Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc

# Mara Pell Thirty-six. She grew up in Lowesport and left it for a state school, not a dramatic one, and came back because the nearshore monitoring job was the job she got. She tells it as a choice. The other half is rent, and the house, and a grant cycle that has been “promising” for two years. The continuation review is on the twelfth. She has been writing the transect as if it were more important than a small station’s counts, which is partly true and partly how you keep a posting. She knows the difference. She keeps knowing it while she does it anyway. Their father, Mark, died of a stroke in the kitchen when she was twenty-two. She was at a poster session. Robbie found him. She has never said “poster session” to Robbie. He says “school” like it was a party, and she lets him, and then she uses the let against him later in her head. Their mother, Adele, works reception at a clinic two hours inland and calls when the harbor is on the news, wanting it smaller. Mara makes it smaller for her and is short with her afterward, which Adele files under personality. She is exact where a mistake can be traced to her and careless where it can’t. Sample labels are neat. The truck registration has been in the glove box under a tape measure since March. She eats instant noodles in the cab because the station kitchen smells like the cooler, and she is a month behind on a podcast she uses to fall asleep. She will not start a transect without the thermos. The one time she did, the engine overheated, she had to be towed, and the story lasted a year. She calls this preparation. She writes dates day-month because a lab manual did, and she has made it everyone else’s problem. When she is about to soften a sentence in a report, she bites the inside of her cheek. One ear is a little dead from an infection she cleaned badly at twenty-nine. She turns the good one toward recordings and does not mention it, because it would be used to discount her, and she would rather be wrong in private than qualified in public. What she wants, this month, in her own accounting: a file someone serious will take. Not to be Robbie’s sister in the room where that happens. Not to have heard the interesting part second. She is frightened for him and irritated that his fear and hers are not the same shape. She thinks she is trying to stop him being stupid. She is also trying to get the clip into her numbers before it lives in a stranger’s video. Both are true, and the second one arrives first, and she notices, and noticing does not reorder it. She loves him as a duty she is bad at and a person she would rather not watch fail in public. She does not experience this as tenderness. Tenderness, if it shows, looks like a dropped-off bag of groceries and a comment about how he stores them. Her allegiance, written down, would shame her: the record, the posting, him. On the water that order slips. She will not admit it slipped, and she is already composing the note in which it doesn’t. She is not striking and not trying to be. Five-six, knot of brown hair that gives up by noon, gray she has decided to treat as weather. Darker on the neck and hands than on the arms. A zip-tie split on the thumb, half healed, which she keeps reopening. Glasses on her head, one arm loose. She walks a little forward, as if the next station were late. On a boat she is easier than on a dock. Her face lags her voice or runs ahead of it: mild sentence, furious mouth. People at the plant call her cold. She thinks she sounds friendly. She doesn’t hug. She hands people things, already turning toward the next task. When she is listening in a loud place she angles the good ear and looks impatient, which loses her information and makes her sharper. “Put the amount in a text. I’m not listening to a voice note in the cooler.” She caught herself hoping the afternoon haul would be worse than the morning, because worse was a cleaner figure. The hope was small and practical and she stepped on it, and it got up again while she was labeling the jar. # Robbie Pell Thirty-three. He didn’t finish the two-year technical course. He deckhanded, then bought the Nadine with what was left of their father’s insurance after the funeral and a bill their mother wouldn’t let Mara pay. The name was on the boat already. He says the paperwork is a hassle. There is a plastic saint on the dash that came with it. He taps it because his hand knows where it is, not because he has taken up anyone’s religion. He is a little ashamed of both facts and will joke about them before you can. He lives in their mother’s old house and has not kept it. The good pan is missing. The porch light is out. He is behind on an engine part by about two hundred dollars and a guess; it might not even be the right part, which he knows and does not lead with. There is a woman, Lena, at the fuel dock, who has told him not to call after ten. He mostly doesn’t. That is the whole of it. He is not lonely in a way the month invented. He was already a man whose week is a list of small shortages. He talks more than Mara, and he moves the interesting part of a story to the front, which makes her trust the rest less, which makes him decorate the rest. He is not stupid. He knows which buyer is bluffing, which inspector is tired, when to come in. She treats that as instinct and her own work as method. He has stopped arguing the distinction and started invoicing it, badly. He is decent at cards and hopeless at forms. His phone wallpaper is a photo of the engine. He sends voice notes because typing makes him sound simpler than he is, and she doesn’t get to the end of them, which he has noticed and answered by making them longer. He drinks a few beers, sometimes more on a Sunday, and gets defensive before anyone has said anything. He wears a knit cap into weather that doesn’t need it, then complains about his ears. He can tie a knot without looking, while talking, and has used this in an argument as if it were a degree. The knot holds. He once sold a cooler to a tourist at a markup, felt flush for an hour, saw them about to ruin it on a public grill, and went back to show them how. He came home with no markup feeling and no story he could tell Mara, because it made him look kind or foolish and he didn’t want either. The kitchen has been in his pocket for eleven years. He hates the version of himself that spends it. He spends it anyway when she manages him in front of other people. About once a year. They are due. He is not trying to speak for the harbor or offer himself to anything. He wants the week to pay, and he wants her to admit he heard something. If it had his name in it, even once, that is the first time in a long while the interesting thing picked him first. He will not say that. He will say he can still sell what isn’t herring if he can find it. Going out is money, and stubbornness, and the radio. Turning the radio off feels like agreeing with her. That is as close as he gets to a motive she would call a motive. He is a bit taller than her, broader, stooped in her doorway without noticing. Burn scar on the left wrist from a muffler, “the stupid one.” One black nail. Weight on one leg, always, as if the floor might move. He looks at mouths when the harbor is loud, which reads as intensity and is actually trying to catch the sentence. He smiles too early when a conversation turns. The flannel with their mother’s mend is for any room where he might be written down. In it he feels like he is lying, so he jokes, so the room relaxes, so nobody writes down what he actually heard. His allegiance is the boat, then a couple of men at the dock who will lend a tool and repeat a rumor, then her, in the way you stay loyal to someone you also need to win against. He will help haul carcasses if Dale asks and there is a fee. He will not attend a meeting about what any of it means. “You can be right and still lend me the two hundred. People do that. Strangers do that.” He had the handset down by his knee so she wouldn’t see him not hanging up. It wasn’t his name. It was almost his name. Close enough that he stood there and let it be close, the way you let a check clear when you already know. # Dale Vickers Fifty-eight. Cold storage and the floor at the plant, which means he is the person who decides what the bay does with a mess. He hired their father for a season decades ago and has known Mara and Robbie since they were in the way. He is not a mentor. He is a man with overtime, a failing compressor, and a cousin on the county side who calls him before the news does. He talks in practical units: bags, hours, who signed. He does not want a theory. He wants the fish off his floor before someone arrives to look concerned and slows the line. He liked Mark, finds Robbie unreliable but not worthless, and respects Mara in the specific way of a person who thinks she got out and then came back to count what she got out of. He would never say the sad part. He will say she is the only one who labels a crate so he can read it with wet gloves. He is heavy in the chest, soft-voiced, hard to interrupt because he doesn’t speed up. Gray stubble, a knee that makes the metal stairs honest, reading glasses he hates and wears on a cord he hates more. He stands with his hands in his coat pockets until there is a box, and then he is faster than either of them. He will not be on camera if he can help it. If a clipboard appears he becomes stupid on purpose. That has saved him before. He is loyal to the shift and the paycheck, not to the story the town is about to tell. If there is a fee for hauling, his guys get it in writing. If Mara’s numbers threaten a closure, he will stop being helpful without raising his voice. He has already done the math on a bad week. He does not owe the harbor a feeling about it. “I don’t need you to call it anything. I need it out before noon and I need a name on the slip. Yours is fine. His, if he’s the one getting paid.”

The next station was written on her wrist, and the radio told her anyway. “Three’s open, Pell. Thing on your left, don’t wander.” “Copy.” She didn’t look. It sat over where the water tower used to show, and keeping it on her left would get her there. The thermos sat between her boots. Coffee in it meant she was allowed to start. She’d skipped it once, overheated, and been towed, and the story had outlasted the repair. The good ear was toward the handset. Her glasses were up on her head. They salted over if she wore them out here, and she could see the tray well enough without. Yesterday’s numbers were still on the board from the first time she’d copied them wrong. She dated the sheet the way the lab had taught her, day then month, then station, then count. At the top she’d written 30. That was her count. The news had started the month on a Friday, when the local said megastructure and meant the thing. The herring had started after. She hadn’t picked which date the file was going to wear. People gave directions by it now. A driver had sat in Dale’s lot yesterday until Dale told him past the fuel dock, not the ladder, unless he was here to look, in which case he wasn’t here. On sixteen, where he shouldn’t have been, somebody asked if the channel had moved. He was told to leave the thing to starboard and quit being clever. He asked if the fish thing was still happening. Nobody answered. Mara put her thumb on the mic and took it off. She had a cooler that already wouldn’t latch, and she didn’t need her voice on somebody’s phone. She’d passed the Nadine on the way out, still moored, tarp over the console. The part was in the mail, he’d said. Last week he’d said it too. There was a voice note she hadn’t played to the end. She wasn’t going to play it now. She’d done one and two already. Thirty, then twelve. After the second she’d stopped writing similar on the line, because twice made it look like she was arguing something. Those crates were in the well. The bilge pump kicked on while she idled, the same rattle she’d been meaning to look at since March, and didn’t. Station three was a red nun and a point she trusted less than the nun. She cut the engine early. The jars knocked. A label from yesterday had lifted at the corner. She pressed it down and the zip-tie split on her thumb opened again, and she got the net over before she dealt with the thumb. The haul was small. That wasn’t the trouble. Four years on these stations. This week should have been herring in a volume she wrote as est., and the rest thrown back if it still had a kick in it. The volume wasn’t there. Nothing in the net had a kick in it. Forty-one. Under a hundred, you counted. She counted them into the tray. The slime was the usual slime. Her back wasn’t. Station two had been a bad angle, and the tray walked toward the gunwale every time she shifted, until she hip-checked it and paid for that with the thumb. Mouths open. Not the usual, working at the air and then done. Finished already, jaws at the same tilt, close enough she checked the light. The light wasn’t doing it. She wrote jaws fixed, similar. No box for it. She put 41 in the box that existed, DOA, which was not what anyone was going to ask. Yesterday west of the nun had been twenty-six. Those were in the cooler at the dock. She hadn’t written similar then. She’d thought about it and gone for fuel. A flounder came up under them, dead, gill mashed where she’d hauled too fast. Its mouth was a mouth. She put it on the board. Relief, small and stupid: one that didn’t match. She got annoyed at the relief in the same minute. No pattern yet. A lean was how you ruined a set. She knew it, and she still wanted the flounder alive or not in the net. The rinse in the bottle had been tea. The deck smelled like the cooler. The cooler smelled like the truck, and the plant had said they were about done taking waste she couldn’t code as anything a buyer might touch. She should have called Dale before she left the ramp. She hadn’t wanted his noon. The phone buzzed in the dry bag. Glove stayed on. Grants office, or her mother with a picture. Last night’s message was still sitting there: was she submitting the continuation as scoped, given events. Review on the twelfth. She hadn’t opened it. She knew the voice she’d use. Even. A little glad. She ate the noodles cold, standing, and they tasted like the glove, and she ate them anyway. Somebody’s music bled onto the working channel for half a minute, a song she hated. She was glad to hate it. Then it cut. Eighteen at station four. She measured a jaw so the margin could stay empty. About twenty degrees off the body. About wouldn’t hold. Second one matched. She stopped before a third could turn into a method. A crab came up alive. She logged it and put it back. It stayed down. At five she thought she’d missed. Nine herring. She held the net up as if the rest were late. They weren’t. She copied the new counts under the morning’s in the order the page wanted, which made them look like weather. 1, herring 30. 2, herring 12. 3, herring 41, flounder 1. 4, herring 18. 5, herring 9. One hundred and ten. Last year this week she’d given up at two hundred and written est. and sworn at the bycatch. She slid the page into the sleeve. The cooler lid didn’t want the crate. She knelt on it until the latch took, and the smell came up into her face, a haul somebody had to take before it cooked worse. The phone buzzed against the jars. She let it. One hundred and ten. One flounder.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably controlled piece of writing. The model has executed its plan with unusual discipline, resisting nearly every temptation that would have made it worse. The chapter opens in medias res with Mara already at work, and the prose immediately establishes her voice through action and habit rather than exposition. "Coffee in it meant she was allowed to start" is a clean, character-revealing sentence that does real work. The thermos backstory is delivered efficiently and without sentimentality. The chapter plan called for the thing on the horizon to already be a landmark people give directions by, and this is handled with exactly the right lightness—Dale's instruction to the driver ("past the fuel dock, not the ladder, unless he was here to look, in which case he wasn't here") is the best line in the chapter, doing triple duty: characterizing Dale, establishing the town's weary relationship with the structure, and being genuinely funny without trying to be. The fish counts are rendered with procedural authenticity. The detail about writing "similar" and then stopping because "twice made it look like she was arguing something" is excellent—it shows Mara's scientific self-awareness and her vanity about the record simultaneously, without the narration pointing at either. The jaw angle detail ("About twenty degrees off the body. About wouldn't hold.") is the kind of specific that earns trust. The flounder is handled well. The relief at finding one that doesn't match, and her immediate annoyance at the relief, is psychologically precise and consistent with the character profile's description of her catching herself hoping for worse numbers. The narration doesn't editorialize; it just records the thought and the self-correction. The chapter plan called for ending on numbers, not an omen, and the chapter delivers: "One hundred and ten. One flounder." This is exactly right. It refuses the portentous closing image while still landing with weight. Where the chapter is slightly weaker: the zip-tie split on the thumb is mentioned twice (consistent with the profile, which notes she keeps reopening it), but the second mention feels slightly mechanical rather than organic. The phone buzzing in the dry bag and the grant email are handled efficiently but the transition between them is a little abrupt. The Robbie material (the Nadine, the voice note) is appropriately brief but feels slightly inserted rather than woven in—though this may be intentional given the chapter plan's focus on the transect. The dialogue is minimal and functional, which is appropriate. What exists ("Three's open, Pell. Thing on your left, don't wander." / "Copy.") is exactly right in register. No dialogue is wasted or false. The prose avoids purple entirely. There are no forced metaphors. The one moment that could have gone wrong—"The deck smelled like the cooler. The cooler smelled like the truck"—is actually a good, grounded chain of association rather than a reach. The writing is consistently flat in the best sense: it trusts the material. The chapter is coherent, follows the plan closely, and is faithful to the prompt's established world. The structure is already integrated into daily life. The fish are dying in a specific, documented way. The mouths are noted as a protocol problem, not an omen. The grant sits unanswered. All of this is exactly as planned. The main limitation is that this chapter, by design, is not emotionally engaging in a conventional sense—it's deliberately withholding, procedural, and flat. This is a defensible artistic choice and consistent with the plan, but it does mean the emotional register is narrow. The chapter earns its flatness rather than defaulting to it, which is the distinction that matters. The county lab email was waiting when she got the cooler onto the cart. No analytes above reporting limit. They’d run the panel she’d paid the rush on, the one with a name she could have put in a box if it had come back dirty. It had not. She read it twice on the ramp, thumb leaking into the phone case, and wheeled the cart inside before the smell turned into a text from Dale. The station was one room and a closet with a freezer that hummed louder than it cooled. She labeled what she hadn’t labeled on the boat and ate the rest of the noodles over the sink. They were worse. She ate them. The grants message sat under the lab email, still unopened. She photographed the sheet instead. The call came while the photos were sending. A man, name too fast, an office he called coordination. He had her transect through last week. He wanted this morning. He wanted a sentence. “For the afternoon note,” he said. “Something that won’t travel.” “The screen was negative.” “That’s not a sentence.” She had the phone on the good ear. The freezer kicked and she missed the next part, and asking him to repeat it made her sound like she was stalling. He wanted no evidence tying the mortality to the object offshore. He said object. She looked at the crate. One hundred and ten, and a flounder with a mashed gill, which she was not going to offer him. “I don’t have a mechanism.” “Then the counts are depressed and the likely stressors are under review. You can live with that until Thursday.” She bit the inside of her cheek. “Counts are down. The screen was clean. I’ll send the sheet.” “By four, if you can.” He hung up as if they’d agreed. She stood with the phone at her ear because the room was loud and she wanted a second of nobody. She had not agreed to Thursday. She had not disagreed. Robbie was in the doorway when she turned. Cap on, weight on one leg, the flannel with the mend. He’d thought there might be someone here besides her. There wasn’t. He took the cap off and put it back on. “You don’t answer notes.” “Put the amount in a text.” “It’s two hundred. That’s the text.” “You said the part was in the mail.” “Pelham had it. He wants it paid before it leaves the counter. I wasn’t going to call you for a maybe.” “You sent a voice note.” “And you didn’t get to the end of it, so.” He smiled too early. “You can be right and still lend me the two hundred. People do that. Strangers do that.” She rinsed the fork. The crate needed the freezer and the freezer needed room. She had the two hundred. The truck was due, the twelfth was the twelfth, and in February she’d paid for a coil he’d called the last one. “Not today.” “You can.” “Not today.” He nodded like he’d come for the nod. He didn’t leave. His eyes went to her mouth, the way they did when a room had a motor in it. “I was on her this morning,” he said. “Waiting on Pelham. Had the VHF up so it wasn’t just me sitting there. Forecast came in late. Like a delay. One word wrong. I don’t know which. Don’t look at me like that.” “I’m not.” “The point, maybe. Visibility. It wasn’t a thing. I’m not putting it anywhere.” She almost said the jaws were the same on three stations. It would have sounded like the pages he was swearing he wasn’t on. She dried her hands and didn’t say it. He took the silence the way he usually did, her keeping the real version for a room he wasn’t in. He wasn’t wrong. He also wasn’t owed the sheet. “All right,” he said. He left with the cap in his hand. The truck with the tick took the turn by the fuel dock. She didn’t go to the window. The file was open. She typed the morning stations under last week so the sheet and the folder matched, and added a line at the bottom: jaws fixed, similar, stations 3–4, not all individuals examined. It looked like someone trying not to say sign. She left it. Higher up, in the notes she sometimes forgot to strip, she had already written, while he was still in the door: VHF forecast delayed, one word off, R. Pell, unconfirmed. She deleted that line. The jaws stayed. She attached the file, wrote See attached, and sent it at ten past four because the man had said if you can and she was tired of the screen. Then she opened Robbie’s note, heard “It’s two hundred, and Pelham—” and closed it, and went to make the freezer take the crate.

What the chapter does particularly well is honor the plan's instruction to let Mara be wrong in the prose, not only in dialogue. The chapter follows its plan with high fidelity: the toxin screen comes back useless, the agency caller wants a file and a calming sentence, Robbie mentions the VHF, she's short with him, she doesn't tell him about the mouths, he leaves without the money, she adds the line and deletes the radio note. "Nobody asked you to pray," Griggs said. It wasn't the joke from the meeting. He heard himself and shut up. He finished the knot. Mara had the phone up late. The recording was the forecast, the drop, Griggs, her own coat against the mic. She played it back under the ramp light with the volume low. The fish wasn't on it. She played it again. Still the coat. Luis leaned in, listened, and straightened like he'd been offered a bad price. "R," he said. "Or nothing. Don't write R if you didn't get R." She had Dale's slip in her pocket. She turned it over. The first version she wrote was two beats and a lift, no letters. The second grew a consonant while the kid was talking. The third she wrote after Robbie said his name again, slower, as if speed had been the objection. It looked like his name if she let the last mark lean. She didn't let it. She crossed the third out and the cross-out left a ghost of it, which was worse. She asked the kid what the prayer had been. He said if he said it, it would be him saying it, not the fish. She asked Griggs. "I heard me," Griggs said. "That's the part I can swear to." She folded the slip. The versions were already leaving. In her head the middle one had picked up the end of fifteen. On the paper it hadn't. She put the pencil away so she'd stop helping it. Out past the nun, the thing was where the morning had left it. She had no range on it and no reason to get one. A work light on the plant roof made the near water orange. The rest was the rest. If it had moved, she couldn't have proved it, and she didn't get the binoculars out of the truck. Griggs lifted a bag and said nothing, which was its own version. Mara got a glove on. The herring at the edge had the mouth it had come in with. She shifted the crate. Nothing came out of it. Strangers do that." are excellent—they reveal character while advancing the plot. The dialogue never feels written; it feels overheard. The central conceit—that first contact is happening through dead fish and radio interference, and that the protagonist's primary concern is whether she can put it in a box on a form—is both original and thematically rich. The story is about epistemology, about the gap between experience and reportable data, about how institutions shape what can be said. This is sophisticated science fiction. Weaknesses: The piece occasionally risks opacity. Some readers will find the procedural density of Chapter 1 alienating before they've been given a reason to trust the voice. The "jaws fixed, similar" motif is effective but slightly overworked. The ending, while tonally perfect, may feel too withholding for some—the story earns its ambiguity but doesn't quite earn the full emotional release that eight chapters of restraint might promise. The line "They're finishing a sentence we already had on the radio" (which Mara crosses out) is the story's most explicit thematic statement, and its self-cancellation is clever but also slightly too neat. There is almost no purple prose, no forced metaphor, no unearned transformation. The darkness is consistently well-earned. The piece is faithful to the prompt in the most interesting possible way—it takes the prompt's three beats (megastructures, fish dying, speaking) and makes them the skeleton of a story about something much more interior. This is genuinely impressive literary work. It has the texture of a real writer who has thought carefully about what kind of story this should be and executed that vision with discipline. + Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Darkly Comic British YA Fiction Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸 -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. Model Output:
# Brainstorming The prompt is almost nothing and almost everything: one message, just after midnight, three blood drops and no words. British YA dark comedy lives in the gap between what that looks like and what it actually is. Eight chapters at roughly a thousand words each is a short novel’s spine, not a sketch, so the idea has to be able to change shape every thousand words without outgrowing a single night, a single group chat, or a single comprehensive school. **Ways the text could land** - A private message from an unknown number. The protagonist, half-asleep, assumes a prank, then notices the number is their own. - A group chat called something embarrassing (GCSE Sufferers, Lads Who Cry At Adele, Year 11 Netball Except Dave). One person sends the drops and immediately goes offline. Everyone else starts detective work with the confidence of people who have watched one true-crime podcast. - A message from Mum. She has recently discovered emojis and uses them with the accuracy of a faulty satnav. Three blood drops might mean “pick up tampons,” “your brother has a nosebleed,” “the Sunday roast is leaking,” or “I love you,” depending on which Facebook graphic she last screenshotted. - A message from a younger sibling who is not allowed a phone after ten and is therefore texting from the family iPad in the airing cupboard. - A message inside a school email system that should not be active at midnight. Subject line blank. Attachment: nothing. Just the drops. - Read receipts only. The protagonist sent the text. They do not remember doing it. Their notes app has a draft that is also just the drops, timestamped 00:00:00. - A chain. First the drops. Then, over subsequent chapters, other people receive the same text from the person who received it last, like a horrible pass-the-parcel. **What the drops might actually mean (wide net, not a shortlist)** - A code agreed in the lunch queue and then forgotten: three drops means “I’m outside, let me in,” or “the sleepover plan is off,” or “bin the evidence.” - Autocorrect carnage. Someone tried to type a place name, a band, or “brb” and the phone, set to some demonic predictive mode, offered blood. - A theatre thing. School is doing *Carrie*, *Macbeth*, or a well-meaning devised piece called *Periods: A Celebration*. The midnight text is a cue, a prop note, or the director (a supply teacher who cries) method-acting. - Medical and mortifying. A period-tracker widget, a nosebleed during a mock exam that became folklore, a haemophilia alert mis-forwarded, a blood-donation appointment reminder redesigned by someone who thinks Gen Z only reads pictograms. - Butcher, chippy, or kebab-shop stock system. The protagonist’s Saturday job. “Blood” is the code for the drip tray under the doner, or for black pudding running out, and the manager texts like a Victorian ghost. - Sport. Rugby, boxing club, or a five-a-side where someone has split an eyebrow and is texting for a lift because their mum will “make it a thing.” - A charity stunt or sixth-form fundraiser gone feral. Fake blood, a GoPro, and a plan that sounded ironic at 4 p.m. - Supernatural, played straight just long enough to be funny. A vampire who has joined the wrong WhatsApp. A cursed emoji that spreads like nits. British folklore with none of the glamour: a redcap who cannot operate a touchscreen and keeps sending the only symbol he understands. A ghost in a new-build estate where the signal is better than the living residents’. - An urban legend already circulating at school. If you get the drops, you have until the next midnight to forward them or you bleed from the eyes. Nobody believes it. Everybody forwards it. Comedy is in the hypocrisy; darkness is in the one person who doesn’t. - A misread crisis. The sender is not in danger of bleeding. They are in danger of being dramatically misunderstood by their friends, and the rescue attempt is the thing that goes wrong. - Something that looks like a threat and is a love language. In this friendship group, concern is expressed only through bits. Three drops means “I am not fine, do not ask me with words.” - A scam. An account cloned after someone clicked a link in a “free Nando’s” email. The scammer’s entire persona is three emojis because they are working from a script that got truncated. - The text is evidence in a much smaller crime: shoplifted fake blood from a joke shop, a snatched phone, a lie told to a parent. The dread is social annihilation, not death. - Time loop or repeated midnight. Each chapter is the same 00:01, slightly worse, and the protagonist is the only one who notices the group chat is filling with duplicates. - The drops are a map. Three locations in town where something red has been left: a scarf on the rec, Ribena on the war memorial, a drama-department blood capsule in the disabled loo. A treasure hunt designed by someone whose sense of humour has outrun their risk assessment. **Possible protagonists (British, school-age, not a chosen one)** - A chronic overthinker who narrates in footnotes they do not have time to write. Good at exams, bad at buses, keeps a notes-app list called PEOPLE WHO HATE ME (CURRENT). Receives the text and treats it as a controlled assessment. - The group’s designated Sensible One, who is not sensible, only loud. Will call 999 and then have to explain to a tired call-handler that the emergency is “vibes.” - A kid who has just moved from one British nowhere to another (coastal town to estate, or the reverse) and does not yet know which legends are jokes. - A teen carer. Midnight is not a mystical hour; it is when they finally look at their phone. The drops might be about the person they look after, or might be the first thing all week that is not. - The school newspaper’s only remaining member, who smells a story and is wrong in a way that is useful. - Someone already in mild disgrace: exclusion looming, a rumour about a party, a teacher who has Said Their Name in briefing. The text arrives when they can least afford another incident. - A dry, ambitious theatre kid who would quite like a haunting if it improved their personal statement. - Two co-protagonists forced to share a chapter each: the sender and the receiver, neither reliable, both convinced they are the reasonable one. **Supporting cast that can carry comedy without needing their own plots** - A parent who is kind, tired, and catastrophically online. Or a parent who is not online and therefore interprets “emoji” as a type of Italian bread. - A younger sibling who understands the situation immediately and will not share this knowledge without a tariff (control of the remote, silence about a broken mug). - A form tutor who wants to be an ally and keeps saying “I see you” until nobody can see anything. - A group-chat lurker who has not spoken since March and whose single message will be either the twist or a picture of a crisp. - A local oddball with a harmless reputation (the man who power-walks in a high-vis at dawn, the goth who works in the library, the vicar who does open-mic). Useful as a red herring; dangerous if the story starts requiring them to be a villain. - A friend who is genuinely frightened and therefore ruins the bit. Dark comedy needs one person who will not play along, or the darkness is just noise. **Tone options** - Deadpan first person. Horror described like a disappointing trip to Greggs. The laugh is in the adjective choice, not in jokes that announce themselves. - Ensemble chat-log chapters alternating with prose. Risk: chat-logs eat word count and date fast. Reward: British teen speech is the joke. - Polite dread. Characters say “sorry” while bleeding, haunting, or accusing. Nobody raises their voice until chapter seven, and when they do it is embarrassing. - Slapstick that keeps almost becoming sad. Fake blood on a school shirt that is also the only clean shirt. A haunting interrupted by a boiler fault. - Satire of online bravery. Everyone is a detective until a real adult asks a question, at which point they become eight years old. - Folk-horror in a cul-de-sac. The old gods have to contend with a ring road and a Tesco Express that closes at ten. - Pitch-black but not cruel. The comedy punches up at institutions (school comms, rumour, parents’ WhatsApp) and sideways at the protagonist’s own self-mythologising. It should not punch the kid who is actually scared. **Story-beat menus (mixable)** 1. Inciting ping. Phone lights the room. Three drops. Protagonist does the sensible thing, which is the wrong thing: screenshots it, sends it to the group chat, and adds “lol.” 2. The group decides it is a game. Rules are invented on the spot. A location is chosen: the park, the closed pier, the science-block fire escape, someone’s dad’s garage. 3. A parent almost finds out. The lie told to cover the outing is worse than the outing. 4. Physical “evidence” appears. Red on a cuff, on a textbook, on the bathroom tap. It might be squash, stage blood, or a nosebleed. Nobody tests it. Testing it would be sensible and therefore unfunny. 5. Someone is missing from registration, or from the chat, or only missing in the sense that their status says “last seen 00:03.” 6. An adult interpretation crashes the teen interpretation. Teacher, PCSO, older sibling, or the family GP who has been sent a screenshot “just in case.” 7. The protagonist discovers they have already received this text once before and deleted it. Memory becomes unreliable. Comedy curdles. 8. A public humiliation set piece: assembly, bus, family barbecue, match, drama assessment. The drops stop being private. 9. False climax. They “solve” it. The solution is tidy, British, and embarrassing (a butcher’s code, a play cue, Mum). Then another text arrives, same time, and the tidy answer does not cover it. 10. Real stakes, small scale. Not a murder. A friend on a bridge, a lie that will get someone excluded, a medical issue someone was too ashamed to name, a prank that has trapped a person who cannot get home. 11. Confession. The protagonist, or the quiet friend, admits they sent the first one. Motive is petty, lonely, or accidental. The spooky story was a better story than the true one, which is why everyone preferred it. 12. Last-page sting. The rational explanation holds, and then one detail does not. Or the rational explanation is the darkest joke: nothing supernatural happened, and they still managed to hurt someone. **Pacing shapes for eight chapters** - **One night, clock-tight.** Chapters are hours: 00:12, 00:40, 1:15, 2:00, 3:00, 4:30, dawn, the morning after. Tight, stagey, good for farce. Hard to deepen character unless backstory arrives through argument, not flashback. - **One week, one midnight each.** Every chapter opens with the same text. Days are school-shaped; nights are the plot. Allows rumour to grow and allows the comedy of “we have chemistry coursework due.” Risks repetition if the midnight scene is copied rather than escalated. - **Two-day spiral.** Friday night text, Saturday chaos, Sunday confrontation, Monday school consequences split across the last chapters. Fits British teen life (nothing fun happens on a Tuesday). Enough room for a parent plot without a travel plot. - **Investigation parody into something tender.** Chapters 1–3 play Scooby-Doo in cagoules. Chapters 4–5 the suspect list collapses. Chapters 6–8 drop the parody and stay funny only through voice, because the situation has become a friend who needed a word and got an emoji. - **Unreliable escalation.** Each chapter’s narrator is a different member of the chat. Word count stays even; the reader assembles the truth from people protecting themselves. Strong for comedy of contradiction. Risk of eight shallow voices instead of one sharp one. - **Geography-led.** A walkable British town. Each chapter a site: bedroom, bus stop, high street, school, A&E waiting room, church hall, underpass, kitchen table. The emoji pulls them through town. Ending at home makes the scale feel right for YA: the world is not saved; the group chat is. - **Farce ladder.** Every attempt to hide the problem creates a larger visible problem. Word-count budget goes to set pieces (a bottle of fake blood in a school bag at a metal detector that is actually just a strict dinner lady; a séance interrupted by a Deliveroo driver; a confession in a PE cupboard). Needs a simple truth underneath or the ladder falls over. - **Slow dread, late laugh.** Early chapters almost straight unease, jokes only in asides. Comedy arrives when the unease is revealed as social, bodily, or bureaucratic. Harder sell for “darkly comic” if the laughs wait until chapter six, but a stronger aftertaste. **Constraints worth noticing while the net is still wide** Eight thousand words can hold one protagonist, one core friendship (or trio), one institution (school or family), and one mystery. A vampire *and* a scam *and* a missing sibling *and* a folk ritual will read as a trailer. The blood emoji has to remain the engine: if chapter four would still make sense without it, the prompt has been abandoned. British specificity should be sensory and social (bus fares, register, the particular shame of a parent using your full name in public, the smell of a sports hall), not a checklist of slang that will expire. Darkness can be social humiliation, shame about bodies, a lie that spreads, the fear that your friends like the crisis more than they like you. It does not need a body count to feel dark. Comedy can be underreaction, overreaction, and the British refusal to say the obvious sentence until it is far too late. **Opening-image variants** - Phone face-down, buzz, protagonist already composing the reply “wrong number” before they have turned it over. - They are on a night bus. The text arrives as the bus is between stops, which is the least useful place in Britain to have an emergency. - They are at a sleepover, everyone else asleep, and reading the text aloud would make it real. - They are in a hospital corridor for a boring reason (sibling’s asthma, grandparent’s tests) and the drops feel like the building has learned to text. - They have just been told off for being on their phone at the table. It is 11:58. They look anyway. **Ending temperatures** - Warm-sour: the group survives, someone is owed an apology, the chat name gets changed to something worse. - Cold laugh: the explanation is banal, and the protagonist realises they enjoyed being frightened. - Ambiguous folk: the banal explanation works, except the sender’s phone was out of battery, and nobody agrees to mention that. - Public sting: assembly. A teacher says “some of you have been circulating unpleasant images.” Three students do not look up. The reader knows which kind of unpleasant. - Private sting: the protagonist types a real sentence instead of an emoji, deletes it, and sends something smaller. Funny, and a little damning. # Reflection The prompt’s strength is its blankness. Three drops carry threat, embarrassment, slapstick, and superstition at the same time, which is exactly the range dark comedy wants. The risk is matching that blankness with a plan so broad that the eventual story tries to be a haunting, a caper, and a social novel in eight thousand words. Whatever direction holds, the text has to stay active. If it is solved in chapter two and the rest is epilogue, the shape collapses. If it is never interpretable at all, the reader is just being dared, and British YA comedy usually works better when the reader is slightly ahead of the characters, wincing. The most reliable engine in the pile is misunderstanding with consequences, not lore. A code, a parental misfire, a job alert, a theatrical cue, a shame-signal between friends: all of these let teenagers behave at full confidence in the wrong direction. That is funnier, and more painful, than a monster that is simply monstering. Supernatural options are tempting because the emoji already looks occult, and a cul-de-sac folk horror could be distinctive. They are also the easiest way to lose the comedy. Once a curse is real, the register slides toward horror-YA, and the jokes become armour rather than the point. A light supernatural residue at the very end might keep the dark, but the chapters that earn it are probably the social ones. Pure scam or pure prank, on the other hand, can feel thin by chapter five unless the prank lands on something the characters actually fear: exclusion, a parent’s disappointment, a body they cannot talk about, a friend who has gone quiet for a reason that is not cinematic. Voice matters more than mythology here. Deadpan first person fits the word count and the humour; a rotating cast of narrators is clever and likely expensive. Chat-log chapters would nail the British teen specificity and then date, and they can flatten dread into formatting. Better, probably, to let the chat intrude in short bursts inside prose so the night still has rooms, weather, and the horrible brightness of a phone in a dark kitchen. Ensemble is useful — dark comedy needs someone to misunderstand the protagonist in a different direction — but eight thousand words wants one interior and two or three mouths, not a whole year group. A Sensible-but-not friend, a parent who is trying, and one person who will not treat the crisis as content: that triangle can carry tone. A form tutor and a local eccentric are garnish. If they become suspects for long, the story turns into a cosy mystery wearing a school tie. Pacing is where several ideas fail the format. A single-night farce is clean and stageable, and it respects “just after midnight,” but eight chapters of one night can become eight stalls in the same joke unless each hour worsens a different relationship, not just the clue list. A full week of identical midnights risks a chorus. The two-day or long-weekend shape looks more forgiving: Friday’s text, Saturday’s public mess, Sunday’s forced honesty, Monday’s institutional aftermath. It gives school and family enough room to be funny without a travel plot or a villain monologue. Geography-led chapters are attractive for British texture — bus stop, high street, sports hall, kitchen — as long as the town does not become a tour. The reader needs to feel that these are the only places these kids are allowed to be after dark. The emotional temperature needs watching. “Darkly comic” dies if the book is cruel to a frightened teenager, and it also dies if everyone is ironic and nobody wants anything. The version that looks most compelling is the one where the spooky reading is the flattering reading. Being possibly cursed is a better story than “I didn’t know how to say I wasn’t all right,” or “we started a rumour and it ate a friendship,” or “Mum was trying to tell me something ordinary and I built a ghost out of it.” That lets the early chapters be genuinely creepy and silly — fake blood, 999-adjacent farce, rumour as a school sport — and lets the later chapters get quieter without a genre change. A false solution around the middle, then a second text or a second fact that the tidy answer cannot cover, would keep the prompt alive into the back half. A reveal that the protagonist sent it, or deleted an earlier one, is strong only if the motive is small and human. A twist for its own sake would make the midnight feel like a machine. Endings that restore order too neatly waste the opening image. Endings that add a real corpse or a real curse at the last minute betray the comic pact and ask for a different book. The aftertaste that fits is sour warmth or a cold laugh: they get home, someone is owed an apology, the explanation is almost entirely banal, and one detail is left slightly wrong. Public sting in assembly could work if it is short; the kitchen-table ending is probably more in scale. Either way, the last movement wants a sentence someone could have sent at 00:01 and didn’t, because an emoji was easier. That keeps faith with the prompt: the story is not about blood. It is about what three drops let you avoid saying, and the mess you make in the avoiding. Scale check against the brief: one town, one weekend or one stretched night-into-Monday, one group chat, one lie or code that mutates, no chosen one, no graphic cruelty, humour from understatement and social terror. That is enough plot for eight chapters if each chapter turns status — who knows, who is blamed, who has to lie to an adult — rather than introducing a new mythology. The ideas that sprawl into folklore encyclopaedias, scam tutorials, or a large suspect board are the ones that will not fit. The ideas that stay close to a phone in a dark room, and to teenagers who would rather be haunted than embarrassed, are the ones that already sound like the book.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention A darkly comic British YA short story in eight chapters, close first person, past tense, told by Rowan Blake, sixteen, Year 11 at Hailford Academy, an inland town small enough to cross on foot and large enough to have a rumour problem. The voice is deadpan and understated: fright described with the same register as a disappointing bus. Jokes are not announced. Chat intrudes in short bursts inside prose, never as a whole chapter of transcript. British detail is sensory and social — register, a dinner lady, Dad using a full name in public, a sports hall, Ribena, a school email footer — not a slang checklist. The plot is misunderstanding with consequences, not lore. Just after midnight on Friday, Priya Shah, Rowan’s best friend, sends three blood-drop emojis and goes offline. Months earlier, after a mortifying wellbeing workshop, the two of them invented a private code: three drops means come to the war-memorial bench, alone, and do not ask in writing. Priya is using it for real. A teacher has seen stage blood in her bag — she is understudying Lady Macbeth and practising where her house will not hear her — and Priya knows the school would rather have a safeguarding story than a boring one. She wants one friend, in person, before Monday. Rowan’s original sin is to screenshot the text into the group chat with a joke. Callum, loudly sensible and not sensible, forwards it onward. A Year 10 legend (forward the drops or it is your turn) does the rest. Jonah Pike, who runs the production’s socials, piggybacks with a tasteless red trail around town and is briefly delighted to take credit. Each chapter turns status — who knows, who is blamed, who has lied to an adult — rather than adding a mythology. The midpoint “solution” (it was marketing) is tidy, embarrassing, and wrong. Priya’s text predates the stunt. A second midnight text keeps the prompt alive; its banal source lands late. The emotional aim is that the haunting is the flattering reading. Being possibly cursed is a better story than “I couldn’t type the sentence,” and Rowan notices, too late, that she enjoyed the fright. Darkness is social: shame, a friendship used as content, an institution warming up its concern. Comedy punches at rumour, school comms, and Rowan’s self-mythologising. It does not punch Priya. No gore, no self-harm on the page, no methods, no mockery of anyone actually in crisis; the stage-blood misunderstanding is about panic and language, and Priya stays angry and intact. No chosen one, no suspect board, no scam, no real curse, no corpse, no rotating narrators, no romance plot. Scale stays one weekend, one chat, one walkable town, Friday midnight to Monday form time. The ending temperature is sour warmth with a cold laugh inside it. They tell the plain version. Someone is owed an apology. The chat is renamed to something worse. The last unexplained buzz is ordinary, and Rowan is almost disappointed, which is the damning joke. One adult rhyme: Dad, kind and terrible with his thumbs, is also capable of hiding behind a symbol. The last movement wants a sentence that could have been sent at 00:07 and was not, because an emoji was easier. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Just After Midnight** Friday, 00:07, Rowan’s bedroom. The text arrives from Priya: three drops, nothing else. Rowan drafts “wrong number,” does not send it, and does the fatal sensible thing instead — screenshot, group chat, “lol.” Cal invents a plan before anyone has stood up. The legend is mentioned and officially not believed. Dad knocks about the light under the door; Rowan lies a small lie that will not stay small. Chapter turn: a private code has become content. Rowan has not yet admitted she knows the code. **Chapter 2 — The Bench** They get out of the house. The memorial bench is empty except for a dumped Ribena bottle and a red smear Cal photographs like evidence. Natalie, silent since March, types “stop” and is ignored. They write rules no one agreed to. On the walk back, Rowan checks “last seen” and realises Priya went offline before the forward, which should comfort her and does not. Chapter turn: the group now has a quest, and Rowan has had the first chance to say “this was for me” and spent it on a clue. **Chapter 3 — Doorstep** Saturday morning. The screenshot has leaked past the chat. Rowan goes to Priya’s and meets Mrs Shah, precise and badly frightened, who will not put Priya on the doorstep. Rowan misreads fear as hostility. A Macbeth call sheet in the porch becomes a convenient theory. At home, Dad almost sees the phone and offers a voice note of parental concern so awkward Rowan flees it. Chapter turn: an adult is already in the story, and Rowan still thinks she can solve it before the adults name it. **Chapter 4 — The Trail** Saturday afternoon, the sports hall and its side door, then the only places Hailford lets them be. Jonah has left a capsule, a stained programme, a scarf — a marketing breadcrumb trail he pretends is fan behaviour. Farce with the caretaker and a dinner lady who is more effective than any curse. Cal nearly calls 999 and practises the sentence. Rowan is good at this, and the chapter lets her enjoy it. Chapter turn: she knows she is having a better weekend than Priya is, and she keeps going. **Chapter 5 — The Tidy Answer** Saturday evening. Jonah confesses, pleased, then less pleased when he understands a parent is scared. The group relaxes into mockery: of course it was the play. False solution locked, embarrassing and British. Rowan checks timestamps anyway. Priya’s text came first; Jonah only saw the drops because Cal forwarded them. The tidy answer cannot cover the silence. A school line — “unpleasant images,” Ms Grennell’s register voice, even second-hand — arrives before the laughs have finished. Chapter turn: the haunting is demoted, and the real trouble, institutional and ordinary, is promoted. **Chapter 6 — The Second Midnight** Sunday, just after midnight. Another three drops. Rowan does not put this one in the chat. She goes alone to the bench and waits. Nobody comes. She remembers the workshop, the joke code, the one drill they ran and then pretended was nothing. She records a voice note that is still a bit, listens back, deletes it. The chapter is quieter, still funny only through voice. Chapter turn: she finally does what the code asked, a night late, and has to sit with the fact that lateness is the whole plot. **Chapter 7 — Plain Sentences** Sunday afternoon. Rowan gets Priya — bedroom, thin walls, Mrs Shah out for an hour. The truth, said angrily and without swell: stage blood, a teacher’s glance, a mother who found residue in the wash and could not be expected to prefer the theatrical explanation, a Monday meeting already blooming. The code meant come alone. The forward turned Priya into the rumour. They row. The row is comic until Rowan admits the haunting was a better story and she took it. They plan Monday in the least cinematic way available: a plastic bag, the call sheet, and an apology that keeps trying to become a joke. Chapter turn: both of them know the sentence now; neither trusts the institution to hear it. **Chapter 8 — Form Time** Monday. Ms Grennell’s office, not a haunting. The banal evidence works badly and then well enough; concern deflates into embarrassment, which is its own punishment. Cal is useless in a way that helps. Natalie says one precise thing and leaves. In the corridor Dad reveals, mortified, that the second text was his: he saw the emoji, tried to type “are you safe,” and his thumbs sent the drops back. Rhyme, not twist-for-its-own-sake. Rowan sends Priya an actual sentence. Someone renames the chat to something worse. A last buzz — attendance, ordinary — and Rowan feels the small, ugly drop of disappointment before she turns the phone over. End on sour warmth: no curse, an apology still owing, and proof she would rather have been frightened than late.

Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece.
