Model Output:
He stopped where the track widened. She had asked twice. The third time she explained what a day of piss on the boards would do to Keel's price, in detail a man could have done without. Col hobbled the mare and went around to the rail. "Feet first." The ankle knots were his, and they gave. She rolled one foot, then the other, and made a small noise that was half relief. He didn't answer it. Her tail had got into the rail hitch while she sat, the end of it caught under the rope, and when he pulled, it pulled her. "Off it." "I can't see the thing." He lifted the tail clear. Heavier than it looked. Hot. It twitched itself straight back into the knot. She tried to help with her wrist and knocked his bad nail. He swore. She swore at her rib, quieter, not at him. Between them they got the tail out and the hitch off. His elbow hit the rail. It took too long. He tied her wrists in front, short, and took her by the upper arm to get her down. She came off the boards stiff and into him. Hair in his mouth. Warm the whole length of his chest. He got hard so fast he hated her for it, and the cart, and the hour. He stepped back. Not far. Her feet were free and the scrub was right there. "Ten paces. That's it." "Romantic." He turned his face to the mare. Cloth. A button giving her trouble she wouldn't ask about. He looked at the mare's hock and did the purse in his head. Four hundred. Seventy of it Ibbe's. Less if he paid the toll like a fool. The count did nothing. His coat was up on the seat. He was still hard, and there was nowhere to put it. She came back loud through the scrub on purpose. "Still here. Nobody stole me. You can check." He checked. That was the job. She looked at the front of his trousers, one beat, then at his face. "Congratulations," she said. She looked ready to add to it. His face had already gone mean, so she didn't. He got her up without caring about the step. The wrist rope went to the rail and he cinched it, then cinched it again, the hitch biting. She didn't give him a sound. She watched his hands. He tied her ankles. He took the hobble off the mare. He drove. Half a mile on she said, "You can put the coat on. I saw it. The coat won't help you now." "Shut up." "I am being practical." He didn't answer. The mare did the road. He stayed angry anyway. By the time the light thinned, her left hand was wrong. He saw it when he passed the skin and she missed the spout twice. The fingers didn't close. Nail beds dark. She wasn't building an argument out of it. She just couldn't. He pulled off, hobbled the mare, and picked the hitch open with his thumbnail. The rope had sat deep enough to groove the wrist. Blood came back slow and patchy. She flexed. The fingers stuttered, then worked. "That's spoiled," he said. "I don't get the purse if you're spoiled." "You'd have noticed at the gate." She worked the hand, getting the color into it. He started the knot again, rail-high, the way he liked it. "Hands in front," she said. Hoarse, not smooth. "You put them in front and I'll tell you which inns on this road cut a man's throat for the finder's fee, and which ones only take the boots and leave him breathing. There's a difference. You want it. Two nights is a lot of doors." "No." "I'm not dressing it up." "No." He set the knot looser than he'd sworn by in ten years. Two fingers of room. Her wrist sat in the rope, and the rope didn't sit in her wrist. Swelling, he told himself, and went to make a fire out of what the ditch had, small as it would stand. Hard end of the loaf. Cheese that had turned. He set her piece on the board by her knee. She got it to her mouth by ducking, which looked stupid, and talked around it. A dog that had belonged to three yards and answered none of them. A woman at the south gate who shorted the pie filling and dared you to mention it. Whether ditch water was water. How the white wood wouldn't burn, the green pale stuff, it sulked and smoked and made a fool of you. "Birch," Col said. He meant the pale stick already in the fire, dry, burning, her being wrong. It got out as a correction and hung there. She turned her head. "Birch," she said, too pleased. "There he is." He put the rind in his mouth and looked at the mare. She was on the verge, hobbled, eating. The quiet that came after wasn't one of Rue's. Her mouth stayed a little open, the next piece ready, and she didn't spend it. She looked at the slack in the rope, then at the fire. He saw quiet. He took it for the win. The cheese was bad. The day could be over. The mare stamped at nothing. "What's she called?" "She isn't." "Look at the face on her." Rue pointed with her chin. "Minister. Thinks she's in charge. She isn't. She'll put us in a ditch, and she ought to have a title while she does it." Col got up and checked the hobble. It was sound. The name came with him to the mare's shoulder and pushed at his teeth, the first of it, the M. He put his hand on her neck. "Easy," he said.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 2)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter executes its plan with considerable discipline. The writing plan called for a piss stop, a moment of physical comedy with the tail, Col getting hard and hating it, a too-tight knot that damages her hand, a loosened rope as a compromise, fire, food, and the naming of the mare. The chapter delivers all of this in sequence, without editorializing. The prose register is exactly what was promised: cheap paperback, concrete, short when Col is winning. "He got hard so fast he hated her for it, and the cart, and the hour." That's the voice working correctly — the comma-list distributing blame absurdly, the self-awareness without self-pity. The chapter earns its humor without smirking. "Congratulations," she said, and then the note that his face had already gone mean so she didn't add to it — that's a small, precise piece of character work. We see both of them calibrating. The tail business is genuinely good. It's awkward, physical, nobody's graceful, and it does double duty: it establishes the practical difficulty of managing a tiefling in a cart, and it puts his hands on her in a way that is neither erotic nor clinical but something more uncomfortable and real. "Heavier than it looked. Hot. It twitched itself straight back into the knot." Three sentences, no metaphor, and the thing is alive. The hand-going-bloodless section is handled well. He notices it because it's cargo, not because he cares, and the chapter is careful to let him say so: "That's spoiled. I don't get the purse if you're spoiled." Her response — "You'd have noticed at the gate" — is dry and accurate and tells us she's been in worse situations and has done the math. The loosened knot is then correctly attributed to swelling, which is exactly the kind of lie the plan called for. The fire scene is where the chapter's rhythm opens up. Her monologue — the dog, the pie woman, the ditch water, the wood — is the right kind of talk: circular, not chess, filling silence because silence is where other people decide what you are. The "Birch" correction is the chapter's best moment. It's small, it gets out before he can stop it, and her response ("There he is") is perfectly calibrated — pleased but not victorious, interested rather than triumphant. The plan specified she should be "interested, not victorious" when she clocks his reactions, and the chapter delivers that distinction. The ending with the mare's name is handled with restraint. He doesn't use it. The M pushes at his teeth and he says "Easy" instead. That's the right call — it would be too easy to have him slip and say Minister, and the plan was that he "almost uses it." The chapter honors that almost. Weaknesses are minor. "Blood came back slow and patchy" is slightly clinical in a way that works, but "Nail beds dark" is a small reach toward medical precision that sits a little oddly in the register. The cheese-as-bad-day-ending line ("The cheese was bad. The day could be over") is a touch too neat, a little too aware of itself as a closing beat, though it's not egregious. The dialogue is mostly excellent but "I am being practical" from Rue is slightly flatter than her usual voice — it sounds like a line rather than her. The characters are entirely consistent with their profiles. Col's vanity about being hard to work, his self-deception about the loosened knot, his counting the purse when aroused — all present. Rue's talk-as-defense, her not building an argument out of the numb hand, her naming the mare without asking — all correct. The chapter does not moralize, does not ennoble Col for the shove (which hasn't happened yet), and does not give Rue a master tactic. It is a chapter about a piss stop and a fire and a name almost spoken, and it is exactly that. Day two came up grey. He had her on the track before the ditch-fire was properly dead. The wrist looked better. He got two fingers under the rope, found the give he'd left, and said nothing about it. She didn't thank him. She started on the pie woman again, short measure, dare you to mention it, and he told her he'd heard it, and for a while the only sound was the wheel. The milestone stood where the scrub broke. Cut stone, waist-high, the number thumbed down to a stain. He knew it. Two days to Irongate if the mare worked and the toll didn't eat the morning. He said it out loud. Numbers sat better outside his head. "Two if she works," Rue said. "She isn't going to." "She will." "She's hitching." "She's walking." He tried her for a trot anyway. The mare put her ears flat and stayed where she was, one hoof after the other, as if the stone had insulted her. He let the rein out. He took it back. She blew and kept the walk. Seventy crowns of her belonged to Ibbe if the job paid. All of her belonged to Ibbe if it didn't. He didn't say that to the cargo. Rue waited until the stone was a thumb-print behind them. "Straight offer," she said. "No letter in it. No bed that wasn't the right bed. You stop where the track widens. Once. That's the trade. After, you leave the rail rope off till afternoon, and if I take the scrub you count to fifty before you come after me like a man who tried." It came out in pieces that fit. He heard the joins. She couldn't do much else with it. Wrists to the rail, ankles on the board, so the offer had to live in her mouth. She lifted her chin at the wide bit of track ahead, as if she were pointing at a table she meant to clear. "No." "You haven't got the terms." "I've got them." A beat. Then a shake in the last word, small, set on it like a stamp she'd forgot until the page was out. "Please." His laugh got out. Short. A bark with no humor in it. He hadn't meant to spend the thing. It sat in the cart. "Late," he said. "The shake goes on the number. You gave me the toll first and the please after, like I'd feel tall for hearing it. I've had this one. They don't lick a tooth and then remember to beg." He hadn't known he was going to say the tooth. She'd had her tongue on the chip while she built the offer. He was angry at his own lap, and at the clean of it, and the tooth had been sitting there. She went still. The tail, which he wasn't watching, knocked once against the board and went flat. "That was the version with the tremble," she said. Steady now, which was worse than the please. "You're meant to feel tall. It's cheap. You still didn't have to laugh like a clerk." "I didn't take it." "You priced it." Her voice thinned, meaner, and the mean suited her. "And that wasn't a laugh. That was a hinge. I heard the same one off a man who wanted the room to know he wasn't buying. He laughed, and then he bought, and then he told the room he hadn't." "I'm not him." "Then don't sound like his door." He had nothing to put after that that wouldn't make it bigger. The mare hitched left. He asked again, softer, the voice he used on her and on nobody else, and she flicked an ear and did not hurry. The track ran on. He kept them on it. Rue talked at the ditch, fast, filling. "There's washing done past the clay pits. A woman. Pettle. She takes a floor if you — no. You've got two days and a horse that won't, drive the horse." He didn't ask. He put the name where he put the toll and the seventy, and he looked at the mare's ears, and Irongate stayed in front of them whether the mare cared or not.

The toll sat where the track pinched. Two posts, a rope, a shack with its door off one hinge. Col had paid it before. He hated it on principle and paid it anyway. Three of them today. One in the shack doorway, picking at a plate. One on a stool with a cudgel across his knees. The third came out when the mare stopped, and his eyes went to the rail before they went to Col. "Paper," he said. Col got it out. The man read the name, the cargo line, the figure, and smiled with his mouth shut. "Horns in the back." "Listed." The man on the stool stood up to look. Rue had her chin on her knee-rope, watching his hands, not his face. He whistled, short. "We can take her off you. Cut of the fee. You ride on light." A glance at the shack man, who didn't disagree. "Or an hour. Same cut. You wait by the post. She comes back walking." Col folded the paper. His thumb wanted the count. He kept it still. Splitting four hundred with men who owned a rope across a road was how you ended the year walking. He said so, shorter. "I don't share a fee." "Didn't ask you to share. Asked you to be sensible." The stool man had come around the wheel. He caught Rue's ankle-rope and yanked, testing the knot, his thumb on the bone. She made no sound. Her heel scraped the board. Col stepped down. He put a hand in the man's chest and shoved, once, enough to break the grip. The cudgel came up. Col's knife was already out, low, not pointed at anything clever. He looked at the rope across the track. "Cut that and I pay you. Keep your hands off the rail." The shack man set his plate down. Nobody was interested enough to bleed. The rope dropped. Col paid the posted toll, counted it out where they could see, and took the paper back. His name had been in the man's mouth. Col Betts. He heard it land in the cart and didn't turn. He got the mare moving before the stool man finished whatever he was going to call him. A mile of scrub. His hands were steady on the reins, which he noted, and the note annoyed him. Behind him she breathed through her mouth. Not crying. Sorting. Then she filled it. "Your paper's greasy. He held it like a fish. Keel doesn't keep people long enough for the paper to matter, if that's a comfort. They come in, they come out lighter, they don't come back through this pinch. I heard that off a boy, so it might be tall. Boys like a story." "I delivered to Keel in the spring. A woman. She walked in." He watched the mare's ears. "I slept after." It had sounded like nothing when he kept it in his head. Out loud it had a shape. He didn't add to it. Adding would be explaining. Rue was quiet long enough for the wheel to find a rut and climb out. "Salt," she said. "What." "The shove. Thanks for it. Pass it." He hadn't offered her anything. She knew that. The word sat there, small, taking the shine off a thing he hadn't claimed. His face went hot anyway, under the ear, where she couldn't see it if he didn't turn. He didn't turn. "Don't." The track ran on toward Irongate. He left it pointed there. The knife went back in his belt. He checked it twice.

The confrontation is over in a few lines, as planned. Col's motivation is stated plainly and correctly — "Splitting four hundred with men who owned a rope across a road was how you ended the year walking" — which is the character's actual logic, not a moral stance dressed up as economics. The "I delivered to Keel in the spring. A woman. She walked in. I slept after." passage is the chapter's best moment. The plan noted it "sounds worse out loud than it did in his head," and the writing captures that precisely without labeling it. The line "Out loud it had a shape" does the work without over-explaining. This is the chapter's strongest show-don't-tell execution. The "salt" exchange is handled well. Rue's deflation of the thanks — "Pass it" — is in character, and Col's "Don't" is exactly the right response: refusing the gratitude, refusing the moment, refusing to be made decent. His face going hot "under the ear, where she couldn't see it if he didn't turn" is a small, good physical detail. The thumb wanting the count and being kept still is a nice character-consistent detail from the profile. The mare walked. One ear was back, and not at the road. Col watched the ear. The bank was a pale smear at the edge of the track, scrub torn out, last night's water gone down and the dirt left soft. He looked. The bank went under the off wheel like a rug pulled. Not a fall. A slip. The mare sat into the traces. The wheel dropped to the hub. His knee hit the stones. The mare was going to kick the traces apart or take all of it with her. He got to the rail with the knife already out, because his hand was ahead of him, and he sawed the hitch. Wet rope. It fought. She was saying the edge and his driving and something about his mother, one sentence, fast. The last strand went. Her boots were jammed under the canted board. He cut the ankle rope rather than sort it. He got a fist in her coat and hauled. They landed on the uphill stones in a heap. The cart groaned and stayed. Wheel in the hole. Water past the hub, brown, close enough. His hands were on her. Wrists bare. A fresh burn where the hitch had bitten. She had a horn in the dirt and her hair in his mouth. "I almost died listening to you," he said. "I told you not to drive it distracted." Her mouth was right there, open, mid-complaint. He kissed it. Teeth. A bad angle. His hand got under her coat, onto the warm side of her waist, the rib she guarded, and she flinched and didn't tell him off. She caught his belt with a freed hand. The light was up and in the cart. Late, then, before he had his eyes right. His mouth tasted of the split lip and sleep. Coat under him, not on. He sat up and the board stuck to his arm. The knife was in the boot. He touched it and took his hand off. Rue was already sitting. Coat buttoned wrong, one side higher. Hair stuck to her cheek. She looked at the canvas. "Your shirt's done up like a drunk," she said. "Leave it." He did the buttons. One was missing. It had been missing since the ledge. He got down to piss and to see the ground, in that order, and the ground was the worse of the two. The mare watched him with no interest. He came back and the prints were still there, which he had half hoped he'd made up. One set. Heel-nail clear in the soft, worn on the outside. Out of the scrub, up to the wheel, a shuffle where a person had stood and shifted, and back. He walked them to the track. They died on the stones. Gate or ditch, he couldn't say. Close enough, at the wheel, to have put a hand on the canvas while he slept. The tin-string was in the dirt. He'd left the coil on the board. Someone had pulled it down and stopped halfway. It lay unspooled in a dragged arc, tins muddied, not a trap, a mess. He gathered it. A tin bit the pad of his thumb. He swore at the thumb, at the string, at the bag for being open. "Stupid thing anyway," Rue said, when he threw it in. "Tins. A careful man steps over tins." "A careful man sets them." "You didn't." He didn't answer her. He shoved his sleeve up. The scrape from the stones had gone brown and dull. Nothing you'd show a factor. He pulled the sleeve down. "Water," she said. He shook the skin. He didn't like the sound. She drank and left him less than he wanted, and wiped her mouth with her wrist, careful of the sore place. He took it back. He put the coat on. The burned patch sat on the wrong side of his chest. He didn't fix it. "Sit straight," he said. "This goes back on the rail." "It slipped." "It goes on." Two turns, the bite, tail out of the rope. The hitch he could do asleep. His fingers missed the bite. The loop sat fat. He pulled to test and the whole thing eased. She lifted her hands an inch. The lock opened. She pointed at the lump of it with her chin. "I see it." He tied it again, harder, which made it worse. The free end stuck out over her wrist. He left it there. The gag hung on its peg by his knee, stiff from drying. He let it stay. The stones under the wheel had to come out. He kicked them clear. His shoulder had yesterday in it and didn't like the work. The mare was sound. He told her so. She flicked an ear and leaned toward the gate track, the way her head had sat all night. He put her in the traces. She stood sour about it. He climbed up. "Four hundred," he said. "Less seventy. Seventy's Ibbe. She holds the paper on the mare. There's a yard. She feeds me when I come through. Doesn't trust me with a purse. I miss this, the mare's hers. I'm walking. That's the size. Seventy." His thumb had done the four and the seven while he said it. He stayed on the buckle. Rue got a stone out of her boot. The bad hitch allowed it. She flicked the stone over the side. "All right," she said. He waited for salt. She didn't give him any. He picked the reins up anyway. Half a day if he pushed. No stone needed. The mill, the rise, smoke by afternoon if the mare worked. Late could still pay, if he called it a wheel. Keel had paid late and looked at him like a spill on a counter, and paid. If the prints had kept on, the toll man's reading was already ahead of them. Horns. Red hair. His name. The sleeping. He sat. A last drop came off the canvas and hit his knee. He didn't move for it. The mare stamped and looked back. She wanted the pale track. Off to the left the drover scar cut the grass. Old ruts. No posts. The knot knocked. "You dying up there?" "No." He didn't lift the reins. His legs went to pins. Four hundred less seventy sat in his thumb and came out a purse, if he walked her in. "Job's blown," he said. "Gate's how you walk into a knife." He turned her onto the scar. She wouldn't have it on the first ask. He asked again. She went, ears half back, sour in the grass. The split nail caught the rein. He got his teeth on it and took them off. He didn't look at the smoke. Rue settled against the canvas. Her rib caught. She hissed once and shifted an inch, done with it. "What food's left?" "Heel of the loaf, under the board. The cheese. Water, if you don't finish it." "The cheese can walk off on its own." She watched the grass go flat under the wheel. "How far's the north road, past the clay pits?" "Don't start." "White stones. Then a ford, if the rain left it where it was. After that the pits. They'll take a wheel faster than the cut. North road's the far side. I know that bit. Washing out there. [Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of prose that executes its plan with unusual discipline and craft. Let me work through the chapter systematically. The chapter opens with Col waking late — the consequence of sleeping on the job, which the plan specified. The physical details are precise and unglamorous: "Coat under him, not on. He sat up and the board stuck to his arm." This is exactly the register the plan called for: concrete, cheap, no lyric weather. The missing button from the ledge incident is a small, perfect callback that does character work without announcing itself. The footprint sequence is handled with professional economy. The plan called for Col to discover he slept through a near-death, and the chapter delivers this without melodrama. "Close enough, at the wheel, to have put a hand on the canvas while he slept" — the horror is in the understatement. The tin-string detail is excellent: it was supposed to be a warning system, it failed because he didn't set it, and now it's just a mess that bites his thumb. The thumb biting the tin is a small, dumb, real consequence that earns its place. The knot scene is the chapter's best technical achievement. Col ties the hitch badly, she demonstrates it's loose by lifting her hands, he ties it worse, and then leaves the bad knot. This is showing character through action with complete economy. His competence is compromised by what happened the night before, and neither character names this. The plan specified "The knot is bad. She points at it." The execution is better than the plan — she doesn't point, she lifts her hands and lets the lock open, which is more damning. The money speech — "Four hundred. Less seventy. Seventy's Ibbe..." — is exactly what the plan called for: him doing the purse out loud when nervous, sounding small. The detail about Ibbe feeding him and not trusting him with a purse is characterization delivered in the voice of a man justifying himself to himself. Rue's response, "All right," without salt, is perfectly calibrated. The plan said "She doesn't mock the seventy" and the execution honors that — it's a moment of unexpected restraint from her that lands harder than mockery would. The decision to turn off the gate road is handled with the ambiguity the plan demanded. "Job's blown. Gate's how you walk into a knife." The plan noted this is "half true" and the chapter doesn't correct it. He doesn't explain himself further. The mare's reluctance to leave the gate track is a nice touch — even the animal knows this is wrong. The ending is exactly right. Her question about the north road, his "Don't start," her giving him the information anyway while withholding the rest, and his final "How far" — it's the prompt's promise fulfilled. He's listening. He's not going to Irongate. The last line is practical, unwilling, and listening, precisely as specified. Dialogue throughout is excellent. It sounds like these specific people, not like dialogue-in-general. "The cheese can walk off on its own" is the right kind of dumb humor. "You dying up there?" / "No." is perfect in its compression. The only minor weakness is that the chapter is perhaps slightly less emotionally complex than the best chapters might be — the emotional beats are clear but the interiority is kept very tight, which is a stylistic choice that mostly works but occasionally leaves the reader doing more work than necessary to feel the weight of what's happening. This is a feature of the style, not a bug, but it does mean the emotional engagement is intellectual rather than visceral. The chapter follows its plan with impressive fidelity while improving on several specific beats. Characters are entirely consistent with their profiles. No purple prose, no forced metaphor, no amateurish moves. The humor is dumb in the right way. The darkness is earned. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of fantasy erotica that demonstrates genuine craft across nearly all dimensions. Let me examine it carefully. VOICE AND STYLE: The prose operates in a compressed, elliptical register that recalls Cormac McCarthy or early Denis Johnson — short declarative sentences, minimal attribution, meaning carried in what's omitted rather than stated. "He passed the waterskin back without turning. Her fingers hit his, hotter than the afternoon, and he let go too fast." This is economical and effective. The style is consistent throughout all eight chapters, which is a significant achievement for a long piece. CHARACTER: Col and Rue are genuinely nuanced. Col is established through action and restraint — his thumb doing sums, his face going mean, his inability to stop looking at her mouth. Rue is established through her voice, which is the engine of the entire story. She's manipulative but not purely so; her manipulation has texture and self-awareness. The moment she says "That was the version with the tremble" after Col calls her out is excellent — she doesn't collapse, she recalibrates. Both characters have interior lives that are shown rather than told. DIALOGUE: The dialogue is the story's greatest strength. It's distinctive, rhythmically varied, and character-specific. Rue's speech patterns — the way she builds arguments in pieces, the way she pivots — feel genuinely individual. "Congratulations" after seeing his arousal. "Salt. The shove. Thanks for it. Pass it." These are not generic fantasy dialogue lines. Col's terseness is equally well-rendered. PACING: The pacing is excellent. The story builds tension across chapters through accumulation rather than event. The ledge scene in Chapter 6 earns its physical escalation because the emotional groundwork has been laid across five chapters. The sex scene in Chapter 7 is handled with the same compressed, unsentimental style as the rest — "She talked the whole way, because she was her" — which is exactly right. WORLD BUILDING: Light but effective. Irongate, Keel, Ibbe, the toll men — these feel like a real world glimpsed through a narrow window. The fantasy element (tiefling, horns, tail) is integrated naturally rather than foregrounded. The tail detail is used cleverly — it's a tell for her emotional state, and the moment she sits on it to hide that tell is a small masterpiece of characterization. METAPHOR AND POETRY: The metaphors generally land. "A saw in green wood." "Her voice sat low for someone strung to a rail, and it filled the cart." "The name came with him to the mare's shoulder and pushed at his teeth, the first of it, the M." These are earned. Occasionally the style tips toward opacity — "The coat lay wrong across his lap besides" is doing a lot of work that might confuse — but this is rare. PLOT: The plot is simple but the story doesn't need complexity. The final chapter's turn — Col abandoning the job — is the emotional climax, and it's handled with admirable restraint. He doesn't announce it. He just turns the mare. The last exchange ("How far," he said) is a perfect ending. WEAKNESSES: The piece is not without flaws. The Jas reference in Chapter 5 is introduced and immediately buried — it gestures at backstory that never develops. The prints in Chapter 8 (the mysterious visitor) are introduced and then essentially dropped, serving only to establish that Col slept through a potential threat. This feels like a loose thread. The toll scene in Chapter 4 is the most conventional scene — the threat, the shove, the knife — and while competently executed, it's the least surprising moment in the story. The "I delivered to Keel in the spring. A woman. She walked in. I slept after." moment is powerful but perhaps slightly too neat in its moral confession. UNEARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: Col's decision to abandon the job in Chapter 8 is the story's central transformation. It is largely earned — the accumulation of small moments (the loose knot, the name, the laugh, the kiss, the sex, "I like your voice") builds toward it. However, the final turn happens somewhat abruptly. The story trusts the reader to have tracked the accumulation, which is a mark of confidence, but a reader could argue the final decision needed one more beat. EROTICA ELEMENTS: The sex scene is well-integrated and consistent with the characters. It's explicit without being gratuitous, and the dialogue during it ("Not — hang on. Teeth, if you keep at it like you're checking a knot") is perfectly in character. The aftermath — him staying, her staying, neither reaching for the obvious escape — is emotionally resonant. OVERALL: This is a high-quality piece of creative writing that successfully executes a difficult tonal challenge: maintaining a hard-boiled, unsentimental voice while building genuine emotional investment. The prompt is faithfully followed and expanded upon with intelligence. + Cozy-Horror Post Apocalyptic Survival — Mushroom Season (Chapter Avg: 84.4 | Final: 79.3)
Initial Writing Prompt:
Cozy-Horror Post Apocalypse Survival Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: When you're out of food, you get desperate. Who would have thought the spore mutants -- the things trying to kill us -- would be delicious?
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Cozy-Horror Post Apocalypse Survival Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: When you&#x27;re out of food, you get desperate. Who would have thought the spore mutants -- the things trying to kill us -- would be delicious? -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming The prompt hinges on hunger flipping a predator into a pantry. Cozy-horror wants the warmth of a kitchen pressed against something that should not be food. Eight chapters at about a thousand words each is roughly a novella-slice: enough for a small cast, one escalating revelation, and a last choice, not a full war against the spore. Below are directions that could all serve that shape. None of them is chosen yet. **Who is hungry.** A former line cook who still thinks in mise en place, measuring survival the only way they know. A foraging kid who tastes first because kids put things in their mouths and then will not stop talking about how good it was. A medic who has been rationing the last antibiotics and now has to decide whether “delicious” is a symptom. An old greenhouse keeper who recognizes the fruiting bodies and hates that recognition. A pair: one person who butchers, one who will not watch, and the lie they tell the rest of the shelter. A small holdout of six, already down to one can and a jar of salt, so the moral argument has a clock. A lone traveler who has been talking to an empty bowl for weeks and treats the first meal like a guest. **What the mutants are, lightly.** Walking fruiting. Things that used to be deer, or neighbors, or neither, crusted in gills and soft plates that steam when cut. They hunt by spore-cloud and by sound. They are not people anymore, or they are only almost not. Their meat might marble like pork, smell like browned butter and wet forest, pull apart like mushroom and chicken at once. The deliciousness could be ordinary biology (they ate well; fat is fat) or a lure: the taste is how the colony recruits stomachs. Cap, stem, marrow, spore-sac: different cuts, different risks. Some parts numb the tongue. Some parts make you dream of soil. **How the first bite happens.** Accident: a mutant dies in a pan fire and the smell undoes everyone’s discipline. Experiment: the cook skins a small one the way you test an unknown mushroom, one bite, wait, another bite. Trade: a stranger arrives already smelling of rendered fat and will not say what the grease is. Desperation with a witness: the child eats while the adult is out, and the adult comes home to an empty carcass and a proud, sauced face. Ritual: someone insists it has to be cooked a certain way or the spores wake. Comedy of manners in hell: they argue about seasoning while something scratches the boarded window. **Story engines that could carry eight chapters.** A recipe journal, each chapter a dish and the cost of getting the ingredient. A supply plot: salt, fat, acid, heat, and the hunt that stocks them. An infection plot: pleasure first, then cravings, then symptoms that look like comfort (warmth, good sleep, hunger that feels like love). A social plot: once two people know, the shelter splits into those who have tasted and those who will not, and dinner becomes politics. A maternal/paternal plot: feeding a child something that might save them today and claim them next month. A culinary mystery: why is it good, and why does it taste like the cook’s mother’s Sunday roast specifically, not generically. A trap plot: the mutants stop attacking the people who have eaten, which feels like mercy until it feels like herding. A coziness-under-siege plot: the best chapter is the quiet one where bread rises and broth simmers and nobody says what the broth is. **Tone mixes.** Gallows warmth: jokes about wine pairings, then a hand that is not a hand on the cutting board. Tender grotesque: careful washing, careful knives, reverence for not wasting, dread in the sink. Quiet dread more than chase scenes; the horror is appetite, not a set piece every chapter. Dark comedy if the cook cannot stop improving the dish. Grief if the meat remembers a face for one paragraph and then is only meat again. Cozy as resistance: clean plates, shared portions, a rule that everyone sits down, because sitting down is how they stay human. Or cozy as the danger: the meal is so good it makes the ruined world feel optional. **Beat shapes across eight short chapters.** Cold open on an empty pot. A failed hunt. The accident or the choice. The first real plate, written with sensory care and almost no moral language. Morning after: no one is dead, which is worse, because now it is a plan. A trip for “ingredients” that goes too well. A guest, a child, or a skeptic forced to the table. A sign that the food is eating back (dreams, cravings, a tooth loosening into something soft, a mutant that does not attack). A kitchen argument that is really about what they are willing to become. A last meal: either they stop and face the hunger again, or they plate it beautifully and accept the change, or the colony comes to dinner as if invited. Epilogue-scale ending inside chapter eight, not a new war: a plate, a door, a spoon set down or not. **Set dressing that could do theme-work.** One functioning stove. A chipped blue bowl. Salt worth more than bullets. A window that fogs when the oven is on, so for an hour the outside disappears. Names for cuts that start clinical and become menu language. A rule on the wall about what is not food, slowly edited. Rain, because cozy needs weather you are glad to be out of. Spores like flour on the counter, so the cook keeps wiping and cannot tell which white dust is which. **Complications worth keeping in the net.** Eating them might be survival and damnation at once, with no science-lecture answer. They might be delicious only when fresh-killed and harmless, and the horror is what the survivors do to keep the supply. They might be delicious because they are finishing a sentence the eater’s body already started. Someone might refuse and starve in view of a full pot, and the story should not sneer at that refusal. Someone might pretend not to know what they are chewing. The best chapter might have almost no mutants in it, only the smell. **Ways to miss the prompt, so they stay visible.** All chase, no kitchen. All body-horror, no desperate tenderness. A lecture on mycology. A twist that they were eating people and the mutants were a dodge; that betrays the given sentence. A victory feast that forgets anyone was afraid. Eight chapters of the same “we shouldn’t / we did” beat. # Reflection What the prompt actually promises is small and sharp: scarcity, a category error (enemy becomes ingredient), and the shock of pleasure. Cozy-horror fits that better than pure splatter or pure adventure, because the pleasure has to be convincing. If the meal is not, on the page, genuinely good, the joke and the dread both fail. Sensory writing is not decoration here; it is the plot. The reader has to understand why someone would lift the fork. A single cook-focal character, or a cook plus one person they are feeding, is stronger than a large ensemble for eight thousand words. A shelter of six can exist as pressure and voices, but the plate should belong to one pair of hands. The former-cook angle earns the coziness without a speech about it: they already know how to make awful things palatable, which is both their gift and the accusation. A child as the first taster is emotionally loud and risky; it can tip into cruelty-for-shock unless the adult’s response is the real subject. A medic skeptic is useful as friction, less useful as the sole lens, because clinical distance undercuts deliciousness. The greenhouse keeper’s recognition is a good secondary fear (they know what fruiting bodies do) but may crowd the story if it becomes a biology explain-along. The lure reading (deliciousness as recruitment) honors “who would have thought” better than “turns out mutant pork is just pork.” Ordinary calories are a fine first theory and a weak final one. The story wants the characters to earn a practical hope (we can eat, we might live) and then have that hope curdle. Not into a twist that erases the hunger, and not into a monster-manual. Into a choice about whether to keep eating once eating is no longer only hunger. If the meat is dangerous from bite one in an obvious way, desperation feels stupid. If it is dangerous only in dreams and politics for seven chapters, the spore threat goes soft. A delay works: safe enough to rationalize, wrong in a way that arrives late and personally. Pacing should not be eight hunts. The prompt is about food, not about combat prowess. One or two acquisitions can be tense; the rest of the word count belongs to rationing, cooking, arguing, dreaming, and the social fact of a shared secret. Chapter-length around a thousand words favors one scene plus a turn, not braided subplots. A recipe-journal frame is tempting and a little cute; it works if the recipes are really scenes (who was in the room, what was refused) and fails if it becomes a gimmick list of dishes. Dark comedy is a seasoning, not the stock. Too many wine-pairing jokes and the desperation stops being desperate. Grief and ordinary manners (portioning fairly, wiping the table) will carry coziness more honestly than whimsy. The ending that fits the length is not eradication of the mutants. It is a decision about the next meal, made with full knowledge, by people who are still hungry. Stopping cleanly is noble and may kill them. Continuing is survival and may be surrender. A third path (cook it, do not swallow, feed it to the fire) is morally neat and dramatically thin unless the cost is on the page. Ambiguity is fine if the last image is concrete: steam, a spoon, a door, a body that feels better than it should. What does not pull its weight: a late reveal that the mutants were human all along (the prompt already names the enemy and asks us to believe the appetite); a savior cache of real food that lets them avoid the choice; an origin-of-the-apocalypse info dump; a romance that competes with the kitchen; body-horror so constant that “delicious” never gets to land as comfort. What does pull weight: salt as treasure, one repeating dish that improves as the moral situation worsens, a rule on the wall that gets edited, the awful relief of being full, and at least one person who never takes the bite so the eaters cannot pretend there was no other stance. The compelling version is probably intimate, kitchen-forward, and slow to condemn. It lets the food be wonderful. It lets hunger be a real argument. It lets the spore-thing stay a creature, not a metaphor lecture. And it spends the last chapters on what the wonderful food wants back. That is the reflection, not a lock. The cast, the exact mechanism of the lure, and whether the final spoon is lifted are still open.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention A close-third story locked to Lena, a former line cook, inside a boarded roadside diner that a handful of people have turned into a holdout. The prose stays in the kitchen: heat, salt, knives, portions, the fogged front window. Past tense, concrete, lightly lyrical only when a smell or a bite earns it. Humor is scarce and never wins a scene. The coziness is manners under siege—everyone sits, plates match, nothing is wasted—not whimsy. The cast stays small. Lena cooks. Ellis, her younger sibling, is failing from an ordinary infected wound and is the reason a bad meal can look like love. Ade, the medic, never eats and is not mocked for it. Ruiz eats early and jokes, then goes quiet. Nia knows fruiting bodies well enough to be afraid, eats once, and stops. No child taster. No romance plot. No origin-of-the-plague lecture. The mutants are creatures, not a disguise for cannibalism. They are delicious for a reason that arrives late: the taste is a lure, and a full stomach makes the colony treat you as already partly gathered. Early bites do not obviously damn anyone. Fullness is real, sleep is better, the meat pulls like chicken and mushroom and browned butter. Only afterward do the signs collect—hunger that feels like affection, dreams of soil, a mutant that will not attack an eater, white dust that might be flour or spore, a rule on the wall that gets edited. Plot runs on one repeating plate, not eight hunts. Lena’s “Sunday plate” (a seared braise, pan sauce, guarded onion, salt) gets better as the moral situation gets worse. There are two acquisitions of meat, one almost accidental and one that goes too well. The rest is rationing, cooking, argument, and what the food wants back. Salt is treasure. One working burner is the hearth. Ade’s refusal is the other stance in the room, so the eaters cannot pretend there was no choice. The ending is not a victory and not a rescue cache. Lena learns enough to choose with open eyes. She still cooks. The last image is hospitality: a beautiful plate, steam, a spoon, something knocking like a neighbor, her hand on the door. Survival and surrender are the same gesture. The story does not explain the apocalypse, does not reveal the meat was human, and does not let a found stockpile erase the hunger. Aim for sensory conviction, delayed dread, and a last choice that feels domestic. Avoid chase-plot inflation, splatter for its own sake, recipe-gimmick chapters, mycology speeches, and any twist that dodges the prompt’s sentence. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The empty pot.** The diner’s last honest meal is thin and shared. Lena inventories nothing: salt, one onion, a burner, the rule on the wall about what is not food. Ellis is hotter than yesterday. A failed night outside. Something dies in the alley against the flue, and the smell that comes through the boards is wrong in the worst way: it smells like dinner. **Chapter 2 — The first cut.** Morning. A small spore-thing is dead at the wall, half-cooked by the flue. Lena treats it like an unknown mushroom—clean, trim, one bite, wait—because training is the only courage she has. The taste is shockingly good. She does not announce it. She braises a little and feeds Ellis, who sleeps. Ade sees the pan. The chapter ends on Lena’s second bite and the sentence she will not say aloud: we could live. **Chapter 3 — Sunday plate.** She cooks it properly for the room. Ruiz eats and makes the one joke the book will allow. Nia eats, then goes gray with recognition and puts her fork down. Ade refuses; Lena still sets a full plate at Ade’s place and will not clear it. For an hour the window fogs and the road disappears. No one sickens. Fullness feels like mercy, which is the trap’s first success. **Chapter 4 — Groceries.** Hunger returns too soon, especially in Ellis. Lena and Ruiz go out for another. The kill is easier than it should be. A larger mutant scents Lena, lowers what used to be a head, and lets them pass. They come home like people who have been to market. Nia names the fruiting parts without lecturing. Lena salts the new cut as if naming it makes it meat. A small wrongness: Lena was not afraid at the moment she should have been. **Chapter 5 — The good night.** The dish improves—the last vinegar, Nia’s stubborn herbs, a real crust. Dreams begin: soil, warmth, Lena’s mother’s Sunday roast specifically, not a generic meal. Ellis is gentler and hungrier. Ade keeps a quiet symptom list and will not eat. Lena wipes the counter until her arm aches because the white dust will not declare itself flour or spore. Cozy, and the coziness is the dread. **Chapter 6 — What stops hunting.** A mutant waits at the glass the way a dog waits at a door. It tracks only Ade. Ruiz, who has eaten most, walks the lot and is not touched; he stops joking. The holdout splits without a speech: mouths that know the taste, and Ade, who is now the endangered one for having stayed human. Lena portions the pot with perfect fairness, including the untouched plate, and understands she is hosting. **Chapter 7 — The argument.** The kitchen fight is the moral climax. Ade will starve in sight of food and says the colony is finishing them, not feeding them. Ellis asks for more in a voice that sounds like love. Nia sides with stopping and is already weak. Lena states the true case—Ellis dies this week without it; the road will not forgive a principle—and hears how much of that case is appetite. Evidence, not a lecture: a softened tooth, a craving that feels like affection, the thing outside patient as a guest. No one is converted. **Chapter 8 — Come in.** Lena cooks the best plate of her life. She gives Ade the last of the clean salt and the last sealed scrap of real food—one portion, not a miracle—and does not pretend that saves anyone. She sits with Ellis. She eats, knowing. Steam. Clean plates. A knock like a neighbor bringing a dish to pass. The chapter ends on Lena’s hand on the latch and the window clearing just enough to show them waiting, polite, as if dinner was always the invitation.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. Model Output:
The prompt is a campfire brag with a bad conscience: hunger, a category error, and the punchline that the enemy is delicious. A person writing it would usually start from a mouth, not from a theme. They would know how their cook holds a knife, what cheap beloved food the meat unfortunately resembles, who in the room they are sick of, and they would find the ending while the pans are still dirty. They would let a scene run long because the butchering is slippery and hard to get off the hands, and they would let another scene die early because nobody has anything new to say. The eight chapters would leak into each other. Someone would still be owed an apology from chapter 3 in the middle of chapter 6, and the apocalypse would not be the only subject, because trapped people bicker about boots, snoring, and who last washed a fork. That approach is less even than the plan, and also less fair. LLM prose, left alone, tends to write safely, finish with a bow, and sound impressive at the expense of sounding said. It distributes moral positions across a cast so no stance goes unrepresented. It makes the protagonist competent and basically fair, then signals their fall with a tidy set of symbols. It explains feelings in the same breath as having them. It rations humor so a joke can never outrank the theme. It prefers a threshold image to an unfinished bite. Sentences arrive in balanced threes. Objects exist to mean something. The world cooperates with the point. None of this is forbidden in a story, but stacked, it reads as a well-made diagram of a story rather than as people who were hungry first. The intention is already strong about the right large choices: kitchen, not war; the meal has to be genuinely good; no cannibalism dodge; no rescue cache; Ade’s refusal stays available so the eaters can’t pretend. The trouble is that the plan then over-builds those choices until they become a machine. Lena is protected. She portions with perfect fairness, sets Ade a full plate and will not clear it, gives Ade the last clean salt and the last honest scrap, and can state her own dilemma in a clean speech about principle and the road. That is a protagonist the prose is unwilling to dislike. A person cooking in that diner plays favorites, hides a spoonful, takes the crisp bit because she did the work, and feeds Ellis partly to make the asking stop. Perfect fairness is an alibi. The dying-sibling clock is another alibi: the prompt only required hunger, and the plan adds a beloved patient so the first bite is already love. Ellis should be allowed to be whiny, embarrassing, and loved in a sour, ordinary way. If Lena resents them a little, the fork is heavier. The cast is a seminar. Ade is conscience, Ruiz is the joke that will be withdrawn on schedule, Nia is recognition that eats once and stops, Ellis is the reason, Lena is compromised care. Real holdouts have dead weight: someone who eats and has no theory, someone whose refusal is squeamish or pious or vain rather than noble, someone whose grudge predates the spores. “Ade is not mocked” is an overcorrection. Not mocking the ethical one is how the draft stays just. People stuck in a kitchen are not just. Ade can be right and also unbearable, or right in public and already licked the knife. The symbols are too willing. The rule on the wall wants to be edited on camera. The white dust wants to be flour and spore. The Sunday plate wants to improve as the morals worsen. The fogged window removes the road for exactly one hour of mercy. The mutant lets them pass, then waits like a guest, then tracks only the uneaten person, which is proof arriving on time. Each of these is a good idea once. Together they are a thesis kit. A lived version would ignore the wall rule until it is grease-thumbed and unreadable, misread the easy hunt because people overread luck, and fail to confirm the lure in a single demonstration. Suspicion is more human than evidence. If the dish improves every time, the story is allegorical. Scarier, and plainer: Lena cooks worse because she is tired, scorches the pan, oversalts, and the meat is still the best thing in the room. Her skill was never the point. Service-muscle is the point. She worked this diner, or one like it, and hates that her hands know what to do. “Mother’s Sunday roast” is a stock memory. So is browned butter, chicken, and mushroom, which is magazine deliciousness. The prompt’s shock needs a specific, slightly ashamed deliciousness: staff-meal fried rice, a gas-station slice, a family soup she always said was too salty and now wants exactly that way. One ugly precise detail in the butchering will do more than a bouquet: a sac that smells wrong and sweet, fat that beads gray before it goes gold, a chin she doesn’t wipe because she is still chewing. Reverent butchering is competency porn, and the unknown-mushroom protocol is the same thing in chef’s clothing. The first carcass should be half ruined. They eat it anyway. Chapter 7 as “the argument” puts the theme in a debate. By then these people would already have fought about the dishes, the door, and a stolen portion, and the moral content would have leaked out sideways, badly phrased. Lena would not say the true case. She would say something smaller and meaner and only half fair. “No one is converted” is the approved literary result, and then chapter 8 converts the book anyway, into the best plate of her life, the salt-gift, the neighborly knock, and a hand on the latch. That is the bow. Threshold endings, fragment buttons, and “survival and surrender are the same gesture” are impressive and familiar. A human last page is likelier to be petty or muscular: she says “we’re closed” because that is what you say at a diner door; the knock is Ruiz with the door stuck and they laugh wrong; she is mid-chew and Ade is the one who stands up; the burner is still on; nobody has done the dishes. Do not cash out every token. Leave the salt unmentioned. Tone is being policed. “Humor is scarce and never wins a scene,” “lightly lyrical only when earned,” Ruiz’s one permitted joke: that is how a draft stays tasteful and goes gray. The prompt is a little gleeful. Let a joke win, meanly, with a mouth full, and let the win sit there unpunished by craft. Give Lena a work mouth — ticket slang, a repeated swear, contempt for the word rustic — and let sentences be clumsy when she is tired. Not every chapter needs a turn and a title that already sounds like the story’s poem. One chapter can be mostly chores and a card game while the meat sits in the walk-in. One can be almost all physical butchering, with no one interpreting it. Chapters should start with yesterday’s pans still in the sink. The plan knows what the food wants back before anyone has eaten it. A person writing this would leave a few things undecided on purpose: whether the lure is real, whether Ade already tasted it, whether Lena likes being the one who feeds more than she likes Ellis. That uncertainty is the human remainder. The draft can be intimate and kitchen-locked and still less diagrammed, if Lena is allowed to be unfair, the meat allowed to be gross and wonderful in the same bite, and the last page allowed to leave a mess.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention A close-third, past-tense story locked to Lena, who worked the grill at the roadside diner where six people would still be too many and four is already too much. The people stuck with her are Ellis, her younger brother, with a dirty ordinary wound and a voice that grates when he is scared; Ade, a stranded nurse who will not eat and is often right in the most unhelpful way; and Cal, who ran the other grill, eats whatever she puts down, and does not treat it as a position. No fifth moral counterweight. No child. No romance. No origin of the spores. The prompt is the appetite. They are out of food. The spore-things are trying to kill them. The meat is genuinely, embarrassingly good, and that goodness has to be on the page more than once: specific, a little gross, closer to overpeppered breakfast sausage and staff-meal grease than to a magazine roast. Lena’s first swallows are for herself. Feeding Ellis comes after, partly love and partly so she can stand the room. She plays favorites, hides the crackling, resents the asking, and breaks her own pass-rule by eating at the stove. Ade’s refusal stays in the room so the eaters cannot pretend there was no other stance. Ade is not protected from being irritating, and Lena is not protected from being unfair. The wrongness stays deniable. Something in the lot does not always finish a rush. Hunger comes back mean and affectionate. A dream might be exhaustion. A tooth might just be a tooth. Nobody gets a demonstration that would settle a lab. Lena wants a theory mostly so the pleasure will not just be hers. She does not get one. What she gets is a practical bind: the walk-in is dead, so a carcass is a today-problem. That, more than a creed, pushes the next meal. Cozy-horror comes from diner habits still working around the wrong food. Call a plate. Wipe the pass. Say “we’re closed.” Argue about forks. Sit or don’t. Let a joke land and keep landing. The warmth is real for stretches, especially when they are full and indoors, and it is not framed as a lesson. Horror is the chewing, the quiet outside, and how good the second bite still is. Not a chase plot. Two short, ugly trips for meat, both botched, neither a set piece. Voice is work-mouth and tired mouth. Short sentences when her hands know the job. Longer, clumsier ones when she is angry or half-asleep. Sensory detail should be precise and slightly ashamed, not lyrical food writing. Dialogue can interrupt and stay unfinished. Feelings ride on what she does. Do not gloss them afterward. Chapters may carry dirty pans, unfinished fights, and no moral button. One chapter is mostly chores. Avoid a symbol kit (wall-rule, holy salt, fog as mercy, a dish that improves on a moral schedule, white dust that explains itself). Avoid a debate chapter, a fair heroine, a beloved patient as permission slip, a cannibalism twist, a food cache, an eradication ending, and any last line that names survival-as-surrender. The ending is a tired plate and a full mouth. She does not open the door and does not make a better barricade. She keeps chewing. The sink is full. Whether the colony has been invited is not cashed out. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1.** Night, almost nothing left. Lena stretches a thin pot and is already mean about the salt. Ellis complains. Ade counts what is left in a bottle. Cal wants to check the lot. Something hits the flue and the smell that comes through the boards is breakfast-grease and rot. Lena’s mouth waters. She says they will deal with it in the morning because she is tired, not because of a rule. She stays at the pass anyway. **Chapter 2.** Morning carcass, half crushed and half spoiled. The trim is clumsy. She nicks herself, throws out a sweet-wrong bit, and goes back for it. The taste is the shock: hot fat, black pepper, the sausage she used to eat standing up and call trash. She eats more than a taste before she tells anyone, then feeds Ellis a scorched piece and says it’s fine. Ade sees blood on her wrist and asks the wrong question. End on the secret swallow, not on a decision. **Chapter 3.** What they have will turn, so she cooks it. Cal eats standing up, calls it the special, and the joke works. Ade refuses and starts explaining; Lena cuts that off. Ellis wants the meal to mean they are all right. It doesn’t. Someone’s stomach turns and they blame the grease. Lena calls “two up” to nobody out of habit. Cal laughs. She lets the laugh stand. The window is only greasy. **Chapter 4.** No cold storage, and Ellis is hungry again, and so is she. A short botched trip with Cal. They come back with less than they cut loose. One of the things gets close and does not finish them; in the moment she is only trying not to drop the meat. Back inside she shakes, oversalts a fry-up, and eats at the stove before anyone is served. It is still too good. Cal tells the not-quite-attack bigger than it was. Ade doesn’t buy it. Lena doesn’t correct either of them. **Chapter 5.** Chores. Sink, bandage, a stupid card game, who sleeps where. The meat smell is in the curtains. For a little while the room is almost nice, and the niceness doesn’t have to pay for itself. Cal makes the same joke and it still lands. Ellis is a bad patient. Lena sleeps and dreams the ticket rail is full of the same item. She wakes hungry. Her tongue feels thick. She blames the salt. No one interprets the dream. **Chapter 6.** The lot is quiet in a way that proves nothing. Cal goes out to piss and comes back shrugging. Ade says it watched him. Lena finds Ellis in the pot and blows up over a portion, not over a soul. The fight is petty and does not finish. She sleeps in the office, wakes hungrier, and eats cold meat with her fingers in the dark. Cold, it is still the best thing she has had in weeks. She does not wake the others. **Chapter 7.** Ellis keeps down almost nothing except the meat, and he is worse. Ade grabs for the ladle. Lena says something small and only half fair, wins because it is her kitchen, and does not make a speech. One deniable wrongness: a loose tooth, or Ellis smelling like the pan, or her gums itching. She can explain all of it. She cooks. She eats while she cooks. The chapter ends on the sound of Ellis eating, which is relief, which she cannot stand. **Chapter 8.** A tired plate, not a best plate. She has already eaten the crackling. Ellis gets the piece that will stop the whining. Ade’s share sits; she tells herself she will wrap it. A scratch at the door. Mouth full, she says “we’re closed” and does not get up. Cal laughs, wrong, and nobody fixes it. She tells Ellis not to talk while he chews. The burner ticks. Yesterday’s pans are still in the sink. She reaches for another bite. The door stays as it was.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Lena Lena is thirty-six and has worked the grill in this diner for nine years, four of them as the person who actually ran the line. She grew up two towns over, left home at eighteen because the house was loud in the wrong way, and landed here because the sign said help wanted and the apartment over the closed tax office was cheap. She is not a cook in the way people mean when they want a story. She can fry an egg in a pan that isn’t level, stretch a gravy, and tell by the sound when a burger is lying about being done. She cannot bake. She resents anyone who calls the food rustic. She came into the collapse already tired of people. Ellis turning up was not a reunion. He had her address from a Christmas card she almost didn’t send. She let him in because the lot was worse than the dining room, then spent the next weeks wishing she had a second door. She likes Cal in the way you like someone whose bad habits match the holes in yours. She does not like Ade. Ade’s hands are too clean for how much water they use, and Ade looks at the pot like a chart. Her flaw is not temper, though she has one. It is hoarding the good bit and calling it management. She eats at the stove so the portioning looks fair afterward. She hides crackling in a folded towel. She will feed Ellis the piece that stops the noise and keep the piece she wants. When she is frightened she gets precise: she wipes the same six inches of steel, she calls tickets that nobody ordered, she answers a question with the next task. She is capable of tenderness and suspicious of it. If Ellis thanks her she gets angry sooner than if he complains. She is short, thick through the shoulders, with a burn ladder up the left forearm and a white nick across the pad of the thumb from a mandoline she still blames on a lunch rush in 2019. Hair goes in a knot that fails by midmorning. She smells like onions even now, under the meat. She stands with her hip against the counter so her hands stay free. She does not sit to eat if she can help it. When she lies, she looks at the pan, not at the person. She wants the burner to stay lit, her mouth not to be watched, and Ellis not to die in her kitchen where she would have to be the one who deals with it. She is not sure those wants are in that order. She is loyal to the diner as a set of motions, not as a home. Cal gets the truth if it is about the grill and a trimmed version if it is about her. Ellis gets food and a shorter sentence than he asked for. Ade gets whatever keeps Ade from taking the ladle. “Don’t narrate it. Eat it or move.” She thought, greasy-fingered in the dark, that she could wrap Ade’s share in the morning. She also thought she wouldn’t. Both thoughts felt like work, so she licked the salt off her thumb and shut the lid. # Ellis Ellis is twenty-seven and was, until the buses stopped, a parts-counter guy at a warehouse that smelled like cardboard and coolant. He is not handy. He can hold a flashlight and he can talk, which he does when he is scared, in a rush that apologizes three times and still asks for the thing. He came to the diner because Lena was a dot on a map he could reach on half a tank. He told himself she would be glad. She wasn’t. He has been living inside that correction ever since, trying to shrink it with usefulness. He stacks plates wrong. He offers to watch the lot and then doesn’t want to go. The wound is a dirty cut across the shin from a chain-link tear outside a closed gas station, days before he arrived. He cleaned it with a napkin and a splash of something from the glove box. It sulks. It weeps. It is not a war wound and he hates when his own voice makes it sound like one. He picks at the bandage. He asks if it looks better and watches Lena’s face instead of the leg, because her face answers faster. He is vain in a small, surviving way. He still combs his hair with wet fingers. He keeps a plastic lighter that belonged to a girlfriend who didn’t come, though the lighter has been dry for a week. He sits crooked on the stools, one shoe half off, and stands up too fast, which hurts, which makes him laugh so nobody will do the concerned noise. He wants the meal to mean the room is all right. When it doesn’t, he eats anyway and then talks about how it almost does. Under the want to be loved is a meaner want: not to be the reason Lena looks at the door. He will accept the meat, the lie, the “it’s fine,” because refusing would make him the problem in a new direction. He loves his sister in the old way, from before she left, and he is embarrassed by it. He also clocks her portions. He knows she eats first. He has not said so. Saying so would cost him the next plate. He is tall and already thin in the face, with a office-job slouch that the pain has bent further. Freckles across the nose. A jacket that used to be for a job interview, cuffs dark. He smells faintly sweet when the wound is bad, and he has started sitting so the leg is away from people. He touches the counter when he talks, as if the diner is a person who might take his side. He is on Lena’s side and resents the price. He wants Cal to like him and laughs late at Cal’s jokes. He wants Ade to say the leg is ordinary. Ade won’t quite. That silence scares him more than the meat. “It doesn’t even hurt if I don’t stand on it. You don’t have to do the face.” If he said she ate more than she served, she might stop feeding him. So he said the potatoes were fine, which they weren’t, and rubbed the lighter with his thumb until the plastic went warm. # Ade Ade is forty-one, a clinic nurse who was driving to a shift that no longer existed when the car died on the highway shoulder. They walked toward the diner lights with a canvas bag, a half bottle of water, and the certainty that a building with a door was a temporary fact. Three weeks later the temporary fact has a grill cook who will not take instruction. Ade’s full name gets used by nobody. Lena says Ade like a ticket. They are not a saint of refusal. The not-eating started as disgust and a work rule about unknown flesh, and hardened because stopping now would mean Lena was right to start. Ade is hungry. Ade looks at the pot more than Ade admits, and hates the looking. The principle is real and also a way to stay the person with the bag of gauze. They wash their hands in water the room cannot spare. They count remaining packets out loud. They ask diagnostic questions at the moment a person wants a plate, because questions are how Ade holds a floor. Ade’s flaw is the need to be the accurate one in a room that is trying to get through a meal. They correct a story while it is still being told. They say “that doesn’t follow” about a fear that was never trying to follow. They are brave in the lot in short bursts and then ruin it by explaining the burst. Lena thinks Ade wants the ladle. Ade wants not to be infected by somebody else’s appetite, and is afraid the appetite is already in the room, including in Ade’s own mouth. There was a moment, early, when Ade put a finger to a drip on the steel and smelled it and did not lick it. Ade treats that as a victory. It felt smaller than a victory. They have no one left in range to be loyal to except the idea of a clinic that might still be staffed two exits on. The group is a wait, not a family. Ellis gets Ade’s actual worry, delivered badly. Cal gets contempt mixed with reliance, because Cal will walk outside when Ade would rather not. Lena gets opposition, because Lena has the food and the habit of deciding. Ade is spare, long-necked, with close-cropped hair going gray at the temples and a rash from the collar of a shirt worn too many days. They stand as if the floor might be dirty in a way that matters. Gestures are small. The canvas bag stays in reach. When they are angry they get quieter and more exact, which reads as calm and isn’t. “You can heat it all you want. Heat isn’t a test. It’s just hot.” They had the sentence ready about spores and stomach acid and what a negative night doesn’t prove. Lena turned away before the middle of it. Ade held the rest in their teeth and was, for a second, angrier about the interruption than about the meat. # Cal Cal is forty-four and has worked the other side of this line, on and off, since before Lena had a key. Nights, originally, when the clientele was truckers and the radio was stuck on one station. He lives, or lived, in a rented room above a bar that is now a dark hole with a door that banged for a week and then stopped. He came to the diner on the first bad morning because the walk-in still had eggs and because Lena would be there. Eggs went. He stayed. He is not the conscience and not the fool. He eats because it is in front of him and because naming it would make the next hour worse. He knows Lena hides the crackling. Sometimes he finds it and eats that too, then denies it with a face so mild she almost believes him. He tells the lot bigger than it was. A pause becomes a mercy, a stumble becomes a thing that knelt. He isn’t trying to recruit anyone. He is trying to make the story one he can say over a plate without his voice doing something embarrassing. His flaw is that loyalty, in him, looks like agreement and is often just a refusal to be the person who stops the room. He will back Lena against Ade even when he thinks Ade has a point, then mutter the point later into a mug as if that counts. He jokes on purpose. The joke is the special, the ticket, the bit about the health inspector. When the joke works he feels the day click into a shape he understands. He will repeat it. He would rather be repetitive than honest at the wrong volume. He wants the diner sounds to continue: call, plate, laugh, scrape. He wants Lena to keep deciding the next hour so he doesn’t have to. He is fond of Ellis in a rough, impatient way, the fondness of a regular for somebody’s kid brother. He does not want Ellis to die on the premises, mostly because of what it would do to the shift. Ade he treats as a customer who won’t order. Not cruel, exactly. Unwilling to be converted, and unwilling to say the truer thing, which is that the meat scares him and he is eating it anyway. Cal is heavy in the chest, red in the face from years of the pass, with a shiny burn on the right wrist he shows when a story needs proof. He drinks water from a chipped mug that used to say a tire brand. He leans in doorways. He gestures with his chin. His shoes are the good nonslip pair, cracked at the toe, because he could not make himself wear anything else to this building. When he is frightened he gets friendlier. “You want the special or you want to keep talking about the special? ‘Cause the special’s getting cold.” On the way back, meat leaking through a towel against his stomach, he was already fixing the sentence: it came right up to her and it stopped. By the time he told it, the thing had looked at her like it knew her name. He almost believed it. Believing it made the towel less wet.
