+ Romance — Love in the Limelight (Chapter Avg: 85.8 | Final: 86.3)
Initial Writing Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The story takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. The story will progress beyond this synopsis, and it's up to you where it goes.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The story takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor&#x27;s charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. The story will progress beyond this synopsis, and it&#x27;s up to you where it goes. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming The prompt locks a few things and leaves the rest open: a famous actor, a small Welsh town, a bookstore, paparazzi as the reason he comes in, a first scene of mostly talk with unspoken chemistry, him as a charming rogue whose ego needs feeding, her (or their) surface immunity derailing that charm, and an inward fluster she will not show. Actor is specified as “him.” The owner is not gendered in the brief, so that stays a live variable. Eight chapters at about a thousand words each means roughly eight scenes, not a novel’s worth of plot. Dialogue-primary means the plot has to be speakable: what they ask, dodge, mishear, and almost say. **Place, and why he is even in Wales.** Hay-on-Wye is the obvious book town and may be too famous, too full of people who would clock a celebrity and too pleased with its own literary identity. A smaller market or coastal town gives the shop more privacy and the paparazzi less cover: Cardigan, Aberaeron, Llandeilo, a town under the Cambrian mountains, a Pembrokeshire street in the off-season, somewhere on the Llŷn where the last bus has already gone. He might be there because a production is shooting a few valleys over, because a premiere or junket spilled out of Cardiff, because he was stupid enough to stop for petrol in a recognizable car, or because he is Welsh-born and thought a childhood town would be invisible. Each reason changes the wound. A visitor treats the town as a set. A local who left treats it as a verdict. Weather can do structural work a plot twist would otherwise have to do: horizontal rain, a road closed, a landslip, last train gone, his driver spooked by cameras and fled. Being stuck is more romantic than choosing to linger, at least at the start, because choice would flatter his ego too early. **Who he is, beyond “rogue with a fragile ego.”** The charm is a craft, not a personality. He compliments precisely, remembers a detail from three lines ago and hands it back gift-wrapped, laughs at himself in a way that invites you to correct him. The fragility shows when the gift is not opened: he repeats the joke, upgrades it, fishes, goes a little mean, then panics and becomes generous. Possible flavors: a film actor who is secretly ashamed of being better at being liked than at the work; a stage-trained actor who cannot stop projecting to the back of a shop that has twelve customers on a good day; a Welshman who sanded the accent off and now hears it coming back in his mouth like a tell; an Englishman who has played Welshmen and thinks that counts. The rogue element can be flirtation, petty lying, nicking a paperback “on account,” winding up a local just to feel the room move. It should stay charm, not menace. The interesting failure mode is not cruelty. It is need. He would rather be adored than known, and he does not fully realize those are different until someone withholds the applause. Name-texture only, not choices: something that sounds good said dryly over a till, and something the tabloids would shorten. **Who runs the shop.** Surface immunity can come from several different interiors, and they do not play the same. - A person who clocked him in the doorway and decided celebrity is a kind of bad weather: inconvenient, not interesting. - A former bookseller-to-the-tourists who is tired of people performing “I love hidden gems” while photographing the spines. - Someone who was adjacent to fame once—a sibling, a parent, an ex—and knows what being liked-by-everyone costs the person standing next to him. - A Welsh-speaker whose real life happens in a language he cannot enter, so his charm literally cannot land in the room that matters. - A quietly ambitious reader, writing or not writing, who resents how easily he is given an audience. - Someone blunt, short-sentenced, funny without smiling, who answers a flirtation with a fact about the stock. Inward fluster, if the prose stays mostly dialogue, has to leak as behavior: wrong book pulled, sentence restarted, Welsh slipping out and being swallowed, tea poured past the rim, a kindness that arrives too fast and is then retracted. Gender and age are open. Mid-thirties to forties keeps the ego-wound and the shop-responsibility equally adult. A younger owner risks making his charm look like pressure. A much older owner turns it into a different story, mentor-inflected, which fights the romance unless handled very carefully. Secondary people, used sparingly so they do not dilute the two voices: a part-time assistant who is starstruck and therefore dangerous; a regular who wants the shop to stay boring; a publicist on the phone whose language is all optics; one photographer who is not a swarm but a persistent fact; a sister, a mother, or an ex who knows the owner’s tells. **What the chemistry is actually about.** Not “opposites attract” in the abstract. He offers attention as currency. She refuses the currency, which makes him want the person instead of the reaction, which is new and destabilizing. She is immune to the performance and porous to the moment the performance fails. So the scenes that spark are not his best lines. They are the botched ones: a silence he cannot fill, a local reference he gets wrong, a compliment she declines without cruelty, a joke that dies and is not rescued. Books give them a third subject so they never have to name the attraction. They can argue about a poet, a thriller, a children’s book, a memoir of leaving Wales, and both of them hear the other argument underneath. **Tonal lanes.** Warm comedy with bite. Melancholy, rain-lit, more ache than joke. A comedy of exposure, where the joke is always the gap between how he thinks he looks and how the town looks at him. A slightly sharper social story about what a failing shop and a famous face do to each other. Sensuality held in attention rather than in explicit scene-work, since a thousand-word dialogue chapter has little room for set-piece intimacy and the brief is chemistry, not consummation. Welsh specificity as texture—bilingual signage, chapel times, the particular polite nosiness of a small town—not as postcard. The limelight is not only glamorous. In a town this size it is exposure: everyone will have an opinion by tomorrow, and the opinion will stick to her longer than to him. **Engines that could carry eight chapters, any of which could be the plot or only a pressure.** - Containment: he cannot leave until dark, then until morning, then until a road opens. The shop becomes a hiding place and then a problem, because hiding in a retail space means customers. - The wrong film: he is playing a local figure, a poet, a striker, a saint, and the shop holds the letters, the cheap biography, the argument about what the film flattens. She has the knowledge. He has the platform. That is a live wire for ego. - The shop’s actual trouble: rent, a landlord, a chain, a silent partner, a tourist season that no longer comes. His attention could save it or mark it as a celebrity sideshow and kill the regulars. - The photograph: someone gets a picture. The story the internet tells is a fling, a stunt, or a breakdown. He knows how to surf that. She does not, and her inward fluster becomes public before she has admitted it to herself. - The lie he is already living: a staged relationship, a sober narrative, a “back to my roots” profile his team invented. The bookstore threatens the lie by being real. - Language: she speaks Welsh with the regulars and will not translate. His inability to be included is the first room he cannot work. - A public event already on the calendar: a reading, a school visit, a small eisteddfod fringe, a signing he was never meant to do and then cannot resist doing. Limelight invited into the one room that was safe. - Recognition denied: half the town does not know his face. The wound of not being liked because he is not even seen. He may hate this more than hostility. **How eight short, talky chapters might be paced, as alternatives rather than a spine.** One shape is a single long day and night, two people and a bell over the door. Intimate, high risk of sameness. Each chapter would need a new visitor or a new rule (lights off, back room, his phone, her nephew, the kettle, the lock) so the dialogue has fresh obstacles. Another is a week, one chapter a day, locations opening out: shop, lane behind the shop, caffi, sea wall, his ridiculous hired car, the hall where something local is happening, then the shop again after it has been breached. Better movement, higher risk of becoming a travelogue of banter. A third is a tightening noose: private, then one witness, then the town, then the internet, then a choice about whether to be seen together on purpose. The romance and the fame plot share a climax. A fourth is object-driven: a book moves between them. He hides behind a stack. She sells him the wrong thing on purpose. He returns it. A dedication appears. A volume goes missing. The object can carry time jumps the dialogue cannot. Rough beat possibilities, not a commitment: 1. Entry in the rain. Recognition or not. First charm, first dry refusal. A line of his lands wrong. He stays because outside is cameras, and also because he cannot stand the refusal. 2. He tries harder. She puts him to work or refuses his help. A customer nearly names him. His ego flares in a small, revealing way. She is flustered and covers it with stocktaking. 3. Forced cooperation. A task with their hands busy so their mouths get careless. He is funny without trying. She laughs and then resents the laugh. 4. After hours, or a walk that was not supposed to happen. A true thing from him, small. She almost answers in kind. Interruption: phone, sister, photographer, the alarm he set and forgot. 5. The outside voice enters—publicist, tabloid, local gossip, the assistant who posts. He performs for the new audience. She sees the machinery and goes cold. He feels the cold as rejection and becomes more charming, which is the wrong medicine. 6. Rupture in dialogue, not in action. She says the quiet part: he needs to be liked more than he wants to know her. He cannot charm his way out and tries anyway. Something petty or public follows from his hurt. 7. Consequence with the town or the press attached. Separation. He does an unglamorous thing that cannot be photographed usefully, or fails to, and the failure is the information. She has to decide whether protecting him is kindness or self-erasure. 8. A conversation that is finally unperformed. Not necessarily a kiss-and-credits ending. Options range from him leaving and the shop remaining itself, to a deliberate being-seen, to an unfinished stay. The last chapter should answer what “limelight” did to two people, not only whether they want each other. **Voice, since the brief wants distinct talk.** His sentences can run long, ornate, self-interruptive, full of offered adjectives. Hers can be short, specific, slightly late, willing to let a silence sit. When he is derailed, his lines shorten and he starts asking real questions. When she is flustered, hers lengthen, or she answers a question he did not ask. Welsh in her mouth can be a door. Bookseller diction—editions, damage, who it is for—can be how she flirts without admitting it. His tells: he narrates what he is feeling in the third person, as if pitching the scene. Hers: she corrects a fact when she is moved, because facts are safer than the feeling. **Endings worth holding up to the light, none chosen.** He leaves for the job and the shop goes back to itself, with one object changed. They are photographed on purpose, and the story becomes about whether she can survive being a character in his publicity. The town decides it likes him more than she does, and he has to turn down an audience to be believed. A bittersweet staying: not a relationship announced, but a decision to stop performing for one evening. A comic deflation: he is not, in this postcode, as famous as his ego requires, and the romance begins in that demotion. # Reflection The prompt is narrow in its first scene and deliberately open after that, so the danger is either stretching the bookstore banter until it thins, or abandoning the brief’s actual engine—the charm that fails, the fluster that will not show—for a generic fame-and-small-town plot. Whatever comes later has to keep testing that engine. If he becomes simply sincere by chapter three, the rogue and the fragile ego were costumes. If she remains a wall, there is no romance, only a sketch. The interesting middle is a slow leak: his technique degrades in public view of one person; her composure fails in ways she can still deny out loud. Dialogue-primary at this length is a constraint that helps and hurts. It helps because both characters are defined by talk: he uses speech to be liked, she uses speech to keep a perimeter. Distinct voices will do more characterization than backstory. It hurts because “inwardly charmed” is an interior fact, and a reader cannot be asked to guess it from frost alone. Action beats have to carry the fluster—business of the shop, slips, timing—or the owner becomes a straight man and the actor swallows the book. The brief says primarily dialogue, not exclusively, which is the workable reading. Chapters that are wall-to-wall cleverness will also exhaust the fragile-ego joke. His need should occasionally cost him a line he cannot walk back. Eight thousand words is a long short story, not a novel. A plot with a landlord, a film shoot, a sibling, a publicist, a festival, and a secret manuscript will not fit unless most of those stay offstage as pressure rather than onstage as subplots. One external stake is enough if it shares a theme with the romance. The strongest overlap is being seen versus being known. Paparazzi, a struggling shop, a dishonest profile, a film that gets Wales wrong, a photograph that freezes her before she has chosen anything: these all ask the same question his ego already asks, which is whether attention is the same as regard. A stake that does not ask that question—a stolen car, a mystery, a family secret with no bearing on performance—will feel grafted on, however lively. Place is not decoration, but it can become one. Hay-on-Wye signals “books” so loudly it may do the reader’s work and leave the shop generic. A less famous town lets the bookstore be a livelihood instead of a destination, which matters if her immunity is partly a defense of a real business against a man for whom every room is a set. Wales works best as language, weather, class, and the long memory of a small place, not as scenery he compliments while she rolls her eyes. If he is Welsh and left, the charm offensive has a colonial tint even inside one country: he came back fluent in being watched and clumsy in belonging. That version has more ache than the visiting movie star, and it gives her refusals a moral weight that is not just “I don’t date famous men.” The visiting-star version is cleaner comedy and makes the paparazzi more plausible, but it risks a savior plot in which London attention blesses a quaint shop. That version only works if his help is the wrong shape and she is allowed to refuse it without becoming unlovable. Tone should stay comic enough that his rogue-ishness reads as appetizing rather than invasive, and serious enough that the ego is a real flaw. If the story mocks him constantly, her attraction looks like bad judgment. If it indulges him, her immunity looks like a hurdle for him to win. The reader needs to feel, early, why someone sharp would be flustered by him at all: not the fame, not the lines, but the moment the lines stop. That also solves consent and comfort. A rogue who treats a no as a puzzle to beat will sour the romance, especially in a confined shop. The derailment has to include him hearing her. Attraction grows where he becomes less effective, not where he pushes harder. Pacing favors a widening circle over a bottle episode, with a caveat. One location for eight chapters will repeat the same power arrangement—customer and proprietor, guest and host—until the dialogue has nowhere to go. A few steps outside, still inside the town’s attention, give new things to talk around. Jumping to London, a set, or a montage of fame would break the scale and pull the point of view toward his world, where he is competent again. The story is more compelling if the limelight has to come to the shop, not if she is imported into his life. Chapter length also argues for one turn per chapter: an arrival, a mishap, a leak of feeling, a breach, a saying-aloud, a cost, a choice. Trying to land a full relationship arc with obstacles, breakup, and grand reunion will make each beat too short to be felt. An ending that is a decision about visibility, rather than a solved future, fits both the word count and the title. The owner’s gender being unspecified is useful and should not be hurried. The dynamic in the brief is not inherently heterosexual; it is about performance meeting refusal. What matters is that her voice is not written only as the brake on his charm. She needs wants of her own that predate him—the shop, a language, a standard for honesty, a town she has chosen—or the inward fluster has nothing to threaten. His fame should endanger something she already loves, not merely her dignity. What seems most likely to be compelling, without locking it: a rainy, specific, not-too-famous Welsh town; an actor whose Welshness or lack of it is part of the performance; a bookseller whose dryness is competence, not emptiness; chemistry that sparks when his charm fails; one fame-shaped external pressure that makes being liked publicly dangerous to her private life; dialogue that changes length as the masks slip; and a last chapter that chooses what to do with being looked at, rather than treating a kiss as an answer. What seems weakest: postcard Wales, a shop saved by celebrity, an immunity that never cracks on the page, a rogue who does not suffer for his need to be liked, and a plot so busy the two voices no longer have room to miss each other.

Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>

# Intention A dialogue-led romance of about eight thousand words, set over two days in the off-season in Porthllew, a fictional small town on the Ceredigion coast. The shop is Siop y Felin, a livelihood rather than a destination. Wales arrives as weather, bilingual speech, class, and a long local memory, not as scenery. Rhys Calder, late thirties, is a well-known actor shooting a few valleys inland. He plays a historical Welsh poet in an English-language film, and his team has written him a “homecoming” profile. He was born in Wales, left young, and sanded the accent; it returns when he is wrong-footed. His charm is a craft: long, gift-wrapped sentences, self-interruptions, jokes at his own expense that invite correction. The rogue streak is flirtation, small lies, theatrical generosity, and the occasional mean joke, not menace and not a refusal he refuses to hear. His wound is need. He would rather be adored than known, and he does not start the story able to tell those apart. Elen Vaughan, early forties, owns the shop and speaks Welsh with the people her real life is with. Her dryness is competence, not emptiness. She already has a standard, a poet’s reading to protect, and a town she chose twice. She clocks him at once and declines to treat that as interesting. She is not a wall. The fluster shows in dropped books, corrected facts, tea she did not mean to pour, sentences that lengthen, and one laugh she resents. What moves her is not the fame and not his best lines. It is the moment the lines fail. The prose is limited third person, slanted toward Elen in chapters 1, 3, 5, 7, and 8, and toward Rhys in 2, 4, and 6, so her inward crack and his ego are both on the page. Dialogue carries most of each chapter, aiming at roughly two-thirds speech. His lines shorten when he is derailed; hers stretch or answer the wrong question when she is moved. Welsh is used sparingly and not always translated, so some rooms stay shut to him. Books are the third subject they can argue about without naming the attraction: in particular, the small-press poems of the man his film is simplifying. One external pressure only, sharing the theme of being seen versus being known. A managed public narrative, a starstruck assistant with a phone, and a poet’s evening already on the calendar. The shop’s quiet winter trouble stays background. He is not allowed to save it. Attention, if he aims it at the shop, is the wrong shape, and she can refuse it without becoming unlovable. Each chapter turns once. He does not become sincere by the third chapter; the technique degrades in front of one person and reassembles whenever a third person arrives. She does not remain immune on the page. He does not treat her no as a puzzle to beat. The ending is not a solved future and not a kiss standing in for an answer. The decision is about visibility: she will not be a character in his publicity, and if anything begins between them it begins off-camera. A brief, chosen touch may follow that decision. The last note belongs to ordinary shop business, not to the limelight. Aim for warm comedy with bite, and for the ache of a small place where a story sticks to her longer than to him. Avoid postcard Wales, Hay-on-Wye literary cosplay, a savior plot, a grafted mystery, a London third act, mocking him until her wanting looks foolish, and indulging him until her refusal is only a hurdle. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — The bell (Elen).** Rain, a motorbike idling outside, a wet man pretending to browse. He charms the shop, the town, and her; she answers with prices and the state of the stock. He gets a local thing wrong, upgrades the joke, and she lets it die. She knows his face and does not feed it. She lets him wait in the poetry bay only because wet coats spoil books. He hears interest. She knows he has misheard, and is unsettled to find a part of her glad. He has pronounced her name right by accident; she covers the fluster with a publication date. **Chapter 2 — The upgrade (Rhys).** He tries harder: overpaying, restacking a display badly, fishing. Mrs Prys comes in, speaks Welsh, and does not give him the recognition he expects. He almost corrects her. Elen lies, mildly, to keep the customer from having him, and the lie both protects and shrinks him. A small mean joke about small towns escapes; he walks it back too elaborately. He asks, badly, whether she knows who he is. She says yes, with no applause in it. He sees her turn to the till and misses the blush. **Chapter 3 — Hands (Elen).** The road is still shut, so she puts him to work on a wet delivery rather than accept an offer of help. Hands busy, the talk loosens. They circle the film and the poems without him quite confessing the part. A story about a dialect coach stops being funny and becomes a shame about his own mouth. She laughs, then punishes the laugh with a sharp practical note. He does not pounce on the laugh. That, more than the charm, flusters her. She makes two cups of tea and will not sit down to drink hers. **Chapter 4 — After the sign (Rhys).** The closed sign, an eased rain, a walk only as far as the sea wall. He admits the homecoming profile is a brief, and that he does not remember this coast the way the profile will say. He tries to stage her confession back at her; she refuses the framing and answers a smaller question, about coming back for an aunt and staying because leaving twice would become a story. His publicist calls, loud: he is not to be seen with anyone. He performs for the phone. Elen walks ahead. He feels the cold and reaches, wrongly, for longer sentences. She tells him the shop opens at nine and does not say goodnight. **Chapter 5 — The machinery (Elen).** He is back at nine with a prepared apology and a local fact he learned too fast. Lowri, the Saturday girl, is starstruck, and he switches audiences without seeming to mean to. The charm is real and indiscriminate, which is worse. Lowri lifts a phone. Elen takes it. He says he doesn’t mind. She goes cold and tells him he can be liked somewhere else. She warns him that tomorrow’s reading is not a set: if he comes, he comes as nobody. He agrees too easily, already imagining how well he will play nobody. **Chapter 6 — Nobody (Rhys).** She says the quiet part in a few sentences: a third person enters and she becomes the audience too; he needs to be liked more than he wants to know her. He tries to charm his way out with a confession that is still a pitch. She does not pick up the cue. From the wound he gets petty, and partly accurate: her immunity is also a performance. He leaves and, on the way, does a small stupid thing with his hurt — a word dropped in the caffi, a text to Sadie “in case.” He knows it as he does it. The disgust arrives one beat late. **Chapter 7 — Thursday (Elen).** Anwen’s reading, a small room, the leak from chapter 6 arriving as outside attention. Elen protects the evening without a speech, moving chairs, keeping the language of the room. Rhys does not steal the event. He turns up in the lane and draws the attention off badly and unglamorously, refusing the pose and refusing the doorway. It is not a grand gesture. It works just enough that the poet finishes. He does not come back in. On the step she finds the small-press book, an inscription scored out until the page tore, and his number on a receipt rather than on the flyleaf. Alone, the fluster finally has room. **Chapter 8 — Off the sign (Elen).** Morning, cameras gone, the road open. He comes back because she has not called and because nobody was a part he failed. He starts a charming sentence, stops, and stays with short ones. He admits the caffi, the text, the need. She admits she was charmed and that it made her angry, and that she will not be a profile’s anecdote or a boost for the shop. He asks, plainly, if he can come to the door next week as a person, not a visit to a town. She tells him the shop opens at nine. This time she sits. A brief touch follows the decision and does not replace it. He leaves without a look meant to be seen. She watches anyway, then corrects a date on a label, the ordinary work the limelight does not get to keep.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
The useful distinction is not “polish versus mess.” It is whether the story feels overheard or administered. A human writing this prompt would probably start from an overheard sentence and a concrete nuisance, and let the theme show up late, if at all. The current plan starts from a thesis and assigns every scene a job. That is the main risk, and it is already visible in the plan even though no prose has been written. ## How a human might approach this particular piece A working fiction writer given the original prompt would likely treat the first bookstore conversation as the real assignment, and the other seven chapters as whatever that conversation made inevitable. They would write a page of talk before they named the theme. If the two voices did not separate on the page, no amount of sea wall and scored-out inscription would save it. They would also steal from jobs and places rather than from motifs. Bookshop work is repetitive, slightly dusty, and full of pointless speech: a customer who wants “the blue one, the crime one, his wife will know,” a delivery that is three copies short, a card machine that fails, a child with jam on a paperback. Paparazzi, if they have ever been near any, are not a symbol of exposure. They are a person in a wet leather jacket blocking the pavement, saying a name too loudly, getting the shop’s name wrong. A human would put that irritation in the body of the scene and only later, maybe, notice that it rhymes with his ego. Romance, specifically, would be approached as appetite and embarrassment, not as a media-ethics parable. The prompt asks for a rogue who needs to be liked, a woman who will not clap, and the derailment that follows. A human romance writer would decide early what she fancies, and it would be specific and a bit stupid: his voice when he stops selling a line, the way he occupies a doorway, a vanity she finds appalling and attractive. They would also decide what she does not fancy, and let that be unfair. Fame would be embarrassing as well as powerful. She has probably seen him in something naff. He would know she has, and fish for it. On Wales, a human either writes a coast they can walk in their head or does the dull research: which road floods, what the till receipt looks like, what people actually say when they mean “soon,” who is in the shop on a wet Thursday in November. They would not invent a town in order to avoid Hay-on-Wye and then leave it as “sea wall plus bilingualism.” If they do not speak Welsh, they would be cautious. A few untranslated sentences used as a locked door is a device. Code-switching because the customer in front of you is Mrs Davies is just Tuesday. Structurally, a human would under-plan the back half. They might know the rupture and not know the ending. They would let one chapter run long because the talk got interesting, and let another be three pages because nothing else happened. They would allow a secondary person to be vivid past their function. Anwen might be vain, late, and commercially thrilled by an actor in the lane. Lowri might already have posted. The photographer might be one freelance bloke who also does weddings, and that fact would be funnier and sadder than a swarm. Most importantly, a human would let someone be wrong for longer than a chapter. The prompt’s engine is his need and her refusal. It does not require both of them to arrive at a shared, accurate analysis of that engine and then choose a visibility policy. A human ending might be rash, slightly horny, unfinished, or more committed than is tasteful. It would probably not be a contract. ## Telltale LLM habits, and why they do not serve this story **Theme delivered as dialogue.** Models like a character to say the story’s argument in clean sentences near the end of act two. Here that would kill the brief. The chemistry lives in what they will not say. If Elen can already state his condition, the unspoken current has been replaced by a review of the book. **Safety and therapeutic pacing.** The rogue is sanded down until his worst act is petty and immediately regretted. Hurt is confessed in the next available scene. Disgust arrives “one beat late,” which still means the character is morally punctual. This prompt needs a man who can be charming and a little cheap, and a woman who can enjoy that and be angry about enjoying it. If both are reasonable adults managing a boundary, there is no derailment, only a seminar. **The bow.** Objects return, lines return, the last image restates the theme in a quieter voice. Readers feel cared for and nothing snags. Romance can end happily without every motif checking in. A bow is especially damaging to a story about performance, because the neatness feels like his publicist got a pass at the manuscript. **Impressive prose as a substitute for noticing.** Weather doing emotional labor, coastal light, a torn flyleaf, tea as a symbol of withheld intimacy. Fine once. Fatal as a system. This piece wants readable talk, shop business, and the odd ugly detail. A clever cadence makes both voices sound like the narrator. **Equitable interiority.** Alternating chapters so that neither character is misunderstood. That is a fairness instinct, not a dramatic one. The prompt is richer if we are sometimes stuck not knowing. Her fluster is more alive if we only have her hands. His ego is more uncomfortable if we cannot duck into her understanding of it. **Competence romance.** She is never flustered in a way that makes her bad at her job for more than a sentence. He is never desired for a shallow reason. Help is refused on principle. Nobody is tempted by money, status, or a bad idea. Humans in attraction are not this well governed. **Stock geography of romance.** Rain entrance, closed sign, walk to water, phone call that interrupts the true confession, public event as climax, morning-after reckoning with the road reopened. Each is usable. In a row, they are a template wearing a Welsh place-name. **Symbol hygiene.** The inscription is scored out until the page tears, so he has learned not to make her a text. The number is on a receipt, not a flyleaf. This is the model congratulating itself for not writing the cliché, while still using the cliché’s shape. A human object is often mortifying rather than instructive: a slick line he did write, a Mars bar, a parking fine, the wrong opening time. **Prompt restatement.** “He needs to be liked more than he wants to know her” is the assignment, spoken aloud. Once a character says the prompt, the scene can only agree or upgrade it. **Fast, complete arcs.** Thirty-six hours to diagnose a lifelong habit, do penance at a poetry reading, and renegotiate the terms of being seen. That is arc speed, not human speed. In eight thousand words, a smaller change is more believable: he comes back once without a speech; she does not fully forgive him; something has shifted and neither can name it cleanly. **Dignity for all.** Nobody loses face in a way that will still be talked about on Saturday. The town is a chorus that can be managed by good behavior. Real small-town attention is stickier and less moral than that. The story is about limelight. Someone should have to live with a story they did not choose, past the last page. ## Where the intention is already leaning that way The intention is clear, and a lot of it is the right avoidance: no shop saved by celebrity, no London third act, no postcard, charm not menace. The trouble is that the cure has become a second template. “Being seen versus being known” is too complete a thesis. Every pressure is recruited to it: the film, the profile, the assistant’s phone, the reading, the ending. A human draft would let one pressure be thematic and another be merely annoying. The film about a Welsh poet is the loudest example. It doubles the authenticity problem so neatly that Rhys arrives pre-digested. He is already a man professionally guilty about Welshness. That makes Elen’s knowledge of the real poems feel like a key cut for his lock. Dumber fame — a long-running detective part, a meme, a romantic lead who dies wetly in episode six — would make her immunity more credible and his need funnier. It would also stop the bookshop from becoming a moral classroom. The prose plan is administered. Elen in the odd chapters, Rhys in the even, except she also gets the last word. Two-thirds dialogue as a quota. Welsh used sparingly as a door. These are craft rules a model can satisfy without anyone sounding alive. Distinct voice will not come from giving him long sentences and her short ones if both are still issuing thematic acts. Voice comes from what they notice, what they repeat, what they get wrong, and which banal things they say when they are buying time. “He is not allowed to save the shop” is an authorial ban rather than a dramatic fact. If the shop’s trouble never becomes concrete, the ban has nothing to push against, and her refusal of help is theoretical. If it does become concrete — a rates bill, a leak over the poetry, a landlord — then forbidding the save is interesting only if he offers the wrong help in a tempting form and she is actually tempted. Principle with no grease on it is another kind of safety. The avoid-list bans the savior plot and then the chapter list builds a modest heroism in its place: he draws the cameras off, the poet finishes, the inscription has been corrected, the touch is permitted only after the ethics have been agreed. Restraint has become the twist. That can be beautiful when it costs something ragged. Here it is in danger of reading as tastefulness. Class is named and then absent. So is prior life. So is sex. The original prompt is a romance with a charge under the talk. The intention handles charge as fluster, which is faithful to the brief, but the fluster is always legible and well managed. There is no moment yet where desire makes either of them slightly worse at being the person they think they are. The two-day clock serves containment, which is good for paparazzi, and strains the change, which is bad for character. He cannot unlearn an ego in a weekend without the story becoming a fable. Aim for a dent, not a conversion. ## Chapter by chapter **Chapter 1.** Rain, a wet famous man, a bell, a woman who will not feed him. The bones are right. The execution risks are generic entrance, and her fluster already being interpreted in the same scene as the refusal. “A part of her glad” is a narrator handing us the prompt’s inward state instead of making us catch her mis-shelving something. Pronouncing her name right as a tell is very constructed. A human first meeting would include more failed small talk and at least one moment where his charm works and she is annoyed that it worked. **Chapter 2.** Mrs Prys not recognizing him is a useful wound, and the mild lie is the best idea in the early plan. The mean joke walked back too elaborately is safety. Let the joke sit in the room for a chapter. His “do you know who I am?” is on-the-nose; a vainer man circles that question for a long time before he can bear to ask it. Missing the blush is a camera angle. If we are in his head, he should misread something less cinematic: he thinks she is cross about the display he wrecked; we suspect she is cross because she looked at his mouth. **Chapter 3.** Putting him to work is good, physical, and not a walk to a viewpoint. The dialect-coach story turning into shame about his mouth is again the thesis arriving early, and it makes him sensitively self-aware by night one. The laugh she punishes, and the tea she will not sit down to drink, are neat symbols of the same fact. One of them is enough. This chapter wants a useless disagreement — a thriller she rates and he is snobbish about — that does not map onto Wales, fame, or authenticity. **Chapter 4.** The sea wall is the template. The publicist call interrupting the confession is a screenplay beat. “The shop opens at nine” is a button placed for the finale to press. A more human after-hours might be ugly lighting in the back room, or him eating something he has to pretend he likes from the Co-op, or a B&B where he watches a clip of himself because no one clapped. If they do walk, let the walk be short and the talk worse. He should try to stage her confession and get a shrug, not a parable about leaving twice becoming a story. That line is already too quotable. **Chapter 5.** Lowri and the phone are predictable, and Elen taking the phone keeps her competent. “You can be liked somewhere else” and “come as nobody” hand him his lesson title. The coldness is right; the articulation is early. A human Elen might go rude and practical — “Put that down, Lowri, he’s not signing anything, and you, out” — and only later realize she sounded possessive. Let Lowri keep some agency. If the photo happens, Elen does not get to be the person who stopped history. **Chapter 6.** This is the plan’s most model-shaped scene. She says the quiet part in a few accurate sentences. He answers with a confession that is still a pitch, which is good, then she names the pitch, which is the seminar. His return blow — that her immunity is also a performance — is the most human line in the plan, because it is partly true and not fair. Do not cushion it. Then he does “a small stupid thing” and knows it as he does it. That knowledge is the safety rail. Delay the self-disgust until it is too late to be charming. Make the stupid thing concrete enough that chapter 7 cannot fully undo it: a name said in the caffi, a text that sends a photographer to Thursday, a joke that uses her. Vague penance is how a model avoids making its lead unlikeable. **Chapter 7.** A reading that must be protected from becoming a set is a strong pressure, and then the plan turns it into his modest redemption. Drawing attention away “just enough that the poet finishes” is heroism in flat shoes. The protest that it is not a grand gesture is how you can tell it is one. The torn inscription and the number on the receipt are over-cleaned symbols. A human aftermath might be smaller and worse: six people came, Anwen was difficult, Rhys laughed at the wrong line, Elen is furious, the shop smells of wet coats, and whatever he left her is embarrassing rather than instructive. Also, if Anwen is only “real culture,” the story flatters Elen’s side. Give the poet an ego. Two rogues in one lane would do more than a purity test. **Chapter 8.** Mutual admission, terms of engagement, a repeated line with a twist, a permitted touch, an exit that refuses to be watched, a last ordinary gesture so the limelight does not win. This is a bow, however quietly tied. “She will not be an anecdote” is a position paper. “Come to the door as a person” is the theme in invitation form. The label corrected at the end tells the reader what the story meant. A human last chapter might let the callback fail — he tries “you open at nine,” she hears the writer in him and goes flat — or skip the callback entirely. It might end on a decision that is not yet a relationship: she texts him a time, or she does not, and we feel which one it is without a speech. If there is a touch, it should be specific and a little clumsy, and it should not function as a seal of ethical approval. The plan’s touch is a reward for having said the right sentences. Across the eight, the turns are evenly spaced, morally educational, and reversible. Nothing stains. That evenness will read as designed even if the sentences are good. ## Brainstorm: making it more human These are options, not a new outline. The aim is dirt, unevenness, and desire, without throwing out the brief. **Let the charm work once, early, and let her hate that.** If every line dies, the story is a machine proving the prompt. One genuine laugh in chapter 1, which she then spends the rest of the day taxing him for, is more destabilizing than continuous immunity. His derailment matters more if he has felt the old power and then lost it in the same room. **Make the fame less noble.** A poet biopic ties every scene to authenticity. A naff, specific celebrity — catchphrase, old clip, a topless scene she has unfortunately seen, a detective who always squints — gives her something to mock and him something petty to defend. He can still be in Wales for a job. The job does not have to be the theme in costume. **Delay insight.** Nobody should accurately describe the dynamic before the last third, and maybe not then. Elen’s truest line might be “Stop doing the voice,” or “You’re standing like someone is holding a camera,” not a paragraph about being known. Rhys’s truest moment might be asking a real question by accident and then ruining it. Cut any line that could be printed under the title. **Slow the repentance.** If he is cheap in the caffi or on the phone, he should try to manage it, lie about it, or discover she already knows. Self-disgust that arrives on cue is still a performance. Let him be forgiven less than he expects, or not on the page. **Give the betrayal a residue.** A photo that exists. A regular who stays away. Lowri sulking because Elen grabbed her phone. Anwen delighted by the fuss and therefore angry at Elen for suppressing it. The last chapter should not be able to vacuum this up. **Clog them with prior life.** Not speeches. A name in her phone she does not want him to see. His driver’s abandoned car. An ex who works at the garage. A mother who will hear. A boiler that needs switching off if he is going to be stuck. Age-anxious career fear — late thirties, a part he cannot afford to lose — will feed his ego more plausibly than an abstract hunger to be liked. **Put class and money in the objects, not in a speech.** His coat, her card machine, the price of a hardback, the film unit renting every cottage, him trying to pay for a problem in a way that is both generous and insulting. Let her be tempted. Principle is more human when it wobbles. **Bodily, unsexy, and sexy.** He is hungry. She needs the loo in her own shop and resents him for being between her and the back. Cold hands, a paper cut, a laugh that snorts, a near-kiss that bumps teeth, desire that arrives while he is being slightly ridiculous. Decide what the touch in the last movement actually is. “A brief touch” is euphemism, and euphemism here reads as nervousness about genre. The prompt asked for romance. A clumsy kiss that makes the subsequent talk worse would serve it better than a ratified hand on a sleeve. **Let her fluster make her incompetent.** Wrong change. A sharp word to the wrong customer. Recommending a book she has not read because she wants him in the poetry bay and away from her face. Googling him after close and then being short with him for what she found, which is its own confession. **Let him be vain in ways that do not become shame poetry.** Checking the window. Repeating a review and pretending he is joking. Asking if the rain has ruined the hair. Flirting with Mrs Prys for practice and realizing too late that Elen saw the switch flip. The rogue should occasionally be enjoying himself, not only bleeding. **Uneven structure.** One chapter that is mostly shop admin with the attraction sitting in the room like a third person. One short chapter that is a phone call, or him alone failing to sleep. Do not give every chapter a turn of equal moral weight. Allow a scene whose only yield is that they got through forty minutes without him performing, and he did not notice, and she did. **Break the scenic route.** Replace the sea wall with somewhere fluorescent: the stockroom, a chip queue, a B&B hallway, the doorway while she locks up, a car that will not start. Limelight is more ironic under tube lighting than on a wall above the sea. **Complicate the locals.** Mrs Prys can fancy him and be shrewd about it. Lowri can post anyway, or ask him for rent money advice, or already know his ex’s Instagram. Anwen can want the cameras. If the town is not a pure place he might stain, Elen’s protectiveness becomes possessive, snobbish, or frightened, which is more interesting than custodial. **Welsh as habit, not key.** If it stays, let it be routine: a greeting, a number, a swear, a conversation he catches one word of and misinterprets. Avoid the locked-room metaphor as a repeated beat. And do not invent picturesque place-names as a substitute for knowledge. A plain fictional street with real textures — Co-op, chapel-now-a-house, A-road flood, radio rugby — will feel more lived-in than Porthllew and Siop y Felin, which already sound chosen for their soft Welshness. **Stupider objects.** A note with a typo. A book he inscribed slickly, so she now owns the crime. Biscuits he bought for the reading that nobody ate. His number saved under a fake name and then saved properly, which is the actual romantic event. If a symbol remains, it should embarrass the symbol-maker. **Let the ending be unbalanced.** She can want him and still refuse the profile without delivering a charter. He can ask badly. One of them can be more in it than the other. The last line can be ordinary without explaining why ordinariness is the point — she undercharges someone, the bell goes, she does not look at the door. If a repeated line must return, let it sour, so we see him trying to write the scene and her declining to be in that draft. **Smaller change, stain left in.** He is still a man who needs liking. She is still more moved than she will say. What has changed is local and maybe temporary: he did one unphotographed thing, or he failed to, and she knows which. That is enough for this length. A full cure will feel like the model finishing its worksheet. **Read-aloud test, when prose starts.** If a line could caption the chapter, cut it. If both characters would be at home in the same essay, the voices have not split. If a paragraph makes the theme clearer than the scene did, it is helping the reader too much. Leave one joke that does not land and is not revisited. Leave one fact that never pays off: the uncle’s van, the damp in the corner, the name of the photographer. Human attention does not reconcile its books. The plan as it stands would produce a competent, gentle, symmetrical romance about performance. The prompt can hold something livelier: a funny, slightly unfair attraction in a shop that has to keep trading while two people fail to behave as well as they think they are behaving. The human version is less sure what it means, more specific about what it wants, and a little stained at the end.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention A dialogue-led romance of about eight thousand words, mostly one scene per chapter, set over three ordinary days in off-season Cardigan. The shop is Vaughan Books, a side-street livelihood with a sticky bell and a dead February, not a destination. Wales is the weather, the high street, bilingual chat with customers, and the speed of local talk. It is not scenery and not a lesson in authenticity. Rhys Calder, 39, is known for eight series as a sarcastic TV detective with a catchphrase people do back at him, plus one soggy romantic film he hopes she has not seen. He is between jobs and in the area because a unit is filming up the coast. He has ducked the co-star rumour and walked into a new one. The rogue is flirtation, vanity, a mean joke, theatrical generosity, and a public lie he tells himself is kindness. He is not a menace, and a clear no about being touched or posed with is a no. His ego still needs feeding. He would rather be liked than left in a room where the laugh died. Charm is his craft: long sentences, self-deprecation that asks to be corrected, a precise compliment, the same joke upgraded when it fails. It derails when she does not clap. That is when he starts wanting her, and wanting makes him worse at the craft, not cured of it. Elen Vaughan, 42, owns the shop. Dry, specific, funny without smiling. She knows his face and declines to treat that as an event. She is not a wall and not a moral guardian of the town. Early on, one unplanned joke gets a real laugh out of her. She spends the rest of the story taxing him for it. The inward fluster is never explained as a theme. It shows up as incompetence: the wrong book, the wrong change, tea she regrets offering, a lock she holds too long, his jacket under the counter so no one will see it. What gets to her is not the fame. It is the moment the performance drops, and also, annoyingly, the moment it works. Voice stays in the talk. Close third, mostly Elen, so the prompt’s inward charm is available as botched action and the odd plain thought, not as metaphor. Two chapters sit nearer Rhys — the second, when the failed charm turns into want, and the sixth, when he does something cheap and does not repent on cue. No even alternation, no fairness quota. His lines run long and get shorter when he is wrong-footed. Hers are prices, stock, and corrections, and they spill when she is moved. Welsh is habit with regulars, a greeting or a number, not a locked door. Prose stays plain. If a sentence could caption the chapter, it does not go in. One pressure only, and it is allowed to be merely annoying as well as exposing: a single freelance photographer, Chris, who also shoots weddings, plus Lowri, the Saturday girl, who wants a photo for her mam. The stain is small and local and does not get hoovered up. A slow winter sits in the background so his offer to “bring people in” is tempting and wrong. He does not save the shop. No poet film, no homecoming profile, no landlord plot, no London third act. The change is a dent. He is still a man who needs liking. She will not perform wanting him. By the end something private and uneven has started, and a photo she did not choose still exists. Nobody states the prompt. Nobody is rewarded for having the right sentence ready. Aim for readable talk, embarrassment, appetite, and a joke that fails and is not reused. Avoid the bow, the seminar, scenic water, symbol hygiene, modest heroism, a rogue sanded down into a lesson, and impressive prose. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Wet coat (Elen).** Rain, a motorbike at the kerb, a man pretending to browse. He charms the room. She answers with prices. A line dies. He upgrades it. She lets it die. Then an unplanned stupid joke — a Welsh-language paperback he cannot read, a crack about detectives — gets a real laugh. She is harder on him immediately after, and hands him the wrong book. Chris at the glass. She sends Rhys into the back bay because wet coats wreck stock and the photographer is blocking the door, not because he is welcome. She hears herself offer tea and regrets it before the kettle is on. He hears interest. She will not look at his mouth. **Chapter 2 — Leave it with me (Rhys).** He has decided to win her. He restacks a table badly, overpays, fishes. Beti Jones, a regular, does not know him, then does, and quotes the catchphrase. He feeds on it and flirts with Beti on autopilot. Elen sees the switch and is abrupt with the till. After Beti goes he makes a small mean joke about a town knowing your business by lunchtime. It was about himself. It lands on the shop. He does not walk it back cleanly, and she does not rescue him. He circles the question of being known. She says she watched one series with flu and the detective talks too much. That stings worse than ignorance. He misreads her colour as anger about the display. He stays because he cannot bear the missing clap, and tells himself it is the cameras. **Chapter 3 — Returns (Elen).** His driver has gone. The car can sit. She puts him on returns so he is out of the window. Talk stays on paperbacks. He sneers at a thriller, then finds his own name on the back in small type. She had not clocked it. The moment is awkward and funny, not a confession about fame. Too close in the stockroom. She gives a customer the wrong change because he is in the doorway. She laughs once when he makes a mess of the tape, then is brisk about the mess. Tea. She sits by accident and stands up again. He does not pounce on the laugh. That flusters her more than the charm did. A set anecdote starts in his mouth and dies for lack of an audience. The boiler knocks. Neither of them fixes it. **Chapter 4 — Sandwiches (Elen).** After close, strip light, Co-op sandwiches he paid too much for. She clocks the price and eats anyway. He says one true small thing: he left the unit hotel because a photo with the co-star would have been a lie he was tired of, and he has made a different photo instead. He tries to steer her into a matching confession. She tells him the shop was her aunt’s. His publicist comes through the phone, speaker by accident. He does the client voice. She keeps eating. She is not a hotel. The B&B is on the high street. He is charming at the door. She shuts it on the sentence. Her hand stays on the lock too long. **Chapter 5 — Lowri (Elen).** Morning. He is back for a jacket he will manage to leave, and for her. Lowri is starstruck. He lights up. The charm is real and indiscriminate, which is the unpleasant part. Elen is short with the wrong regular. Lowri asks for a photo for her mam. Elen says no. Rhys says it’s only Lowri, let her have it. Lowri takes it. Elen is too late to stop the phone and will not wrestle a nineteen-year-old. He does not understand the size of it. She tells him he is in the way. He leaves smiling, which is worse. No speech about being nobody. **Chapter 6 — Fan (Rhys).** On the pavement he meets Chris and handles him. To be liked, and to kill a romance headline, he says Elen is a fan, very kind, no story. He feels protective and a little slick. Disgust does not arrive. He goes back in to tell her it is handled. She has heard enough through the door. He repeats the fan line as reassurance. She goes cold and says not to call her a fan, and not to call her anything. He tries charm, then a confession that is still a pitch. She does not pick up the cue and does not diagnose him. From the wound he gets petty and partly accurate: she likes the shutting of the door. It is a bit of a performance too. She does not answer. He leaves thinking he was honest and she was cruel. **Chapter 7 — Dead February (Elen).** Same day, later. Looky-loos. A nephew text. Lowri sulking. Someone says “lucky you” and does not buy a book. Elen recommends a novel she has not read and snaps at a person who was only browsing. Rhys comes to the back with a bad apology and an offer to do a signing, bring people in, February is dead, let him help. It is tempting and insulting. She refuses, not nobly. He explains he did not want Chris writing it the other way, then adds a joke and ruins the sentence. She tells him to go. He goes, and leaves the jacket. She puts it under the counter so the shop will not have a famous coat on a chair. She looks at Lowri’s post. She does not make Lowri take it down yet. **Chapter 8 — Jacket (Elen).** Next morning. Cameras thinner. He comes back because the jacket is there and the car is still at her cousin’s garage, and because he wants her to like him again. A charming sentence starts and stops. The apology is incomplete: the fan line was cowardice, and he half liked sounding wanted. She does not absolve him and does not issue terms. She is visibly flustered, denies it badly, and tells him he can text if he can do it without being clever. She writes the number on whatever paper is by the till because his phone is in the jacket. He leans in as she turns to the till. Mouths bump. Both swear. The bell goes. They spring apart. He takes the coat and does not play the exit. She watches anyway, then gets a customer’s change wrong. Lowri’s photo is still up. He is not fixed. She has not said she wanted that kiss. The shop has to keep trading.

Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc

# Rhys Calder Thirty-nine. Born in Aberdare, gone at eighteen, and the accent mostly went with him. What is left comes out on short words when he is rattled, and he hears it a second after everyone else does. His mam, Glenys, still lives in the same terrace. He pays for the boiler and misses Christmas more often than he means to. She sends him links. He replies with a voice note that sounds like a man leaving a message for a producer. He is known for DI Adam Vickers on *Harbour Road*, eight series, a squint, and the line “Leave it with me.” People say it back to him in queues. He hates it, and he waits for it. There is also *Low Water*, a wet romantic film in which he dies in the rain with his shirt open. The still circulates more than the performance. He is between jobs. The unit up the coast is not his. He was visiting someone on it, a co-star the papers have already half-married him to, and he left the hotel because he could feel the photograph arriving. That flight is the most honest thing he has done this month, and he has already spoiled it by being seen somewhere else. Charm is a trade he learned before he learned to act, and he is better at it. He finds the one thing a person is proud of and hands it back to them, polished. He is funny at his own expense in a way that invites you to let him off. He remembers a detail from three sentences ago and returns it like a gift. If the gift is not opened he does not sit with the silence. He upgrades the joke, then gets a little mean, then overpays for something. The meanness is small and fast. In a green room once he mocked a director’s accent to get a laugh from a room that was slipping from him, and spent a fortnight being beloved at everyone to undo it. He still thinks of that as damage control, not as the actual event. He needs the room to like him the way other people need a light on. A regular who does not recognise him unsettles him more than an insult. A woman who recognises him and does not brighten unsettles him worse. He will flirt with a customer he has no interest in because applause is transferable, and he will not notice the switch until it is too late. He checks his reflection in shop windows and pretends he was reading the display. He quotes a review that called him “serviceable” as if it were a joke he is over. He is not over it. At thirty-nine the hunger is not abstract. If the next part does not come, he does not know what he is for. Being liked is how he checks he is still here. He is a coward about being unwanted, and generous with money in a way that ranks people. He tells small lies to keep a mood intact and calls them kindness. The fan line he will give a photographer is typical: it sounds like protection, it costs her more than it costs him, and he half believes it on the way out of his mouth. He can hear himself pitching a confession. He cannot always stop. He is not cruel as a habit. He is cheap in a panic, and the apology tries to arrive in the same costume as the offence. Trivial tells, which he would deny: he tongues a chipped molar when he is about to lie. He says a person’s name too often. He eats the biscuit before the sandwich and then apologises to the sandwich. He cannot bear loose-leaf tea and will make a whole speech about not being fussy while asking for a bag. His phone is full of drafts to Sadie, his publicist, written before he has spoken to anyone who was actually in the room. He stands as if someone has marked his place on the floor. When a laugh does not come he talks over the place where it should have been. He wants, from his own side of it: to get out of the rain without a photograph Sadie has to eat; to be liked by the one person who did not do the catchphrase; to feel the old click of a room giving way. Under that, ugly and new, he wants Elen. The want arrives when the click fails, which he did not order and does not know how to use. He is not looking to be known. He would settle for adored. The problem is she will not do it, and he stays anyway. Sadie is the person he is most loyal to, and she is paid to be. His mam gets the boiler and a version of events. The driver who left him in Cardigan is already a story he is telling differently. There is an ex, Lara, who said he performed even when there was nobody else there. He thinks that was unkind. He also sometimes checks. No one current. Arrangements, a few of them half publicity, none of them likely to drive to Ceredigion. His allegiance, if forced, runs job, mood, then whoever is standing in front of him. Elen disrupts the order and he resents the disruption at the same time as he chases it. He is just under six foot and used to folding himself down in small rooms, which reads as courtesy and is also a move. Dark hair, expensive cut, ruined by rain; he keeps touching it. Handsome in the way profiles call lived-in, and more ordinary across a till: good mouth, tired eyes, a face that has been lit from its better side for a decade. The smile arrives before the joke. That is the tell. Navy coat that costs more than the shop takes on a wet Wednesday, soft jumper, boots chosen to look unchosen. Hands do too much, then vanish into pockets. Voice trained, warmer than his face, dropping half an octave when he wants something. Mostly a London-actor voice now. On a swear or a “yeah,” Aberdare. He moves like a man who expects to be watched and is trying, today, to look as if he has forgotten that. “No, that’s— I’m not heckling the town. I’ve heckled myself in worse rooms. Smaller rooms. That sounded worse. I’ll pay for this twice, shall I, and we’ll call it even.” “Leave it with me. Don’t— I heard it. You don’t have to do the voice. God, I’m doing the voice. Sadie, I’m in a shop. I’m not in a shop with anyone. I’m buying a book like a person.” He catches his own eye in the dark of the window and thinks, don’t. Then he does. If she saw that, he will die, and if she didn’t, he will have to be funnier. # Elen Vaughan Forty-two. Cardigan born, back from a stretch in Swansea where she did the sorts of jobs you describe by the rota rather than the title. Library shifts, a bookshop chain, a flat with a rotating third housemate. She came home because her aunt Nerys was ill, not because she had a theory about home. Nerys died two years ago and left her the lease and the stock and a drawer of supplier notes written in pencil. Elen stayed because the lease was in her name by then, February was coming, and she could not face another room where the plates were shared. She does not turn this into a story about leaving twice. If asked she says the shop was her aunt’s and the van was already taxed. Vaughan Books is a side street off the high street. Dead in February, faithful the rest of the year to people who want a thriller for a ferry and people who want to talk. She pays Lowri when she can. She knows what the rates letter looks like before she opens it. She is a reader, not a writer, and she is not romantic about paper. She reads the last page of crime novels in the stockroom, a private vice, and will recommend Denise Mina to someone who asks for “something with a dead wife, but good.” She watched one series of *Harbour Road* with flu. She has seen the wet still from *Low Water* and has no plan to tell him that. Celebrity, to her, is other people making a noise in a doorway. It is not interesting. It is in the way. The immunity is partly real. She has been the audience for a charming man before, and she got tired first. It is also a stance she grabs after her own face betrays her. A real laugh got out of her once, through her nose, which she hates, and she has been sterner with him since, as if the till were a court. She is inwardly more thrown than she will admit to anyone, including herself. The fluster is not a glow. It is incompetence. Wrong change. Wrong book. Tea she hears herself offer. A lock held after the door is shut. His jacket under the counter so the chair will not have a famous coat on it. She gets blotchy at the neck and talks about publication dates. She is dry, specific, funny without performing it. She says “right” as punctuation. She calls people by their full names when she is cross. She straightens a book that is already straight when she needs a second. Milk goes in first; Nerys hated that, and Elen still hears it. There is a biro behind her ear more often than not. She eats standing up. She swears in Welsh under her breath, small and automatic, when a pile falls. She is loyal to regulars and short with people who treat the shop as a set. She undercharges people she is fond of and is then irritable with them for it. Flaws she would not put on a list: she is proud. She is snappish, and sometimes the snap lands on the wrong customer. She holds a grudge past the point where it is doing any work. Her protection of Lowri is also control. She can be a snob about noise, and about men who think attention is a present. She is lonely in a practical, unadvertised way, and she treats that loneliness as a preference because a preference does not have to be talked about. She is slow to admit wanting, and unfair once she has wanted something. If he makes her laugh again she will make him pay for the first time as well. She wants, from her own side: to get through the week without the shop becoming a story; to keep Lowri from doing something that cannot be undone; not to be explained to a man with a camera. She also wants Rhys to keep being slightly hopeless in her doorway, and she is angry that she wants it. She will not join his publicity, and she will not give a speech about why. She just won’t. Under the refusal is appetite, embarrassment, and the plain fact that it has been a while since anyone looked at her as if the next sentence she said was the point. Nerys is still the person she argues with. Her mam, in a bungalow toward Newcastle Emlyn, will hear about any photograph before Elen has decided what it was. Her cousin Gareth has the garage and will take the piss for a year if a shiny car stays on his forecourt. Lowri Price, nineteen, works Saturdays and some after-school hours, is starstruck, and is not a child; Elen is fond of her and bad at showing it except as wages and warnings. Beti Jones knows everyone’s business and is not unkind. There is an ex, Marc, ended four years ago, not a villain. He wanted Bristol and a bigger life. She felt mean for not wanting it with him, and still gets a Christmas text she answers late. A friend, Siân, at the library, will text three words and a screenshot. No one in her daily life is going to experience this as a fairy tale. They are going to experience it as news. She is not tall and not small, practical in the body, a grey in the fringe she is not paying to fix until March. Dark hair in a clip. Hands dry from paper and the cold shop, a plaster on one finger from a split thumbnail. Cardigan, boots, sometimes the apron if she has been moving stock. A bad knee from a ladder last winter; she will not mention it and will not sit down to favour it if sitting down means sitting with him. Alert face, mouth ready to disagree. She looks at the book in her hand when she is listening, which reads as indifference. When she looks up it is direct and a beat too long, then away. The blush is blotchy, not decorative. She moves as if she knows where every pile is. The glitch in that efficiency is the only confession she makes. “It’s four ninety-nine. You’ve put a ten down on a paperback. I’m not a hotel.” “Right. Don’t do the squint in here. There’s no room. Lowri, if that phone comes up again you’re stacking the returns, I don’t care whose mam it is.” She thinks: do not offer tea. She offers tea. She thinks about his mouth and immediately about the boiler, which has been knocking since January, and which at least is a problem she understands.

Chapter 1 The bell stuck halfway and gave its sour little ring. She was on the returns. A damp Dan Brown she was not putting out. Rain since nine, and a motorbike idling at the kerb, camera bag on the rider’s chest, as if the side street owed him someone. Rhys Calder came in too quick, collar up. He didn’t look behind him until the door had shut, and then only the once. “Shut the door.” “Yes. Sorry.” He got it shut with his shoulder. The smile was already on, ahead of the sentence. “I’m browsing. That is what this is. You’ve got books, I need a book, the rain’s been having opinions about me since the high street.” She knew the face. Telly over the till in the caffi, three lunchtimes last winter, not interesting then either. Water came off the navy coat onto the ferry table. The coat had cost more than the table would take in a week. The mat took the drip and gave up. “Mat’s there.” “Doing God’s work, that mat. I’ll stand on it and admire you.” He heard it. He went on, because a gap would have shown. “The shop. This is a proper shop. People like me are always saying we’ve found a hidden gem. You ought to have a jar for it. Fines. I’d pay.” “Jar’s for the lifeboat.” He waited. Nothing. “Second jar, then. Crimes against bookshops. I’ll put a twenty in and tell them I was mugged.” The twenty went on the counter, not entirely as a joke. “There. I’ve paid ahead for being unbearable. Does that work on a Friday, or only in London?” “Four ninety-nine,” Elen said, “if you’ve ruined that one.” A Fine Dark had a wet corner. “And no. I’m not a hotel.” “No,” he said. The smile caught up late. “No, you’re not. You were meant to give me a little something, though. Not much. I’m easy. Most people manage a smile.” “You’re on my mat in a coat that cost more than I took yesterday. I wouldn’t call it easy.” “So you do like the coat.” “I like dry paper. Card machine’s there, if you’re buying. It doesn’t always work.” He got off the mat. Wet hair, a spine, wet hair again. Once he looked at the glass, then at the shelves, quick, as if the shelves had been the plan. The Welsh shelf was nearest. He opened a thin paperback, red lighthouse, no English anywhere, and frowned at a line that would not help. “Is there a murder in this?” he said. “I’m only any use if there’s been a murder. Even then I mostly squint.” She laughed through her nose. One short honk. The heat went up her neck so fast she turned it into a cough, and the biro slipped from behind her ear and clicked on the floor. She straightened a book that was already straight and left the biro where it was. “Put that back,” she said. “You’re not buying it. We don’t sell that shelf to people who hold it open like a menu. Put it back.” “I was having a go.” He looked delighted, which was worse. “I’ll get that.” “Leave it.” She took the paperback off him and put another in his hands without looking. “That, then. Four ninety-nine. Same as the one you’ve wrecked, so you can pay for that and go. Don’t do the squint in here. There’s no room.” He looked down. Angling in Brief. Yellow. Nerys had ordered three by mistake and the mistake was still in the shop. “Perfect,” he said, too warm. “I love a fish. I’ll read it cover to cover on your mat. You laughed, mind. I’m not letting a laugh go past. I don’t get them for nothing. I have to have done something first.” “I coughed. Don’t lean on the table. You’re soaking the stock.” At the glass the rider had his visor up. Chris had his palm flat to the window. He did weddings, when anyone was getting married. The bell shivered though the door stayed shut. Rhys stopped smiling. It came back a moment late. “Friend of yours?” “He’ll get bored. He gets bored at weddings.” She nodded at the back, ceiling low over the poetry. “In there. Wet coats ruin paper, and I’m not having him in the door as well as you. Mind your head. It drips if you’re tall.” “I’ll be so quiet you’ll forget I’m anyone,” he said. “I can do quiet. I’m versatile.” “I haven’t said you were anyone.” “You don’t have to. People get a face on when they know and they won’t hand it over. Very still. Very shop.” “That face is waiting to mop. In there.” “Right. Poetry. Very sorry. Thank you.” He glanced at the window. “Is there tea, or do I have to have been better?” The kettle was cold. The twenty stayed on the counter. She got two mugs down, put one back, and got it down again. The second one was chipped on the rim, and still in use. “There’s tea,” she said. “If you’re quiet about it.” Sorry at once. She pressed the switch anyway. He was already under the beam. “I knew you didn’t mind me,” he said. “Kind face. That’s not a line. It is a line. I’ll have the tea and be sorry after, proper order.” “Don’t talk to me from in there.” “All right.” The kettle ticked. He lasted less than that. “Is it a bag? Say it’s a bag. I’m not fussy. I only can’t do the leaves. They get in your teeth, and then you’re talking to someone with a leaf on you, and that’s the photograph. Sadie would have an actual fit.” “It’s a bag,” Elen said. “Stop.” Outside, the bike was still idling. Chris tapped the glass, once. She lifted a hand the way she did at wasps, and kept her eyes on the kettle. If she turned she’d be looking at his mouth. She didn’t turn.
