# Intention A third-person limited story, past tense, held close to Arthur Neegan and written in a calm, slightly formal classic-sf register: institutional manners, dry understatement, and no pulp garnish. Big and small share the same sentences when it counts — a contract date beside a half-life, pit boots on a diplomatic deck — but the history of the rush is never lectured. Retrofuture detail is social and material (paper charters, assay books, filament light, radio protocol, dosimeters, a diplomatic pennant on a military hatch), never costume slang. The spine is a signature, not a chase. Arthur, a first-generation mining engineer, is escorted from his lease to an Antares packet station in high Mars orbit. Factor Leona Quist, of the Office of Strategic Materials, makes the offer. She is not a mask; the mystery is what his consent legally does. Lieutenant Havel commands the retinue: courteous, armed, colonial-born, more informed than he says, never quite a jailer and never a secret mastermind. The opposing pressure is Northreach Combine, mostly paper and one late voice, racing an inspection barge to absorb the lease by ordinary seizure. One indentured driller, Moss Pettit, carries the human ledger. No other factions appear onstage. Azra is explained once, through an object and a correction. Unprocessed and cold, it is shippable; heated and concentrated, its lattice hastens decay in whatever radioactives sit nearby. Arthur’s vein is real and immense. Worked under the domes, it ruins a sector. Lifted cold, under quarantine, it still feeds drives and weapons — slower, and audited, not stopped. That is the story’s one rule, and Arthur is qualified to test it. Quist’s offer is polite and specific: assign the extraction rights, come up as consulting engineer, take the pension and the passage. She will not say “weapon.” Under the colonial compact, a voluntary assay-release lets her skip the public hearing that would start a rush beside the domes. The same schedule’s appurtenance clause assigns his crew, and a rider gives Ordnance first refusal on refined output. She is partly right about the danger and wholly interested in the paper. Her gambit is the sacrifice of Arthur’s obscurity: draw the discoverer up under diplomatic color, so his presence reads as consent before the barge arrives. Arthur’s counter is engineer’s literalism, not escape. He certifies the in-situ danger, which she wants, and signs a narrow release — cold lift, quarantine conditions he remains bound to enforce — while striking persons and refined-output rights, witnessed before a compact notary so the form cannot be quietly widened. Manners never collapse into thuggery. There is no battle, no fleet, no forged vein, no secret identity, no revolution, and no second explanation of the metal. The ending is intellectually complete and emotionally unsolved: both gambits work; the ore moves; Moss is not sold; Arthur keeps the post he did not want, because the cordon holds only while he does. Chapter 1 opens already aboard the transfer vessel, the invitation replayed rather than staged as the start. The offer is withheld until the next chapter, where it is mostly dialogue, vivid, and incomplete. Each later chapter turns once. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1.** Aboard the transfer packet, Mars shrinking in a small port, Arthur turns over the hour he keeps replaying: the retinue at his door, Antares insignia, Havel’s courtesy and the weapons that did not need pointing. He does not know the offer yet, only that refusal was not among the phrases used. Two calendars, a round deadline, a rumor of a hot borehole on the neighboring lease. The chapter ends as the station’s hatch protocol begins. **Chapter 2.** The reception room. Quist beside him, not across a desk; tea in a bulb; his plot already tinted on her map. Mostly dialogue. She offers assignment, a consulting post, passage, a pension, and speaks of safety, hearing, and haste. She will not say weapon. He asks who else has been invited, and what becomes of the names on his payroll, and receives smooth non-answers. A light and Havel at the door prove the meeting is not private. He leaves knowing the ask and not the future it buys. **Chapter 3.** He is not returned. A short decay bench: his own core sample, a dosimeter, a spoiled medical isotope. Someone softens what the curve means; he corrects them. Quist lets the demonstration stand in for a briefing. An inspection notice from Northreach arrives, dated to a barge four ship-days out. The hearing, if he refuses, would post just as publicly. One clock. **Chapter 4.** Radio lag to the camp. Moss Pettit, one contract date, the practical meaning of reassignment if the lease changes hands. Arthur is given the release to “look over” and reads the schedule: appurtenances, and the ordnance rider Quist had folded into urgency. The offer curdles without a speech. Havel, still polite, does not pretend the form is news to him. **Chapter 5.** Arthur states the compact back to Quist: his willingness skips the hearing; the hearing means a rush under the domes; heat and concentration make the vein a slow bomb; cold lift is the less-bad door; the same paper moves his crew and feeds Ordnance. She does not deny it. She calls that clarity, and asks him to sign before the barge. He asks for the charter text and a compact notary, not her clerk. **Chapter 6.** He drafts the narrow instrument — certification of in-situ danger, release for cold lift only, quarantine conditions tied to his own continuing authority — and strikes persons and refined-output rights. The obstacle is procedural: Havel must witness, the notary must be the compact’s, and Northreach’s barge will make any delay look like forfeiture. Quist offers a broader form and a kinder tone. He declines without raising his voice. **Chapter 7.** The signing. Quist shows the gambit: his obscurity was the piece she advanced, a first-generation discoverer being the only competent volunteer who was not already Northreach’s. Inspector Calder protests from a screen, too late and too interested in appurtenances. Arthur signs the narrow copy in front of the notary; Havel witnesses because diplomatic procedure will not let him refuse. The reader sees the width of the paper a beat before Quist does. Courtesy holds, and is worse for holding. **Chapter 8.** Quiet consequence. The narrow release stands. Arthur goes down once, to his own pit head, and posts the cordon himself: dust, his boots, Moss unassigned and out of work, the camp emptying into a quarantine he must stay to enforce. Cold ore will lift. Drives and weapons will still have Azra, slower and under audit. The large picture has moved by a hair; his life has been assigned. He cannot tell whether he played a gambit or only chose which hand advanced him.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
A human writing from the original prompt would probably start from Arthur’s vanity and fear, not from a mechanism. The prompt offers a gold rush, an arms race, indenture, a polite abduction, and a talky offer; it does not offer a puzzle box. A human homage to Asimov would also hear a prose problem the plan solves too elegantly: Asimov is plain, stiff, sometimes even clumsy, and his cleverness arrives late, spoken by people who want something. Modern “vivid description” and Asimov are in tension. A person would likely pick the stiffness, and let vividness mean one true object — a dosimeter, a bad bulb of tea, a core that smells of hot stone — rather than a cinematic Mars. They might not know, at chapter 1, how the paper would be worded. They might discover in the middle that the interesting pressure is not Northreach’s barge but Arthur’s wish to be the man who found the vein, or Moss’s wish to be sold to the higher bidder. Humans let the better chapter demote the outline. They also write unevenly: one chapter wanders, one is almost only talk, one ends on a line that doesn’t know it is an ending. The eight-chapter shape would be a container, not a series of locked turns. **Telltale machine habits, and why they blunt this piece** Smoothness is the big one. Every sentence does work, every image returns as a motif, every character is the right amount of morally legible. Real prose has spare parts: a gripe, a repeated word, a fact nobody needs. On a story this short, total efficiency makes the architecture show through the walls. Safety is next. Exploitation is acknowledged, then arranged so the decent man can refuse complicity and the reader can admire him. Weapons stay abstract and “audited.” Nobody is cheap, horny, superstitious, or stupidly greedy. A colonial gold rush with the ugliness rinsed out becomes a seminar about a gold rush. The bow is a related habit. The last page states the irony the plot has already proved. Asimov does like a click — that part of the brief is real — but his click is usually a revealed implication, not a balanced verdict on the protagonist’s soul. Machine endings often do both: the system is indicted, the hero is exonerated, the last sentence writes the essay. Impressiveness crowds readability. Legal terms, institutional titles, and neatly paired abstractions (“charter and contract,” “large and small”) feel like thought and can be fog. Asimov restates. He lets a character say the plain version, sometimes twice, sometimes badly. A story that is ashamed of plainness will not sound like him, and at a thousand words a chapter it will not have room for people. Other tells that would show immediately here: dialogue in which every reply is a perfect deflection; the stock Mars senses (ochre, ozone, recycled air, copper); triads of worldbuilding props; “not X, but Y” profundity; a threshold hook at the end of every chapter; the title’s metaphor threaded to a final question; an antagonist who explains her gambit on schedule; a symbolic pair of boots walking through the theme. **Where the intention and plan already lean that way** The cast size, the refusal of a battle, and the decision to explain the metal once are sound. They are not the problem. The problem is that the remaining story is a clean machine with a moral alibi. Arthur is never wrong. He asks the ethical question in the first meeting, catches the rider, demands the correct class of notary, drafts the exact instrument, and declines without raising his voice. That is a procedural superhero. An engineer can be precise about rock and still vain, legalistic for the wrong reason, slow to see people, and embarrassed by spin-gravity nausea. If his competence spreads from stone to statute to ethics on a timetable, he will feel designed. Asimov’s prigs are often slightly ridiculous. This Arthur is only admirable. The ending is labeled unresolved and is in fact solved. Moss is not assigned. The domes are spared. Ordnance is slowed and audited. Arthur keeps a tragic post, which is the acceptable price. “He cannot tell whether he played a gambit or only chose which hand advanced him” is a thesis line already written. Readers will feel the bow even if the sentence is cut, because the plot has acquitted him. A tug of war that ends with the hero holding the only decent rope is not a tug of war. Quist is the balanced antagonist: partly right, structurally motivated, never cheap. Havel is the midpoint man, neither jailer nor traitor, whose one plot use is that procedure forces him to witness. Moss is a ledger with a name. Calder appears on a screen to lose. None of them wants something petty. None of them is bad at their job in an ordinary way. The plan knows what each figure means, so they will speak as functions unless something unnecessary is allowed to stick to them. The politics are safe in a way the prompt did not require. Arthur, an employer of indentured labor, is given an early, correct question about his payroll, then a mechanism that lets him strike persons from the form. His complicity is a clause he can delete. Indenture never gets to be normal in his own mouth — which is the more unsettling, more human angle, and also closer to how Asimov actually writes insiders. He defends a system he profits from, or he doesn’t think about it until it inconveniences him. Washing him into the reader’s politics is a contemporary reflex, not a period one, and not a particular man’s. Chapter architecture is visible. One turn each, rising through demonstration, radio, restatement, draft, signing, quiet coda. Chapter 1 ends on hatch protocol, a soft serial hook. Chapter 7 has the reader see the trick a beat before Quist, which is heist grammar. Chapter 5 restates the whole machine to its operator. That last one is very “outline voice”: characters meeting to confirm the author’s notes. Three late chapters of clause-fighting will also read as impressive rather than alive if the jargon is doing the drama. Worldbuilding is a prop list waiting to be distributed: two calendars, pennant, filament lamp, tinted map, pit boots, dosimeter, isotope. Any one of these can be lived in. All of them, placed once per chapter as meaning-markers, will feel like a motif kit. The hot borehole is already booked as a hint. It has not been allowed to be a rumor that turns out trivial, or worse than useful. The gambit language is over-committed. The title will leak into the prose — sacrifice, pawn, hand, move — and the story will interpret itself. A human often uses the title’s word never, or once, carelessly. There is almost no body, no joke that fails, no appetite. Quist does not want a trophy sample, a promotion, or lunch. Arthur does not want the pension in a way he can feel in his hands. Havel’s feet do not hurt. Fear, if present, is dignified disorientation, not the stupid fear of being spaced, which he would then have to be ashamed of when nobody mentions killing. Dignity is the plan’s hidden tone. People under armed courtesy are often undignified. One more mismatch with the prompt: the rush is weather only by decree. “No other factions onstage” protects the word count and strips out the stupid life of a boom — a pamphlet, a liar, a rival geologist who got the grade wrong, a combine man already in the camp repossessing a drill. Scrutiny, in the prompt, is a flurry. In the plan it is an appointment. **Ways toward something more human** Let Arthur want a small wrong thing. He is prouder of the assay than of the people. He is already spending the pension in his head. He is furious that their map colors his plot as if he had not worked it. He hopes, privately, that Moss will not bring up the contract on an open channel. Give him one lie, told badly, and one mistake that is not later redeemed into cleverness. Do not make him a lawyer by chapter 5. Let his intelligence stay local. He understands heat, lattice, and why the neighboring numbers smell wrong. The rider is something he half-grasps; the notary, or even Quist in a careless moment, makes the width of it clear. If he wins a narrow signature, it should be because he is stubborn about wording he can see, not because he out-drafts a ministry. Better: he thinks he has narrowed it, and a practical consequence in the last chapter shows the gap — not as an authorial twist, but as the sort of gap a proud man leaves. Let Moss refuse the role of moral ballast. He may want Northreach’s buyout because the pay clears his term faster. He may think Arthur’s scruple is a leaseholder’s luxury. He may be an indifferent driller and a good mimic of radio voices. Saving him, if Arthur does, might insult him. Not saving him should remain possible. If the story cannot bear that, the indenture thread is decoration and should not be asked to carry the heart. Give Quist an appetite that is not “the paper.” She collects first cores. She is bored of men explaining ore to her and likes Arthur until he starts doing it. She will say “weapon” if it shortens the meeting, and the plan’s refusal to let her say it is a theatrical rule, not a character. Havel can be colonial, footsore, and superstitious about unsigned copies without becoming a secret conscience. Calder, or whatever the opposing pressure is, should do one petty thing early — freeze a supply order, claim a compressor — so the enemy is a nuisance before it is a screen. Break the temperature. One rude person, even briefly, or the politeness has nothing to press against. One failed joke. One bodily fact that affects a choice: thirst, a migraine from the packet’s air, the habit of checking his pockets for a notebook that was taken at the hatch. Allow a chapter to be shorter than the scheme wants, especially the radio chapter, and allow the meeting to sprawl past its “one turn” if the talk is actually good. Drop the self-interpreting close. End on a practical irritation: a form that still needs his thumb, Moss asking whether the pump will be left, Quist’s clerk sending the pension figures with a genuine congratulation. If an irony remains, it can sit in the fact that he is pleased to be consulted. Do not ask the last line to decide whether he was a pawn. Smudge the rush back in at the edges without adding a senate. A station newscast that has his name wrong. A combine geologist who wants to argue strike angle and does not know Arthur is a prisoner. A rumor about the borehole that nobody can confirm. These can be three lines. They keep the world larger than the seminar. On style: plain verbs, some stiffness, an occasional old-fashioned summary sentence of the sort a living writer now avoids (“He had never thought of himself as a man who could be sent for”). Cut triad props. Pick two objects and let the rest be furniture. Avoid gambit, pawn, and chess entirely in the narration. Let people repeat themselves and answer the previous question. If a speech starts explaining the colonial compact, interrupt it with someone who needs the room. The dangerous permission, and the useful one, is to let the plan be wrong in the later chapters. Hold the opening contract — vessel, replayed seizure, an early offer made mostly of talk, hints rather than a briefing, one man of practical competence inside a larger machinery. Release the acquittal. A more human Azimov story might end with Arthur having signed the broad form because he was tired and flattered, and with one small correction that does not fix the rest; or with the narrow form holding and Moss gone anyway, by his own thumbprint; or with the ore lifted cold and Arthur, back at the pit, already writing the next assay as if the work were still his. The prompt asked for a center, not a verdict. The living version will probably be a little unfair, a little undignified, and less sure what the gambit was.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention Third person, past tense, close to Arthur, in a plain and slightly stiff register: summary sentences allowed, dry circumstance rather than jokes, no lyric Mars and no “impressive” diction. The world shows up in talk, paper, and one or two worn objects — his assay book, the core tube — not in a motif kit. Retrofuture means factors, thumbprinted releases, radio lag, indenture rolls, and a sidearm called ceremonial. Big and small sit together when a sentence earns it (a contract’s remaining months, a routing code), and the narrator does not perform that trick on a schedule. Nobody says “gambit,” and nobody explains the rush as history. Arthur is a first-generation mining engineer who is vain of his numbers and ordinary about his crew. He thinks his indenture terms are fairer than the company camps, and he calls the people “the contracts” until that habit stops being convenient. He is good at rock and clumsy with power. He is afraid, in the packet, that they will simply not take him back, and then ashamed of the fear when someone offers him a bulb of tea. He tells one bad lie. He does not become a lawyer. The unknown party is Factor Leona Quist, named only when he is in the room. She wants a voluntary assay-release so a colonial-compact hearing never posts his grade and starts a pit-head rush she would then have to police. Drives and weapons are customers, and she will say so once, lightly, not as a threat speech. She is also pleased by a clean core and bored by men who lecture her. She is right that a public rush beside the domes would be ugly, and she is taking the vein anyway. Lieutenant Havel is tired, colonial-born, and doing a job; the invitation is an invitation the way a locked hatch is a courtesy. Northreach Combine, in the person of a man named Brice, is the other hand on him: a frozen parts order, a shed treated as already theirs, an inspection timed to force the assay into the open. No further factions, no secret identities, no fleet. Azra is said once, by Arthur, because a technician is about to heat a sample. Cold and unrefined, the ore can be lifted. Warmed and concentrated, it hastens decay in whatever radioactives are near it. That is the whole rule. The offer, made in an early scene that is mostly talk, is assignment of extraction rights, a consulting retainer, and a pension. Arthur hears “consulting” and sits up. He does not win the paper. He adds one miner’s sentence — lift temperature, cold — and Quist accepts it because the customers cook the ore at a yard his sentence never reaches. He notices, later, and does not get a speech about it. Moss Pettit, the driller, wants his term cleared faster under a transfer and will not play conscience. Arthur asks him not to thumbprint, has nothing better to offer, and is privately relieved, then ashamed of the relief. He still looks at the pension figures. Chapter 1 opens on the transfer vessel, already wondering; the flurry and the armed descent at his door are what he keeps replaying, in substantial scene and talk, not as a caption. The offer is not completed there. Manners hold. There is no battle and no acquittal. The last chapter ends on a practical exchange — a pump, a note, a routing line — and does not tell the reader what Arthur was. Aim for unevenness: a talky meeting, a thinner radio chapter, a rude moment, a repeated question, a fact that goes nowhere. Avoid a procedural hero, a moral ledger with a person’s name on it, threshold hooks on every chapter, chess language, costume slang, triad props, and any last line that weighs his soul. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1.** Already aboard the packet, watching Mars in a port that is too small. Arthur does not know who asked for him. He keeps replaying the last day: a neighbor’s boundary fuss, a Northreach letter he hadn’t answered, a survey plane, then Havel’s retinue at the door, Antares insignia, the polite invitation that did not include “no,” the sidearm nobody pointed. He tries to radio the camp and is told the channel is reserved. A sandwich arrives. He feels foolish for having thought they might space him, and less sure than before. **Chapter 2.** The room. Quist beside him, a map with his plot already tinted, tea, his boots. Mostly dialogue. She offers the assignment, the retainer, the pension, and says she needs his release before a hearing posts the grade for anyone to read. She names drives and weapons as the buyers, once, as if he already knew. He asks who else is on her list and what happens to his crew, and gets a short answer and a smooth one. He does not sign. He does say he will look, because she talked to him as the man who found it. A clerk puts her head in. The chapter ends on that, not on a revelation. **Chapter 3.** His core is already racked. A technician is about to bake a slice; Arthur stops him and says the rule, irritated, not lecturing. Quist is pleased, which he likes more than he means to. At the edge of the scene: a station cast with his name misspelled, and a Northreach geologist who wants to argue strike angle and does not care that Havel is standing there. Havel’s feet hurt. He will not be drawn. **Chapter 4.** A short radio chapter. Moss: Brice is in the shed, the recycler parts are frozen, the crew want to know if they have been sold. Arthur says nobody is selling anybody. It comes out wrong. Moss talks dates and money — a transfer would clear his term in fourteen months instead of three years — and Arthur is annoyed that Moss is thinking of himself. Afterward Arthur opens the release looking for the tonnage and does not stay on the schedule with the names. **Chapter 5.** Quist, impatient. If he waits, the hearing posts and the rush comes to his ground; Brice’s barge is the clock. Arthur is afraid of that, and also of a funny dosimeter figure in her file from the neighboring lease, which he had called a rumor. He demands to be the one who sets lift temperature. She agrees at once. He mistakes the speed for respect. Temper breaks when Brice, on a relay, calls him a dirt-holder sitting on other people’s adjacency, and Havel has to shut the speaker off like a man turning down a loud neighbor. **Chapter 6.** With the form and a compact notary who is not on his side. He finally reads the appurtenance lines and understands enough to feel sick, not enough to rewrite them. He tells himself the temperature sentence and the retainer will let him look after the crew from inside. He calls Moss and says not to thumbprint. Moss says he has already talked to their clerk, and asks what Arthur is offering instead. Arthur has the lease, which is no longer his to offer. He says he will think. He has no plan. **Chapter 7.** He signs the release Quist brought. His added sentence about cold lift looks small in the margin. She does not make a speech; she needs the name before Brice can force the assay public. Only after his thumb is down does he ask whether the crew go with the lease. She says the schedule is standard, and that they may contract onward if they wish. Havel witnesses because that is the procedure. Arthur wants to feel he was careful. The routing slip already says cold to the yard. He does not, today, read the yard’s line. **Chapter 8.** They send him down to post the cordon in his own face. Dust, the shed, a pennant on the nail where his chart hung. Moss is packing, asks whether the pump stays, and does not ask to be rescued; his thumbprint is already on the transfer. Brice is on the ground and late. The samples are gone. The pension figures are better than Arthur expected, and he looks. He reads the yard code, understands exactly where his sentence stops, and writes the cold-lift note anyway, because a botched packet would carry his name. He answers Moss about the pump.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Arthur Neegan Arthur came up from Earth at twenty-two on a settler’s technical contract and is forty now, and he treats those two facts as a credential. Eighteen years on the same lease, most of them thin, the last two finally showing color. He trained as a mining engineer and still says it that way when asked, as if the lease were a posting and not a life. He has no one waiting off-world. He had a partner in the early years, a driller who took a company job at better rates; they write at New Year and neither of them mentions the vein he has not, in any case, told her about. He sleeps in his shirt. He keeps his assay book in pencil because ink cakes up here, and he numbers the pages himself where the print has worn off. The book lives in his left breast pocket. If it is taken from him he will touch the pocket before he thinks. He is vain of his grades and ordinary about his people. He believes his indentures are fairer than the company camps, and he has said so to a supply clerk, who changed the subject. What he means is that he does not skim the food indent and that he lent Moss a heater coil last winter without writing it down. What he does not count is that sick days sit outside the term, a template clause he accepted because it was already printed. He says “the contracts” for the crew and “we” for the pump. He is good at rock. He can smell a bad dosimeter figure the way other men smell weather, and he is clumsy the moment a person wants something he can’t measure. He under-explains and then, when he sees he has not been understood, over-explains and gets pompous. His lie is not clever. In the radio talk he tells Moss that nobody is selling anybody, in the voice he uses for grades, and he adds a detail he invents on the spot — that the forms he saw were tonnage only — because a short lie feels ruder than a long one. Anyone listening can hear the extra piece. He is slightly deaf in the left ear from a compressor and turns that ear toward questions he does not want. He checks the pocket when he is nervous and then pretends he was after a pastille. He came up afraid of vacuum, specifically of a training film in which a man forgot a tether, and he is ashamed of still having that film in his head when the actual event is a sandwich and a reserved channel. He wants his name on the discovery as it was logged. He wants Quist to talk to him as the man who found it, and when she does he sits straighter, which he would deny. He wants the pension and means to look at the figures only once. He wants Moss to act grateful so that Arthur can go on being the decent employer. His allegiance, if he were honest, is to his own competence, then the lease, then the crew, and he would swear he had that list reversed. He has never read the colonial compact. He dislikes Northreach because their letters assume he is late on something. He is not tall, and broader than station people, with a squint from visor glare and dust still in the creases of his neck after a wash. Low ceilings have rounded his shoulders. His smile is a press of the lips, which strangers take as agreement. Mineral stain under the nails; a thumbnail split by a core clamp and grown back ridged. Earth is still in his vowels. On station they hear it at once. “The grade is the grade. You can tint the map whatever you like.” He had been about to say the contracts were free to go at term, which was true, and also the sentence a man reaches for when he has already started lying. # Leona Quist Quist is a factor, not a diplomat. The Antares pennant flies on her packets because a diplomatic hull gets a berth and a materials hull waits. She came up through freight numbers, took the materials desk when someone died in post, and has spent twelve years moving things that other offices prefer to call strategic after they have arrived. She is fifty-one. She has a room on the station and a drawer of first cores, labeled, which she will show to a competent man for about four minutes if it will shorten a signature. She is not romantic about them. A core proves a file. She once burned the web of her right thumb on a hot sample and never tells the story; the scar is just there when she holds a bulb. She is impatient with fear and with gratitude, and she fills a silence with terms. She assumes that a man who can stop a technician from baking a slice can also see where a sentence ends. That is not a trap she has polished. She needs the thumbprint before Brice’s barge makes the grade public, and if Arthur’s margin note comforts him and does not bind the yard, she will not volunteer the distinction. She would not call that a kindness. She would say she answered what he asked. Drives and weapons are customers. She will say so once, in the same tone as tonnage, because coyness wastes the hour, and then she will not say it again. She is right that a posted hearing would bring a rush to his ground. She is also taking the vein. Both of these sit in her head without a speech between them. She calls people by their trade until the document needs a name, and then she says the name as it has to be spelled. She remembers Arthur’s grade and misremembers whether she offered him tea. She has a good pen and a gray jacket she wears twice running, and she is a little vain of not seeming vain. The station’s citrus cleaner makes her sneeze; she hates the sneeze because it makes her look uncertain. She eats whatever is already in the room. She is bored by men who explain ore to her, and she likes Arthur for the three minutes he is simply right about heat, and she is finished liking him when he begins to watch her face for the effect. She dislikes Brice because he is loud, and loudness makes hearings. She does not remember Havel’s given name and does not feel the lack. Her allegiance is to the desk, to the quarter’s movement figures, and to not having a riot on a lease she could have lifted quietly. She does not wish Arthur harm. She does not intend to think about him after the routing slip is stamped. Square face, hair cut short for a liner and gone iron at the temples, a habit of sitting nearer than station people like because the rooms she uses have always been small. She looks at hands when the talk is about work. Her voice is low and quick and does not rise when she is opposed; it gets shorter. “I’m not here to admire it. I’m here before it goes in somebody’s circular.” “Write your temperature in. Write it in the margin if you want. I need the name before the barge, not a essay.” # Lieutenant Havel Havel was born in a dome the corp still abbreviates wrong on its forms. He is thirty-six, a lieutenant because that is where colonial officers stop without a patron, and he has made his peace with the rank by keeping his kit legal and his record dull. He sends his mother a line every month and never mentions the guests. There have been seven this rotation. He remembers three. Arthur is one of them, for the pit boots on the clean deck and for apologizing to the deckhand, which Havel found mortifying and, in a corner he will not open, decent. He has not decided to be Arthur’s friend. Remembering is not an allegiance. He believes that if the procedure is followed he has not done anything, and this belief is how he sleeps. Fright annoys him because it lengthens the job; he is shorter with frightened people than he means to be, and then tells himself they preferred efficiency. His boots were issued a size small. He has a corn he cuts badly with a penknife, and he stands anyway, because sitting while armed reads as waiting and waiting reads as a threat, and he was trained not to advertise one. Some of his courtesy is that. Some of it is manners he actually has. He will not be drawn into Arthur’s questions, and he will shut Brice’s speaker off the way he would turn down a loud neighbor, because noise is disorder, not because he has chosen a side. He chews a resin pastille for the dry air on packets. The smell is medicinal. People misread it as drink, and he has stopped correcting them. He is good at cards and will not play on a watch, and he resents that this makes him look stern rather than careful. He dislikes Earth factors on principle and has never let the dislike move an order. He does not like Quist. He does not like Brice. He likes a hatch that cycles the first time. His allegiance is to the packet, to the twelve years left before his own pension, and to not being the man who drew. He will witness the release because a witness is what the line asks for. If Arthur looks at him afterward for some human countersignature, Havel will be busy with the pen. Tall for dome stock, narrow, a haircut growing out at the neck, a shaving nick on the jaw he keeps opening. The holster is new and stiff; the sidearm in it is old. His working face is a blank. When he is angry he blinks longer, which Arthur, if he notices, will take for thought. “The invitation stands, Mr. Neegan. The boat’s already warm.” If the man was going to be sick, Havel hoped he would manage it before the hatch, where there was a grate. # Moss Pettit Moss signed the indenture at twenty-six because a dome clinic bill had his name on it and the surface work paid the bill down faster than air-plant work, which was also killing his uncle’s cough. He is thirty now. Four years on Arthur’s lease, three left on the term, fourteen months if a transfer clears him. He does not tell the clinic story. He is not collecting a moral. He has the dates in his head the way Arthur has grades, and he trusts them more than he trusts speeches. He is a good driller and a better hand with the recycler than Arthur is, and both of them know it, and Arthur has never said it, and Moss has stored that with the other things. He hears Arthur say “we” for the pump and “the contracts” for the crew. He has not made a point of it. He calls Arthur “Neegan” to his face and “the lease” when he is talking to the others. He thinks Arthur is the best nose for bad rock he has worked under, and he thinks Arthur’s picture of himself as a fair employer is a luxury of people whose names are already on the paper. He will not perform gratitude for the heater coil. He used it. It worked. That was the transaction. His flaw is simple and he does not dress it up: he will take the shorter term even if the next boss is worse, and he will not spend a day he can’t afford warning the other contracts if warning means his own stamp waits. He sulks. The question about the pump is half practical and half sulk. He wants Arthur to say, in plain words, that he is leaving and the equipment is leaving, so Moss does not have to supply the feeling for both of them. He is superstitious in a way he finds stupid: a washer on a cord, checked before he goes down, never mentioned. He whistles two notes, not a tune, when a drill is about to bind. Arthur has never noticed the notes. The crew has. He is not afraid of Brice exactly. Brice stood in the shed and talked too loud and put a lock on a cabinet that was already failing; Moss disliked the noise and the presumption and then went back to counting months. Quist is not a person to him. She is a shorter number. He does not want to be rescued, and he does not want Arthur’s relief either, though he will see it. He packs his own kit. He asks about the pump because an hour stripping a pump is money, and because he will not carry Arthur’s reason off the lease for him. Wiry, visor-tan in a patchy V at the throat, a canine missing that he could have fixed at term and didn’t, because the term was the point. Hands quicker than his talk. He stands with his weight on one hip even when there is nothing to lean on, which Arthur reads as not attending. When he is deciding something he looks past the other man’s shoulder. That is concentration. Arthur has always taken it for shiftiness. “Fourteen months is fourteen months. You can say nobody’s selling anybody with their lock already on the shed.” “Leave the pump if you’re leaving it. I don’t need the reason written out.” # Alan Brice Arthur never learns the Alan. On the relay and on the ground he is Brice, Northreach claims, the man who says “with respect” and then the insult. He is forty-four and has never held a lease. He works adjacency: if the neighbor’s grade is real, Northreach’s ground is worth a filing, and if the assay can be forced into the open there are shared-works claims, access, a forfeiture on a technicality if the small holder is sloppy. He is good at technicalities. He is not the arms race. He is a man who needs this recorded in his docket before the quarter closes, because his supervisor has already asked twice. He froze the recycler parts over a coupling invoice he believes is unpaid. It may even be unpaid; he has a gift for finding the item that is almost true and using it all the way. He had the shed lock put on because an unsecured shed looks, in a photograph, like abandonment. He will be late to the cordon because he was finishing the notice that was supposed to make him early, and he will experience the lateness as his office having failed him, not as Arthur having done anything impressive. He holds grudges against files. When a file has a man’s name, he gets personal, and then he is only rude. Calling Arthur a dirt-holder has worked on small leaseholders before. He uses Arthur’s first name without asking, a habit he thinks is plain dealing. He gets sick on barges and chews ginger and considers this the hard part of the job. He picks up other people’s survey pegs and does not think of it as stealing; they were in the wrong place, and he has a box of them. He smiles with his mouth open, already in the correction. Soft in the middle from months of transit, a field jacket new enough to keep its crease, sunburn only on the tops of his ears, a slate in the chest pocket that drags the jacket crooked. He is afraid of Central in the specific way of a man who has been copied on a complaint. His allegiance is the claims bonus and the supervisor’s silence. He does not hate Arthur until the thumbprint lands first. After that he hates him in a narrow, durable, office way. “Arthur, with respect, you’re sitting on other people’s adjacency and calling it weather.” If the factor had the thumb already, the factor could explain it to Central. Brice had sent the notice. That much would be in the file even if nothing else was.

Arthur Neegan sat with his pit boots on a clean deck and watched Mars through a port the size of a plate. His knees had started in. By the bulkhead clock, which kept station hours and was no use on the lease, the packet had been under way the better part of an hour. No one had told him where they were going. No one had told him who had asked. He had the assay book. They had not taken it at the hatch, and he had not offered it. It sat in the left breast pocket, the pencil working through the cloth against his ribs. He put his hand there and took it away. A deckhand had wiped his fines off the deck once and then given it up. Arthur had apologized. The man had not looked at him. He had never thought of himself as a man who could be sent for. The morning had been ordinary, by which he meant he was behind on a letter. The recycler was singing in the shed. Moss was on the east face with the other two. The Northreach envelope had sat three days under a wrench, and Arthur had left it, because he did not send numbers out unfinished. The second core had come up richer than he meant to put in anyone's letter. He was willing to think that much before coffee, and no more. The woman from the next lease but one was at his pegs before he opened it, scarf on, one of his rods in her fist, saying a pin had moved. He went out in his undershirt. The pin was where he had driven it in March. He said so. A plane, she said, had been over at first light, and they shifted pins when it suited them. Planes did not shift pins. He said that as well. She left angry. Walking back, he was pleased he had not raised his voice. He had the letter open when the plane came again. Shared works, a request for his latest assay, the word voluntary sitting in the sentence and doing nothing. They had him by lease number, not by name. He was finding the line he meant to refuse when the sound overhead changed. Not a pass. A landing, east of the shed, where the contracts kept the crawler. Four of them came down the ramp. The hull was still ticking. The mark on the hatch was Antares, the diplomatic star and the folded banner, the same one they printed on freight notices. It had been painted over an older panel, and the paint stopped short of a corner where something had been burned off. The officer was tall and narrow, hair grown out at the neck. His holster was new. The pistol in it was not. Another man had a rifle on a strap, muzzle down. Nobody pointed anything. "Mr. Neegan. Lieutenant Havel." He was chewing something that smelled of a clinic. "You're asked to a meeting off-world. The invitation stands. The boat's already warm." Arthur still had the letter in his hand. "I've got men on the face," he said. "And I don't go to meetings that won't give me a name. The pump isn't shut down." "If you'll come along." "Who's asking?" "You'll be told on station." Havel looked past him into the shed, not unkindly. "The boat's already warm, Mr. Neegan." "You've said." "Yes." Someone had gone inside. Arthur heard the chart drawer. He stepped that way, and the man at the ramp shifted his feet, a small shift, the kind you make when a hose is about to kink. No voice went up. Arthur's face heated. He could walk, or he could make them carry him. Walking was the one he could tell Moss about afterward without sounding as if he had been dragged. He set the Northreach letter on the crate by the door. A note on the back would have been the decent thing. Every note he could think of sounded as if he had agreed. "I'll call them from the boat." "From the packet," Havel said. It had the sound of a sentence he had been given. "If you'll come along." Halfway up the ramp Arthur saw, unwanted, a training film from the crossing: a man off his tether, mouth working, the suit doing what a suit did. He had been twenty-two. He was forty, and the thought was a disgrace, and it stayed with him. He turned his bad ear toward Havel, the ear the compressor had taken, in case there was an order he would rather not catch whole. Havel said nothing more. The hatch came down. On the packet he asked at once for the camp channel. The crewman with the headset listened and said it was reserved for the duration. "By who?" "Don't have that, sir." Arthur asked a second time. It made the thing worse. The man pointed at a couch, and Arthur sat. He tried it in order, the way he tried a reading he did not like. Northreach, tired of their letter. A buyer with the plane's pictures. The board, after some fee. Last, and he did not enjoy it, was the chance that someone already had the second core. He had not sent the second core anywhere. None of these people came to a door before lunch in a diplomatic boat. He finished the list and began it again. It did not improve. The deckhand brought a sandwich and a bulb of water and set them on the couch arm. The bread was pressed flat, dry at the edge. The Antares star on the wrapper had been stamped hard enough to crack grease through the paper. "Thank you," Arthur said. It came out thin. He did not eat at once. On the ramp he had thought they might put him out a lock if he made trouble, and the thought had been the film again, and now he had ham in his hand and was ashamed of it. The shame did not clear anything. They had reserved his channel. They had brought him food. A man you meant to space, you did not feed. He was hungry all the same, and resented it, and ate too fast. The salt stayed on his lip. He folded the wrapper into the couch seam so it would not drift if they maneuvered, and opened the book. The pages were his grades and nothing else. In the port, Mars had gone too small to be any use.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of writing that demonstrates genuine mastery of the Asimov retrofuturist register while maintaining its own distinct voice. Let me work through the key elements carefully. The chapter opens with Arthur already aboard the packet, exactly as planned, and the retrospective reconstruction of the morning's events is handled with considerable skill. The writing avoids the trap of flashback-as-summary; instead, the events unspool with the texture of a man replaying them in his head, which is precisely what the plan called for. The neighbor with the survey pin, the Northreach letter under the wrench, the plane's second pass — these accumulate naturally rather than being itemized. The prose register is consistently achieved. It is plain without being flat, slightly stiff without being wooden. Sentences like "He had never thought of himself as a man who could be sent for" carry enormous weight through understatement. The retrofuture world-building is embedded in objects and procedures rather than exposition: the Antares star stamped through grease on a wrapper, the paint stopping short of a corner where something had been burned off, the bulkhead clock keeping station hours that are no use on the lease. This is exactly the Asimov method — the world revealed through incidental detail rather than lecture. Character work is excellent. Arthur's psychology is rendered through behavior rather than statement. The training film about the man off his tether is a masterstroke — it appears twice, the second time with "the thought was a disgrace," and the shame of having feared something that turned out to be a sandwich is handled with real delicacy. His turning his bad ear toward Havel to avoid catching an order whole is a perfect physical gesture that carries psychological truth. His eating too fast and resenting the hunger, then folding the wrapper into the couch seam so it won't drift — these are the details of a man who is frightened and competent simultaneously. Havel is rendered efficiently and accurately to his profile: the chewing that smells of a clinic, the new holster with the old pistol, the repeated "the boat's already warm" that has "the sound of a sentence he had been given." The small shift of feet when Arthur moves toward the shed is exactly the kind of controlled threat the profile describes. The dialogue is spare and functional in the best sense. "You've said." / "Yes." — this exchange is perfect. It establishes the power dynamic without melodrama. The dialogue never over-explains and never performs. The plan called for Arthur to try to radio the camp and be told the channel is reserved, for a sandwich to arrive, and for him to feel foolish for having feared spacing. All of this is executed, and executed well. The chapter ends on the assay book and Mars gone too small — not a weighted final line, just a man with his numbers and a shrinking view, which is exactly right. If there are criticisms to make: the piece is almost too controlled. There is very little that surprises at the sentence level — the craft is in the restraint and the accumulation rather than in any individual moment of unexpected beauty. This is appropriate to the Asimov register, but it means the chapter earns its effects through consistency rather than brilliance. The "forced poetry" risk is essentially zero here, which is a virtue, but it also means there are no moments of genuine lyric surprise. The chapter does exactly what it sets out to do, which is both its strength and its slight limitation. The plan's note about the training film appearing and Arthur being "ashamed of the fear when someone offers him a bulb of tea" is executed with precision. The plan's instruction to avoid "threshold hooks on every chapter" is honored — the chapter ends quietly, on a practical gesture. One minor quibble: "His knees had started in" is slightly opaque as an opening sentence — it's trying for the plain-spoken but lands a touch awkward. But this is a small thing in an otherwise very strong piece. Overall, this is writing that knows what it is doing and does it with discipline and intelligence. The Asimov retrofuture vibe is achieved without pastiche. The characters are consistent with their profiles. The chapter plan is followed faithfully. The prose earns its effects. The station smelled of the cleaner they used on the rails. Arthur followed Havel along a corridor painted one color, his boots sticking and letting go. The spin was a little high for a man who had been on Mars that morning. He did not ask whose station it was. Havel would have given him a designation. They stopped at a door with no plate. Havel knocked once, as a man knocks when he is not asking, and stood aside. "Mr. Neegan." The room was small. Two chairs on the same side of a table, which Arthur did not understand until the woman in the near one looked at his hands and said, "Sit." A wall screen had been left on a map of his ground. His plot was a dull green he would not have used. The neighbors were blank. A bulb of tea sat at the empty place. Another sat in front of her, not drunk. He sat. The chair was light. His arm had nowhere to go that was not her sleeve. She wore a gray jacket that had been on her yesterday, and a pen better than the jacket. She did not stand. "You're the engineer. I'm Quist." Then, as if a form had occurred to her, "Factor Leona Quist. Materials." "I didn't ask for a meeting." "No. I need your release on the assay before a hearing has to post it." "I didn't ask for a hearing either." "If you don't release it, I post it. Anyone can read a posting." She said it low and quickly, and did not lean on the words. "Northreach already wrote you. The rest don't have the grade. I'd like to keep it that way." He turned his good ear toward her and was annoyed that he had. "You took the charts out of my shed." "Someone did. They're last month's. You'll have better." Her eyes went to his pocket and came away. She did not reach. "I don't need the better ones in here. I need your name, so the ore can be assigned and lifted before it goes in a circular." The western pin on her map was off by a little. He nearly said so. It would have sounded like the woman with the scarf. "Assigned to who?" "To the office. You'd be retained. Consulting engineer. There's a pension. It isn't generous and it isn't an insult. You can read it before you tell me which it is." He had come up ready to refuse a buyer. Retained was a different word. She had said engineer as if the plane had not found anything, as if the grade were his. He sat up before he meant to. "I'm not looking for a job." "You're looking at a hearing with your name on it. I'm offering the other door." She took up the pen and did not write. "The buyers are the drive yards and the weapons people. They'll have it either way. I'd rather they had it through a desk than off your ground in a rush." She said weapons as she had said yards. Then she waited. The cleaner was stronger in the small room. She sneezed, once, and looked as if the sneeze had argued with her, and went on shorter. "That's the offer. Release, retainer, pension. Before this gets loud." Arthur looked at the green. "Who else is on your list?" "You," she said. "And Northreach, who already think they're on it. If I post, the list gets long. I don't want the list." He had wanted names. He got that. His letter was still in his head, the word voluntary doing nothing in it. "I've got three contracts on the lease," he said. "What happens to them." "They follow the lease. That's standard. They won't be turned off at a day's notice. A hearing would do worse." She set a form by his hand, face up, not pushed. "Read it. It isn't a trick paragraph. I haven't got the afternoon." He did not pick it up. The top line had his name spelled right, which the Northreach letter had not managed. Neegan, Arthur. Leaseholder. The pleasure of that was stupid, and he felt it. His mouth did the press he used instead of a smile. She took it, he thought, for something nearer to yes. "A posted number isn't a log," he said. He heard himself starting in, the way he did when a man at the supply desk had not understood a grade. "Without the—" "A number is what gets read," she said. "I don't need the lecture. I need the name before it gets loud." "I'm not signing this now." "I didn't say this hour." "You sent a boat." "The boat was warm." It was Havel's sentence. Arthur looked at the door. Havel was not in it. "Read it. Write on it if you have to. Come back with a question that isn't a speech." He had questions. Whether the pump went with the paper. Whether Moss's term sat in the standard line. Who paid a sick day if the office held the lease. They were not in an order he could say without explaining his own ground to her, and he had already started that and been stopped. He put his hand to the pocket and made it a search for a pastille. He had no pastille. She watched the hand. "I'll look," he said. Because she had called him the engineer, and the name was spelled right, and consulting was a word he had not expected to want. He heard it leave him. It was not a refusal. She nodded, done with the part of the hour that had been his. The door opened without a knock. A clerk with a slate to her chest put her head in and stopped when she saw him. "Factor, there's a—" "Not in front of him," Quist said. The clerk stayed in the gap. Arthur had the form under his fingers. Nobody asked him to go, and nobody finished the sentence.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of writing that demonstrates genuine mastery of the Asimov-adjacent retrofuturist register while maintaining its own distinct voice. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions. **Craft and Voice** The prose is disciplined and precise in a way that earns its plainness. Sentences like "Havel knocked once, as a man knocks when he is not asking" do real work — they characterize Havel, establish the power dynamic, and advance the scene without announcing themselves as clever. The register is consistently maintained: dry, slightly stiff, observational without being lyrical. The writing plan called for "plain and slightly stiff" and the execution delivers exactly that without becoming flat. The detail work is excellent. "Two chairs on the same side of a table, which Arthur did not understand until the woman in the near one looked at his hands and said, 'Sit'" — this is economical and revealing. The physical arrangement tells us about Quist's method before she speaks. The pen better than the jacket. The map with the western pin off by a little. These are the right kind of details: functional, character-revealing, world-building without being decorative. **Dialogue** The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. Quist's voice is exactly as profiled: short, quick, not rising when opposed, getting shorter. "I don't need the lecture. I need the name before it gets loud." This is perfect. Arthur's dialogue captures his tendency to over-explain when he senses he hasn't been understood — he starts in about the posted number not being a log, gets cut off, and the reader understands exactly what he was about to do. The exchange feels like two people with different kinds of intelligence negotiating in real time, not performing a scene. "The boat was warm" as Havel's sentence, attributed to Quist, is a nice touch — it shows how institutional language circulates and how Quist deploys it without owning it. **Character Consistency** Arthur's vanity about his grades, his pleasure at his name being spelled correctly ("The pleasure of that was stupid, and he felt it"), his hand going to the pocket for a pastille he doesn't have — these are all precisely consistent with the character profile. The moment where he sits up straighter when she calls him "the engineer" is exactly what the profile promised: "He wants Quist to talk to him as the man who found it, and when she does he sits straighter, which he would deny." Quist is rendered with equal fidelity. Her sneeze that "argued with her" is a small perfect detail consistent with the profile's note about hating the sneeze because it makes her look uncertain. She eats whatever is in the room (the untouched tea). She fills silence with terms. She is bored by men who explain ore to her and cuts Arthur off mid-lecture. **Plot and Stakes** The chapter does what the plan requires: it presents the offer (release, retainer, pension), establishes the competing pressure (Northreach, the hearing), and ends on an interruption that withholds resolution. The stakes are communicated through implication rather than exposition — "The buyers are the drive yards and the weapons people" said once, in the same tone as tonnage, exactly as planned. The ending — the clerk in the doorway, "Not in front of him," Arthur holding the form with nobody asking him to go and nobody finishing the sentence — is genuinely good. It's ambiguous in the right way: is he being kept, forgotten, or tested? The chapter earns this suspension. **Minor Criticisms** The chapter is almost too controlled. There's a slight sense that every sentence has been audited for excess, which occasionally produces a kind of flatness in the middle passages. The line "He had come up ready to refuse a buyer. Retained was a different word" is good but perhaps the most "writerly" moment in a piece that otherwise avoids that quality. The "woman with the scarf" reference — "It would have sounded like the woman with the scarf" — is slightly opaque. It's clearly meant to evoke some prior social embarrassment Arthur has, but without context it reads as a gesture toward interiority rather than actual interiority. This is a minor flaw in an otherwise precise piece. The chapter follows its plan faithfully: the room, the map, the tea, the offer, the short answer about who else is on the list, the smooth answer about the crew, Arthur not signing but saying he'll look, the clerk interrupting. Every planned beat is hit without feeling mechanical. **Asimov Fidelity** The retrofuturist texture is present without being costumed: "bulb of tea," the spin being high, the designation Havel would have given. Arthur stopped so short that Havel nearly walked into him. "That's not last month's charts," he said. "No," Havel said. The bench was materials, not a room anyone would receive a man in. She let the last of his name fall off and went on to a lost slate. "That's me," he said. "Don't correct it in the corridor," Quist said. She was already less interested. "It makes a crowd." She left. The technician hovered for his dish. Havel pointed him at a stool, and they went out. The speaker had moved on to mess hours. A Northreach man was waiting by the lift as if the wall had been assigned to him. Field jacket, survey slate held up like a ticket. He did not look at the holster. "Neegan? Kerr. Geology, not claims. He did not lower his voice for Havel. "Twenty is what a camera does to a face. I walked your pegs last month. You weren't there." Moss was not hot. Arthur had no answer ready for that. "He told them a transfer clears faster than waiting on you. Fourteen months. I've got three years on the paper. I didn't say I believed him. He said the number where they could hear it." Fourteen. The anger arrived before Arthur had a place for it. His cabinet, his coupling, his letter still on the crate, and Moss had come into the eight minutes with his own term already counted, as if the pump might wait its turn. He nearly said he had lent Moss the heater coil in the winter and never written it down. It came up like a proof. He let it die. Said in a booth, with a lieutenant in the door, it would have sounded like a bill. "We've got the pump to keep in one piece," he said. "The east cut is still live. You don't take a term off a man talking in a shed." "Fourteen months is fourteen months. You can say nobody's selling anybody. His lock's already on the cabinet." "The form was tonnage." "You said." A pause that was not the lag. "You want the part number, if you're still the one ordering." He wanted it. He wrote it large in the assay book, because a number was work he could finish and the book was in his pocket. Moss read it back once, slow, a shift gone if a digit was wrong. He did not ask who had Arthur. He did not ask when anybody was coming down. Arthur was still hunting a sentence that would make the first one true when the clock cut them to a tone. Havel did not speak. The clerk put his head in for the log and the set. Arthur got the form out while the man's eyes were on the slate. He had folded it badly. The crease went through his name. If it gets loud, your grade goes in the answer.” She spoke as if she were late for the next room. “I can lift it quiet if you assign it. A column of readings he would have thrown out of a book for being too even, and then one that was not even at all. High. Two weeks old. A hand that was not his had written possible instrument in the margin and drawn no line through the figure. “Who took this?” “Her operator. She sent it up because her lights flickered and she wanted a part.” Quist did not look at the sheet. She had already decided how much of it she would say. “They’ll call it a bad tube.” “They can call it what they like. That isn’t a tube.” He was starting. He heard it and could not get the brake on. “If they’ve had warmth in the ground over there, not a bake, just warmth, and a medical store in the same shed, the store goes first. You don’t wait on a tube story. You pull the store. You don’t let a barge crew camp on the pegs and cook coffee on a hot plate next to—” “Write it,” she said. “If that’s what you need.” He stopped. “Write what?” “The lift. Cold. Your sentence, your hand. I’ll have it in the margin if that’s how you want it. I don’t need an essay on her lights.” He had expected an argument. An office liked a hot plate. An office would tell him moisture, and he would have to fight for the line. She had given him the line before he had finished being afraid. Afraid for the store, yes. Afraid, under that, of Brice reading the same figure and calling a hearing in which Arthur would have to say it out loud, with his name already in the answer. She had heard the fear and handed him the work. His chest did the stupid thing it had done at the bench. “I’d be the one who sets it,” he said. “Not a yard clerk. Temperature, in the instrument. Consulting, the way you said.” “Fine.” The speed of it ought to have been a warning. It felt like being spelled correctly. He almost sat. The relay cracked open on the wall, loud enough that she sneezed and looked murderous about it. A man’s voice, too near his own microphone, the cheer of someone who has practiced plain dealing. “Arthur. Brice. With respect. You’re sitting on other people’s adjacency and calling it weather. I’ve got a coupling you want and a board that wants your assay. We can do this like neighbors.” “Get off the line,” Quist said. “Your office took my notice late, Factor. I’m talking to the leaseholder. Arthur, the pegs are where a careful man would have—” Havel reached past Arthur and shut the speaker. He did it as he might have turned down a set in a mess, one motion, no interest in the pistol. The cheer went out in the middle of careful. Havel’s weight came off the bad boot a half second later. The questions were the right ones and they had no dignity next to a medical store and a barge, and next to a woman who had agreed with him before he had finished. “I’ll write it,” he said. “Tonight,” she said, and left him the file as if he had asked to keep it.

He knew heat. He did not know clauses. The pencil left a gray dot. He rubbed it out and smeared the months. The retainer, he told himself. Consulting. The notary had the lamp over the pad and his eye on the clock. He locked it at twenty. Quist came in without sitting. The jacket was the same. She looked at the margin, then at Arthur’s hands. “Fine.” He had written small so the sentence would fit. Lift cold. No heat on the load. Temperature set by A. Neegan. Against her type it looked like a note left for the next shift. His name was there, and his name was in the top line, the one the notary had pressed flat. He read the pencil once more. The letters were his. “Brice’s wire is on the board,” she said. “If this isn’t in a sleeve, your grade goes in the answer. I need the name.” She did not tell him what the answer would cost. The barge had been the cost for two days. She was done naming it. The notary turned the form to the box and waited, thumb gray to the crease. The schedule was the third sheet. Arthur did not turn to it. If he asked about the names, the page went back, and the notary would say so in front of her, and twelve minutes was not a rewrite. He had read the retainer in the corridor until the sentence sat still. Consulting engineer. A man on that line could still order the coupling. He could still speak for the pump. The pump was what he had always meant when he said we. “Thumb.” He pressed it into the pad. The ink was cold and stood up over the graphite. He set it in the box and lifted straight, as he lifted a core when he did not want a smear on the face. The print came clear. He was pleased, and shut his mouth on it, which settled nothing. The notary had begun the copy from the body, line by line, not from the pencil. Arthur watched the hand skip his sentence as if a margin were not a line. He drew breath to say so. Quist was already clipping a slip to her sleeve, and the first box on it was COLD, in a clerk’s block. His name under it, spelled right. He let the breath go. The word was on the routing. That was where a temperature did its work. A copy was manners. “Witness.” Havel came off the door and took the pen the notary held out. It was not Quist’s. He signed under the print, small, and blew on the line once though the ink was already dulling. Arthur looked at him to see if he had read the margin. Havel was getting the cap back on. It stuck. He worked it square, stepped to the jamb, and let the bad foot take his weight. He blinked the long blink. Then he was only the door. Arthur’s thumb was wet when he got it out. “The crew. Do they go with the lease.” “The schedule’s standard.” She was fitting the sleeve. “They may contract onward if they wish.” He turned his good ear and got nothing further. Onward meant Moss’s fourteen months, said without the shed in it. The names were already in the sleeve. He had told Moss not to print, and then he had printed, and he did not put those two facts where she could look at them. She had answered what he asked. A kinder word would not lift the thumb out of the box. “Temperature stays with me,” he said. “You wrote it down.” She turned the slip so he could see he had been given it, because he was still standing there. Under his name there was a yard mark and a run of code. He did not start it. The notary drew the rag across the pad. The rag had been gray a long time. Havel’s pastille was the loudest thing in the room. Arthur took the slip off the clip. She let it go without watching it go. He folded it once, the yard line to the inside, and put it in the breast pocket with the book. The book bent. He left it. The codes would keep until he had a table. She sneezed in the corridor and spoke shortly to the air. She did not come back. The notary turned his key as if the clock had caught him mid-wipe. “Don’t touch the wet.” Havel held the door. Arthur went through with his thumb held off his coat. The pocket rode hard against the book. He did not take the slip out.

Let me examine it carefully across the requested dimensions. The prose style is deliberately spare and functional, with a bureaucratic texture that suits the subject matter perfectly. Sentences like "Against her type it looked like a note left for the next shift" and "The rag had been gray a long time" do real work without straining for effect. The writing earns its compression — nothing here feels like padding, and nothing feels like showing off. Character nuance is exceptional. Arthur's self-deception is rendered with surgical precision: "He was pleased, and shut his mouth on it, which settled nothing." The moment where he watches the notary's hand skip his margin sentence, draws breath to object, then sees the word COLD on the routing slip and lets the breath go — this is a masterclass in showing a man rationalize his own defeat as a kind of victory. His vanity about the clean thumbprint ("He was pleased") is perfectly calibrated against the larger context of what he's just surrendered. The detail of him folding the slip "the yard line to the inside" — hiding from himself what he hasn't yet read — is quietly devastating. Quist is rendered with equal precision. The sneeze in the corridor — that small vulnerability she hates — lands perfectly as a closing grace note. Havel's long blink, his stuck pen cap, his bad foot: these are the details of a man who has witnessed too many of these signings to be present for this one. The dialogue is exceptional. "You wrote it down" is perhaps the best line in the chapter — it answers Arthur's assertion about temperature with a completeness that is also a dismissal. The moment of Arthur telling Moss not to print and then printing himself, held privately ("he did not put those two facts where she could look at them"), is the moral center of the chapter, handled with exactly the right restraint. No speech. No ledger. Just the fact, sitting there. If there are weaknesses, they are minor. The chapter is so compressed that a reader coming to it cold might struggle slightly with the notary's procedure. The line "twelve minutes was not a rewrite" is slightly opaque on first reading. But these are small complaints against a chapter that consistently earns its effects. The retrofuturist Asimovian quality is present not in any surface decoration but in the texture of procedure — the notary's clock, the sleeve, the routing code, the compact notary — and in the way large stakes (an arms race, an interstellar economy) are entirely absent from the room while entirely present in the document being signed. This is exactly right. The "well-earned darkness" criterion is met with distinction. The chapter's emotional weight accumulates through restraint, not statement.
