They put him down east of the shed and told him the notice had to be up before the packet lifted. The clerk came as far as the ramp and stayed there. Arthur walked the track in his own boots. The dust was the same. It got into his collar before he reached the door. The chart was off the nail. An Antares pennant hung in its place, star and folded banner, the cloth too clean for the shed. He put the cordon under it, because that was the nail the contracts looked at, and pressed the tack with his thumb. The station ink left a gray half-moon on the paper. Closed. No heat. No one past the pegs. His name at the bottom, as the man posting. Hobbs was in the doorway and watched him do it. Arthur turned the bad ear. He did not ask Hobbs to come in. The core locker stood open. A freight tag on the shelf had yesterday's station mark and his lease number. He put his hand on the empty place where the second tube had lain, and took it off, and shut the door. The cores were in a net by the ramp. He could see the clerk's boot against the webbing. Moss was at the bench with his kit in a crate, weight on one hip, looking past Arthur at the pennant. "They said you'd hang it." "It's hung." "Pump." Arthur had a sentence about fixtures. It was a reason, and it was long. "Does it stay or does it go. If it goes I need the hour. I'm not taking it down so you've left something running." "Leave it." "That's not the question I asked." "It stays. Don't strip it." Moss nodded once, as if a grade had finally been readable, and went back to a shirt. The gray smear of a thumb was on his right hand, fresher than Arthur's. He did not hide it and he did not offer the paper. "Printed this morning. Their clerk held it to the shift, the way she said. Fourteen months." The other fact arrived before the decent one. There would be no argument in the shed, no refusal in front of Hobbs, nothing Arthur had to answer with a lease he had already given. The relief was small and immediate. He heard it, and was ashamed of the order, and said the next thing too fast. "Pell?" "Waiting on whether they pay the clinic before he prints. Hobbs printed. You don't have to stand for it." He stood anyway. His hand had gone to the pocket. The book was there, and the routing slip, and a brown envelope the clerk had given him at the hatch with the pension printed on the outside, so there had been no use pretending it was something else. Brice came in off the track with the ginger still in his teeth and the slate pulling his jacket crooked. He was late. He looked at the pennant as a man looks at a clock that has made him late. "Arthur. With respect. My notice was in before her sleeve. I've got a barge on the pegs and a board that—" He stopped. "You thumbprinted." "On station." "You could have called. Neighbors call." The tops of his ears were burned. He saw the empty locker and got personal, which was the only other register he had. "Dirt-holding, and then running upstairs. I'll have the access in the file if I can't have the grade. Central will have my notice either way." "Grade's on the door," Arthur said. He did not want the rest of it. Brice did. Arthur gave him the bad ear and let him go to the cabinet, where his own lock was still on a door that would not shut. The flash was bright and ordinary. Brice took two pictures, in case the first did not show the lock. Arthur opened the envelope while the flash recharged. The figure was better than Quist had made it sound. Not an insult. Nearer the other thing. He read it twice. He did not put it away as quickly as a man refusing would have. He slid it into the assay book so it would not crease, which was a decision, and shut the book on it. The routing slip was the next paper. He had folded the yard line inside on the station and had not started it. He started it now. Cold to the yard. Then the yard's own mark. Heat. A concentration code he knew from a table, not from anything he had written. The pencil sentence bound the lift. It stopped at their dock. They would cook it where his name was not on the temperature. He saw it the way he saw a bad strike, in one reading, and his mouth pressed, and nobody in the shed was watching his mouth. The net was still on the ramp. He went out with the tag the clerk had left blank for the last instruction, and he wrote on it in the same hand as the margin, small and clear. No heat in transit. Neegan. He wrote it because a hot packet would spoil on his name, and the posting already had his name, and a botched load would be his grade in somebody's circular. The yard was a different paper. He knew that while the pencil moved. He wrote the note anyway. The clerk took the tag without reading it aloud and hooked it to the webbing. When he came back in, Moss had the crate on his hip. "Pump stays," Arthur said. "You said." Moss shifted the weight. "Hobbs can hear it from you, if you're still in the doorway. I'm not telling him." "I'll tell him." "All right." He went past the pennant without looking up at it. At the crawler he set the crate down, checked the lid once, and did not turn to see if Arthur had anything further. Brice's flash went off again at the cabinet. Arthur still had the part number in the book, and the pension, and the yard code he could have read yesterday. He told Hobbs the pump stayed.

[Analysis] This is a remarkably controlled piece of writing. The chapter executes its plan with precision and restraint, and the restraint is the point — this is Asimov's tradition of letting the weight of events press through ordinary surfaces rather than announcing itself. The Moss scene is the chapter's center and it's handled with real skill. The model follows the plan's instruction that Arthur "is privately relieved, then ashamed of the relief" with precision: "The relief was small and immediate. The plan specified this exactly, and the execution is clean: "He knew that while the pencil moved. He wrote the note anyway." This is the chapter's moral center, delivered without a speech. The self-knowledge is there, the limitation is there, and neither is dramatized beyond what the moment requires. The pension envelope is handled with similar restraint. He reads it twice, slides it into the assay book "so it would not crease, which was a decision." The chapter ends on a practical fact, as planned, without weighing Arthur's soul. Where the chapter is slightly less successful: the Hobbs character is present but thin — he watches, he prints, he hears about the pump, but he's more a witness-function than a person. Also, "The dust was the same" is a small moment of atmospheric writing that works, but "It got into his collar before he reached the door" is the kind of detail that earns its place. The dialogue throughout is genuinely strong — short, functional, carrying subtext without performing it. "Grade's on the door" is Arthur's best line: dismissive, accurate, and a refusal to engage on Brice's terms.
